stamp: SIMULATED instruments only — judge-score gating joins when verdicts persist to run dirs

items.stem: A student computes matrix products by multiplying matching entries: if A=[[1,2],[3,4]] and B=[[5,6],[7,8]], they say AB=[[5,12],[21,32]]. What is the best correction?
options: That is correct because matrix multiplication is entrywise.
That is incorrect because AB is formed from row-by-column dot products, not entrywise multiplication.
That is incorrect because matrices can never be multiplied.
That is correct only when A and B are square.
items.explanation: The fix is to use the rule for the product: the (i, j) entry of AB is the dot product of row i of A with column j of B. In other words, "The product AB combines rows of A with columns of B via dot products; the entrywise product is a different, rarely used operation."

items.stem: A 2×2 matrix has a zero determinant, but its entries are not all zero. Which conclusion is correct?
options: It must be invertible because it is nonzero.
It is nonzero yet has no inverse.
It is invertible only if its entries are positive.
It has an inverse because every square matrix does.
items.explanation: This is the key correction: "A square matrix with a zero determinant — for example one with two equal rows — is nonzero yet has no inverse." Nonzero entries do not guarantee invertibility; the determinant/pivot test does.

items.stem: Which statement best describes dimension?
options: Dimension is the number of vectors in the space.
Dimension counts basis vectors, not members.
Dimension is the number of spanning sets a space has.
Dimension is the number of coordinates in any vector written in the standard basis only.
items.explanation: Dimension is tied to bases, not to how many vectors happen to live in the space. Put plainly: “Dimension counts basis vectors, not members; R^2 has infinitely many vectors but dimension 2.”

items.stem: Two vectors in R^3 are parallel and nonzero. What is their span?
options: Always a plane
Always all of R^3
A line
A set with no zero vector
items.explanation: Parallel vectors do not give a two-dimensional span. As the corrective says, "If the two vectors are parallel (or one is zero), their span collapses to a line or a point; the span's dimension depends on independence."

items.stem: After row reduction, which statement best describes rank?
options: The number of nonzero entries in the original matrix
The number of pivot columns after elimination
The number of rows in the original matrix
The number of free variables
items.explanation: Rank is read from pivots, not from raw appearance. A matrix full of nonzero entries can still have rank 1 if its rows are proportional, so "Rank counts pivots AFTER row reduction; a matrix full of nonzero entries can still have rank 1 if its rows are proportional."

items.stem: A matrix A has a zero eigenvalue. What must be true?
options: A is the zero matrix
A is singular, because some nonzero vector is sent to zero
A is invertible but not diagonalizable
Every vector is sent to zero
items.explanation: A zero eigenvalue only means some nonzero vector is sent to zero — the matrix is singular, not necessarily zero. That is the key distinction: zero eigenvalue does not force every entry of A to vanish.

items.stem: A student claims the zero vector is an eigenvector because A0 = 3·0 for every matrix A. What is the best correction?
options: Yes, because any vector that satisfies Ax = λx is an eigenvector.
No; eigenvectors must be nonzero, and A0 = λ0 holds trivially.
Yes, but only when λ = 0.
No; the zero vector can never be multiplied by a matrix.
items.explanation: No; eigenvectors must be nonzero, and A0 = λ0 holds trivially. That equality identifies nothing about the matrix, so the zero vector cannot count as an eigenvector.

items.stem: Which condition correctly checks whether age is between 14 and 18 (inclusive on 14, exclusive on 19)?
options: age > 13 and age < 19
If age > 13 and < 19 is valid, chaining the second comparison without repeating the variable.
age > 13 and age = 19
items.explanation: Each comparison needs its own operands joined by and: age > 13 and age < 19. The bare < 19 has nothing on its left.

items.stem:
Suppose lst = [10, 20, 30]. You run:

for v in lst:
    v = v + 1

After the loop, what is lst?
options: Reassigning the loop variable inside a for loop changes the underlying list it came from.
It becomes [11, 21, 31] only if lst contains strings
An error occurs because assigning to v is not allowed
items.explanation: The loop variable is a fresh binding to each element in turn; assigning to it does not edit the container. To change list contents, index into the list directly.

items.stem: Consider nums = [10, 20, 30, 40, 50]. A student writes nums[5]. What happens?
options: It returns 50 (the last item).
It returns 10 (the first item).
It raises an IndexError.
It returns None.
items.explanation: “Indexes run from 0 to length minus 1, so a 5-item list's last index is 4; lst[5] is out of range.” Therefore nums[5] raises an IndexError.

items.stem: You have: grades = {'Ava': 95, 'Ben': 88}. What is the result of grades['Ava'] after executing: grades['Ava'] = 97 ?
options: 95, because the original value stays
97, because assigning to an existing key overwrites the old value
It raises an error because 'Ava' is already a key
It returns both values as a list: [95, 97]
items.explanation: This overwrites: the key 'Ava' is unique in a dictionary, so grades['Ava'] = 97 replaces the previous value. The rule is: assigning to an existing key overwrites its previous value rather than adding a second entry.

items.stem: Which statement is correct about duplicate keys in a Python dictionary?
options: A dictionary can hold duplicate keys; it will store both values
Keys are unique; assigning to an existing key overwrites its previous value
Duplicate keys are allowed only if they appear next to each other
Duplicate keys are converted into a list automatically
items.explanation: “a dictionary object cannot hold duplicate key values.” That’s why a dictionary has unique keys: assigning to an existing key overwrites its previous value rather than adding a second entry.

items.stem: A student writes: d = {'name': 'Ava', 'age': 20}. They say, “I can read d[0] to get 'Ava' because dictionaries are like lists and 0 is the first element.” Which response is best?
options: They are correct: dictionaries use numeric position like lists, so d[0] gives the first value
They are almost correct: d[0] gives the key, so it returns 'name'
Dictionaries are accessed by key, not position; you should use d['name']
You must convert the dictionary to a list before indexing; d[0] will work only after that conversion
items.explanation: The misconception is: “I can read d[0] to get 'Ava' because dictionaries are like lists and 0 is the first element.” Correct rule: Dictionaries are accessed by key, not position; use d['name'] to get the value stored under the key 'name', not d[0].

items.stem: You start with: grades = {'Ava': 95}. Then you run: grades['Ava'] = 88; grades['Ava'] = 91. How many values for 'Ava' does grades contain, and what is the stored value at 'Ava'?
options: Two values are kept for 'Ava', and grades['Ava'] is 88
Two values are kept for 'Ava', and grades['Ava'] is 91
One value is kept for 'Ava', and grades['Ava'] is 91
One value is kept for 'Ava', and grades['Ava'] is 95
items.explanation: The key misconception here is expecting two values to survive for the same key. Keys are unique; assigning to an existing key overwrites its previous value rather than adding a second entry—so the final stored value is 91.

items.stem:
Misconception check (read carefully):

"I can call read() twice on the same file object, and it will just give me the full contents again both times." 

Is that belief correct?
options: Yes—read() always returns the entire file contents from the start
No—after the first read() reaches the end, the next read() returns '' until you reopen/reset
Yes—readline() does that, but read() is different
No—read() returns a list, so the second call fails
items.explanation: Reading advances a position marker through the file; once read() reaches the end, a second read() returns '' until the file is reopened or the position is reset.

items.stem: Consider a student function description: “I wrote a recursive function, but I didn’t include a base case; it just keeps calling itself.” What is the most likely outcome in Python?
options: It immediately returns None because recursion is optional
It eventually terminates because inputs get smaller automatically
It never terminates and overflows the call stack (e.g., RecursionError)
It skips recursive calls and runs only the base case
items.explanation: The corrective idea is: “Every recursion needs a base case — a simplest input solved directly without another call — so the chain of self-calls eventually stops.” Without a base case that stops the self-calls, recursion never terminates and overflows the call stack.

items.stem: A student wrote: g(n) = 2 * g(n) for n > 0, and there is a base case g(0)=1. The code calls g(n) on the same value of n each time (not n - 1). What happens when you call g(3)?
options: It returns 6 because the base case at 0 guarantees termination
It enters infinite recursion because the problem is not shrinking toward the base case
It raises an error immediately because g(n) is not valid for n>0
It returns 1 because g(0) is defined
items.explanation: Even with a base case present, the recursive call must move toward it. The corrective is: “Each recursive call must move toward the base case by shrinking the problem (e.g. n - 1), or the base case is never reached.” Here g(n) calls itself on the same-size input, so it never reaches 0.

items.stem: You write `class Dog: ...` then create `a = Dog()` and `b = Dog()`. You set `a.name = 'Rex'`. Which statement is correct about `b.name` (assuming you never changed `b.name`)?
options: b.name also becomes 'Rex' because both instances share the same attributes
b.name becomes 'Rex' because the class stores the name attribute
b.name does not automatically become 'Rex'; each instance carries its own copy of the attributes
b.name is undefined because only classes can store attributes
items.explanation: “Each instance carries its own copy of the attributes, while the methods defined by the class are shared by every instance.” So changing `a.name` affects only instance `a`, not instance `b`.

items.stem: A student says, “If a model helped once, it is always safe to use it again anywhere.” Which response best corrects that belief?
options: A model is a tool whose conclusions hold only while its assumptions approximately hold.
If a model is useful once, it is true in every situation.
Assumptions do not matter once a model has been taught.
A model becomes more accurate when we apply it to a very different setting.
items.explanation: No — the model is not a permanent truth machine. A model is a tool whose conclusions hold only while its assumptions approximately hold, so you still have to check whether the assumptions fit the new setting.

items.stem: A student says, 'Since the lecture video is online and free, watching it has no cost.' What is the best response?
options: Correct: free always means no cost
Incorrect: the student ignores the value of the next best use of time
Correct: only money counts as cost in economics
Incorrect: the video must have a hidden fee
items.explanation: No money changing hands does not make the choice costless. Always ask what the next best use of the time or money was; that foregone value is the real cost. Here the student's own mistake is counting only the money paid and ignoring the value of the foregone alternative.

items.stem: A student says, “The best consumer choice is whichever bundle gives the highest satisfaction, even if it costs more than the budget.” What is the best correction?
options: The optimal bundle is the best one the consumer can actually afford, not the most desirable one.
A consumer should choose the bundle with the most goods, even if it exceeds the budget.
Budget constraints matter only after utility is maximized.
The best bundle is always the cheapest bundle.
items.explanation: Not quite. The reading defines consumer choice as utility maximization subject to a budget constraint, so the best bundle has to be feasible. In other words, “The optimal bundle is the best one the consumer can actually afford, not the most desirable one.”

items.stem: The price of wheat rises, and farmers plan to sell more wheat this month. What is the best description of what happened?
options: The supply curve shifted right because the higher price increased supply
The quantity supplied moved along the supply curve because the good's own price changed
The demand curve shifted right because buyers want more wheat
The quantity supplied stayed fixed because supply never changes with price
items.explanation: This is a move along the supply curve, not a curve shift. The key rule is: 'A change in the good's own price moves along the curve; only non-price factors shift the curve.'

items.stem: A frost destroys part of the coffee crop. What happens in the coffee market?
options: The supply curve shifts because input conditions changed
The quantity supplied moves along the curve because coffee's price changed
The demand curve shifts because consumers now want less coffee
Nothing changes because quantity supplied is a fixed stock
items.explanation: A frost changes a non-price factor, so the whole supply curve shifts. That fits the rule that only a change in the good's own price moves along the curve; input costs or technology shift the curve.

items.stem: A student says, 'When the price of apples rises, the supply curve shifts right.' Which correction is best?
options: Yes, because any price increase shifts the supply curve
No, because a change in the good's own price moves along the curve; only non-price factors shift the curve
No, because price changes never affect quantity supplied
Yes, because the supply curve is fixed and cannot be moved
items.explanation: That sentence confuses a move along the curve with a shift. Say it plainly: 'A change in the good's own price moves along the curve; only non-price factors shift the curve.'

items.stem: A student says, “If the market is in equilibrium, nothing is happening.” Which reply is best?
options: Correct—equilibrium means buyers and sellers stop acting.
Incorrect—equilibrium is a balance of ongoing opposing pressures, not a frozen market.
Correct—equilibrium only happens when the government sets the price.
Incorrect—equilibrium always means there is a shortage.
items.explanation: The key correction is that equilibrium is not a frozen market. Equilibrium is a balance of ongoing opposing pressures, not a frozen market.

items.stem: A new drug has a patent and no close substitute. Which statement best fits the market structure and pricing power of the seller?
options: It is a monopoly, so it can raise price by restricting the quantity it sells.
It is a perfectly competitive firm, so it must accept the market price.
It is a monopoly, so it can charge any price it likes with no limit.
It is a market in equilibrium, so price cannot change.
items.explanation: Correct: the patent-protected drug matches a monopoly, and a monopoly is a price maker. But that power is not unlimited; as the reading says, "a monopoly is constrained by the demand curve: to raise price it must sell less."

items.stem: A regulator raises the price of a monopolized product. The seller responds by reducing output. Why is that response consistent with monopoly behavior?
options: Because a monopoly is a price maker: it can raise price by restricting the quantity it sells.
Because equilibrium means the quantity sold never changes.
Because raising price always increases quantity demanded.
Because the firm is now operating like a perfectly competitive firm.
items.explanation: This is the basic monopoly tradeoff: "a monopoly is a price maker: it can raise price by restricting the quantity it sells." The point is not that it can choose any price, but that price and quantity move together through the demand curve.

items.stem: A household saves part of its income, and a bank lends that saving to a firm for new equipment. In the circular flow, what is happening?
options: The saving has left the economy forever.
The saving is a leakage that is re-injected as investment.
The saving counts as an import.
The saving makes leakages larger than injections automatically.
items.explanation: That path is exactly a leakage being put back into the flow: saving is not destroyed; in balance it re-enters the flow as investment, government spending, or exports.

items.stem: A firm buys new equipment this year. Which statement best matches the reading’s idea of capital accumulation?
options: The capital stock jumps immediately by the full amount of the purchase.
The capital stock rises gradually over time as net investment stays positive.
The capital stock falls whenever gross investment rises.
The capital stock changes only if depreciation is zero.
items.explanation: The reading says the capital stock “rises through gross investment and falls through depreciation,” and that “the stock grows only when net investment is positive.” So higher investment can raise the stock, but it does so gradually over time; the stock does not jump when the flow changes.

items.stem: A student says, “When firms invest more this year, the capital stock doubles right away.” What is the best response?
options: Yes, because investment and capital stock are the same thing.
No; higher investment raises the stock gradually over time; the stock does not jump when the flow changes.
Yes, as long as depreciation is positive.
No; gross investment never affects the capital stock.
items.explanation: That belief confuses the level with the flow. Higher investment raises the stock gradually over time; the stock does not jump when the flow changes. The factory example makes the same point: one year of higher spending nudges the trajectory, it does not double the stock overnight.

items.stem: You are explaining why the inner core is solid even though it is hotter than the outer core. Which explanation is correct?
options: Hotter material is always liquid, so the inner core must be molten.
The inner core is solid because immense pressure keeps the iron solid.
The inner core is solid because it has no iron or nickel.
The inner core is liquid because all parts of the core are molten.
items.explanation: This is one of the key corrections for today: “The core has both a liquid outer layer and a solid inner layer; the inner core is solid despite being hotter, because the immense pressure keeps the iron solid.”

items.stem: A student brings you two igneous rocks. Sample A has large, visible crystals. Sample B has tiny crystals you can barely see. Which explanation best fits both samples?
options: Sample A cooled slowly at depth, and Sample B cooled quickly at or near the surface.
Sample A cooled quickly at the surface, and Sample B cooled slowly at depth.
Sample A is lava, so it has large crystals; Sample B is magma, so it has tiny crystals.
Sample A formed from more silica, so it must have larger crystals even if cooling was fast.
items.explanation: Slow cooling at depth gives crystals time to grow large (coarse, intrusive); fast cooling at the surface freezes tiny crystals (fine, extrusive). That is why crystal size tracks cooling rate, not just composition.

items.stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes magma from lava?
options: Magma is molten rock below the surface; once it erupts onto the surface it is called lava.
Lava is molten rock below the surface; once it cools underground it is called magma.
Magma and lava are just two words for the same thing, so the location does not matter.
Lava is always cooler than magma because it has already erupted.
items.explanation: Magma is molten rock below the surface; once it erupts onto the surface it is called lava, and the two cool at very different rates. Keep the location in mind first, because that is what separates the terms.

items.stem: A student says, “If a rock melted, that is metamorphism.” Which response is correct?
options: Yes; metamorphism is when a rock partially or fully melts
No; metamorphism happens in the solid state, and if the rock melts it becomes magma
Yes; melted rock is called sediment
No; melting only happens in sedimentary rocks
items.explanation: Metamorphism happens in the solid state; if the rock actually melts, it becomes magma and the igneous part of the rock cycle begins instead.

items.stem: A sandstone layer is buried, heated, and squeezed until it becomes quartzite. Later it melts and cools again. Which sequence best describes the rock cycle path?
options: Sedimentary → metamorphic → magma → igneous
Igneous → sedimentary → metamorphic → magma → igneous
Metamorphic → sedimentary → igneous → metamorphic
Sedimentary → igneous → metamorphic → sedimentary
items.explanation: The rock cycle is not a one-way ladder; rocks can move through many paths and repeat over geologic time. The corrective says: “The cycle has many paths: any rock type can become any other; metamorphic rock can erode to sediment, or melt to magma and re-crystallize as igneous rock.” This path matches a rock that becomes metamorphic, then melts to magma, then crystallizes as igneous rock.

items.stem: A seismometer on the far side of Earth detects P waves from a strong quake but no S waves. What is the best explanation?
options: S waves are slower than P waves, so they just have not arrived yet.
S waves cannot travel through the liquid outer core, which creates an S-wave shadow zone.
P waves stop in the mantle, but S waves pass through it.
The earthquake did not release any seismic energy in that direction.
items.explanation: This pattern points to Earth’s interior, not to a weak quake. P waves travel through solids and liquids, but S waves only through solids. The S-wave shadow zone is exactly why we know the outer core is liquid.

items.stem: Which statement best describes what happens just before an earthquake along a locked fault?
options: Energy is created at the moment the fault slips for the first time.
Rock bends elastically for years, storing energy until the fault slips and releases it suddenly.
The plates stop moving completely, so no energy is involved.
Magma rises and pushes the fault apart, causing the quake.
items.explanation: The key idea is elastic rebound: the energy is stored over years as rock bends elastically along a locked fault; the quake releases it suddenly when the fault slips. That is different from energy being created at the instant of shaking.

items.stem: Which example shows chemical weathering rather than mechanical weathering?
options: A boulder splits along a frost crack into smaller blocks.
A stream carries gravel downstream.
Feldspar alters into clay.
A landslide moves loose sediment downhill.
items.explanation: Feldspar altering to clay is the key clue. Mechanical weathering physically breaks bedrock into smaller pieces, but chemical weathering changes the minerals themselves into new substances.

items.stem: A student says a rock layer is 'about 120 million years old' because it is below another layer. What is the best correction?
options: That is relative dating, not absolute dating; being lower only tells you older or younger.
That is absolute dating, because lower layers always have a numerical age.
That is original horizontality, because lower layers are always younger.
That is superposition, because it gives the exact number of years.
items.explanation: This is the common mix-up: "Relative dating only orders events as older or younger; numerical ages in years come from absolute dating methods such as radiometric dating." The lower layer can be older, but the number of years requires absolute dating.

items.stem: A company says its customer survey proves everyone loves its service. The survey was emailed only to repeat buyers. Which statement is the strongest critique?
options: Repeat buyers are the best customers, so the survey is fine.
The survey may overstate satisfaction because unhappy customers who already left were excluded.
The dataset is objective fact, so no critique is needed.
The method cannot matter if the sample is large enough.
items.explanation: This is the classic provenance problem: the collection method leaves out a group that matters. The collection method and its purpose can bias what the data can support, so the survey can overstate satisfaction. Ask who collected the data, how, and why before trusting what the numbers say.

items.stem: A student looks at a study showing that people who carry lighters are more likely to have lung disease and says, 'Carrying lighters causes lung disease.' What is the best statistical response?
options: Yes, because a strong association proves causation.
No: the association could be explained by a confounder, so causation is not established.
Yes, if the sample size is large enough.
No: observational studies cannot show any association at all.
items.explanation: That claim goes too far. In an observational study, an association may be due to a confounding variable rather than a causal effect, so the safe response is: association is not causation until plausible confounders are ruled out.

items.stem: A study reports a p-value of 0.03. Which interpretation is correct?
options: If the null hypothesis is true, data this extreme would happen about 3% of the time.
There is a 3% chance the null hypothesis is true.
The effect size is 3%.
The alternative hypothesis is true with probability 0.03.
items.explanation: This matches the definition: a p-value is the probability of getting a test statistic at least as extreme as the observed one, assuming the null hypothesis is true. The 3% is about the data under the null, not about whether the null itself is true.

items.stem: Which statement best describes what a small p-value tells you?
options: The observed data would be unlikely under the null hypothesis.
The null hypothesis is probably true.
The sample mean must be close to the population mean.
The effect is definitely large.
items.explanation: A small p-value indicates that the observed data would be unlikely under the null hypothesis. That is exactly the corrective to the common confusion: “It is a probability about the data given the null, not about the hypothesis given the data.”

items.stem: A p-value of 0.03 is best translated as which sentence?
options: If the null were true, data this extreme would occur 3 percent of the time.
There is a 3 percent chance the sample is random.
The null hypothesis has a 3 percent chance of being true.
The population standard deviation is 0.03.
items.explanation: Use the worked example directly: “A p-value of 0.03 means data this extreme would occur 3 percent of the time if the null were true.” That translation keeps the conditional structure intact and does not turn the p-value into a probability of the null.

items.stem: In a hypothesis test, which quantity is being described by a p-value?
options: The probability distribution of the statistic under repeated samples, assuming the null hypothesis is true.
The probability the alternative hypothesis is true after seeing the data.
The size of the sample mean.
The population standard deviation divided by the square root of the sample size.
items.explanation: The p-value comes from the distribution of the test statistic under the null. It is tied to how unusual the observed statistic is in that null world, not to the probability of the hypothesis itself.

items.stem: A regression output shows a very strong R-squared. Which conclusion is most defensible from this lesson’s perspective?
options: The model is trustworthy because a strong R-squared guarantees the assumptions are valid.
The model may still be misleading if assumptions like independent errors are violated.
A strong R-squared proves the data were generated by a linear model.
A strong R-squared means the model keeps every important feature of the data.
items.explanation: The high fit does not settle the real question. The text says the model can be “misleading even if it fits the sample well,” so you still check whether assumptions like linearity and independent errors hold before trusting the conclusions.

items.stem: A student says, “This model fits the sample well, so its assumptions must be fine.” What is the best reply?
options: Yes—good fit and valid assumptions always go together.
No—good fit does not guarantee valid assumptions; check the assumptions, not just the fit.
Yes—because assumptions are only important when fit is poor.
No—because a model can never fit the sample well.
items.explanation: That statement is exactly the trap. The corrective is: “Good fit does not guarantee valid assumptions; check the assumptions, not just the fit.” A sample can look good while the model’s assumptions are still broken.

items.stem: A student wrote a while loop but it never stops. They say: “Every while loop runs forever unless I used an if-else inside the body.” Which fix matches the real cause and addresses it?
options: Add an if-else inside the body; that guarantees termination
Update the variable used in the loop condition so the condition eventually becomes false
Change while to if so it repeats automatically
Remove the condition and always run the loop body
items.explanation: Termination depends on making progress toward ending the loop expression. Corrective: “Every while loop must change something the condition depends on; a counter loop needs n = n - 1 (or += 1) inside the body so the condition eventually becomes false.” If the condition never becomes false, the loop can be infinite.

items.stem: A student writes: “range(5) produces 1 through 5, so my loop runs one time too few or accesses the wrong indices.” What is the issue with that reasoning?
options: range(5) does produce 1 through 5, so the student is right
range(5) starts at 0 and stops before 5, giving 0 through 4
range(5) produces only 5 values from 1 through 4
range(5) produces 1 through 6, so it runs one time too many
items.explanation: The corrective is: range(5) yields 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 — it starts at 0 and stops before the endpoint, giving exactly five values. It does NOT produce 1 through 5.

items.stem: A while-loop hangs because the condition never becomes false. Which change addresses the problem by ensuring progress toward ending the condition?
options: Remove n from the condition so it can’t block termination
Add n = n - 1 (or n += 1 if the condition is written accordingly) inside the body
Change the loop to a for loop but keep the same condition unchanged
Set n equal to itself inside the body (n = n)
items.explanation: Corrective: “Every while loop must change something the condition depends on; a counter loop needs n = n - 1 (or += 1) inside the body so the condition eventually becomes false.” Without updating, the loop can run forever (an infinite loop).

items.stem: A student writes: last = lst[5] to get the last item from a 5-item list and says “that should work because the last index is 5.” What is the best correction?
options: Use last = lst[4] because indexes run from 0 to length minus 1
Use last = lst[5] but add try/except
Use last = lst[0] because the first item is the last item
Use last = lst[-1] because lst[5] is the first item
items.explanation: The wrong belief is that a 5-item list’s last element is at index 5. In Python, “indexes run from 0 to length minus 1,” so the last index is 4 and lst[5] is out of range. Use lst[4] for the last item.

items.stem: Which code structure best ensures the file is closed automatically even if an error occurs while reading?
options: Use `f = open('data.txt')` and never close it; the OS will handle it.
Use `with open('data.txt') as f:` so Python closes the file automatically even if an error occurs.
Use `open('data.txt')` inside a function, because functions close files automatically.
Use `readlines()` because it closes the file after returning the list.
items.explanation: Always close the file when done, or open it in a with statement so Python closes it automatically even if an error occurs. That’s exactly what the `with open(...) as f:` structure provides.

items.stem: You want factorial(n) to always stop. Which change most directly fixes a version that recurses until it crashes?
options: Add a base case such as: if n == 0: return 1
Change the recursive call to: factorial(n) instead of factorial(n - 1)
Remove the return statement so the function prints the answer later
Move the base case after the recursive call
items.explanation: Recursion needs a place to stop. The fix is to add a base case so the self-calls eventually stops: “Every recursion needs a base case — a simplest input solved directly without another call — so the chain of self-calls eventually stops.”

items.stem: Consider this recursive idea: f(n) should reach a base case, but it calls itself with the same argument each time (f(n) calls f(n)). What will happen?
options: It will work but be slower than necessary
It may eventually reach the base case anyway
It never reaches the base case and keeps self-calling
It will always return 0 for n > 0
items.explanation: If the recursive call does not shrink the problem, the base case is never reached. The rule is: “Each recursive call must move toward the base case by shrinking the problem (e.g. n - 1), or the base case is never reached.”

items.stem:
Let x = 3. Then run:
y = x + 2
x = 10
What value does y hold?
options: A variable stores the expression itself, so they expect it to update when the inputs later change.
y becomes 7
items.explanation: “Assignment stores the value computed at that moment; if y = x + 2 runs when x is 3, y is 5 and stays 5 even if x changes afterward.” Changing x later does not rewrite the already-stored value in y.

items.stem: You’re checking an age range. Which condition correctly means “age is greater than 13 and less than 19”?
options: If age > 13 and < 19 is valid, chaining the second comparison without repeating the variable.
age > 13 and age < 19
13 < age and 19 > age
items.explanation: Each comparison needs its own operands joined by and: age > 13 and age < 19. The bare < 19 has nothing on its left.

items.stem: True or false: “The loop expression is tested only at the top of each iteration; the rest of the current pass still runs before the condition is checked again.”
options: True
False
True only if the loop body contains an else clause
False only if n changes inside the body
items.explanation: Correct. This directly addresses the misconception: “The loop expression is tested only at the top of each iteration; the rest of the current pass still runs before the condition is checked again.” So if the body changes n, the change won’t prevent the *current* pass from finishing—it affects the decision for the *next* iteration.

items.stem: Timing check: In a while loop, when is the loop expression evaluated relative to the body’s statements?
options: Only after the body finishes running for that iteration
Only in the middle of the body immediately when a variable changes
Only before the body runs for each iteration (at the top)
Never; it runs once at the start and then ignores it
items.explanation: The loop expression is tested only at the top of each iteration; the rest of the current pass still runs before the condition is checked again.

items.stem:
Consider this code:

def add_five(n):
    temp = n + 5

result = add_five(10)
print(temp)

What best describes what will happen?
options: It prints 15 because temp is created inside the function and Python keeps it around.
It prints None because add_five returns nothing, but temp is still accessible.
It raises a NameError on print(temp) because temp is local to the function call.
It raises a SyntaxError because temp must be declared global before use.
items.explanation: temp is a local variable created during the function call, so it exists only inside that call. If you want to use the result outside, the function must return it and the caller must capture the returned value, for example: return temp, then result = add_five(10).

items.stem: Which option correctly explains when the body of a function runs?
options: The body runs immediately when you write def greet(): ...
The body runs only when you call greet(), such as greet().
The body runs only when you assign the function to a variable, like f = greet.
The body runs when the file is imported, but not when called.
items.explanation: Defining a function only stores it; the body runs when the function is called by name, such as greet(). Writing def greet(): does not execute the body immediately.

items.stem: A student says: “Defining a function only stores it; the body runs when the function is called by name.” Which of these actions will trigger running the body?
options: Writing def greet(): print('hi')
Calling greet()
Doing greet = def greet(): print('hi')
Importing the module that contains the function (without calling it)
items.explanation: Defining a function only stores it; the body runs when the function is called by name, such as greet(). Simply defining it does not execute the body.

items.stem: A 5-item list lst causes an error when doing lst[5]. What is the correct reason?
options: Indexes run from 0 to length minus 1, so a 5-item list's last index is 4; lst[5] is out of range.
lst[5] is the first element after the list starts at index 1.
Slices use exclusive end, so lst[5] should still work like lst[0:5].
Index 5 is valid because Python counts positions starting at 1.
items.explanation: Indexes run from 0 to length minus 1, so a 5-item list's last index is 4; lst[5] is out of range.

items.stem: Consider: grades = {'Ava': 95, 'Ben': 88}; grades['Ava'] = 97. What is grades['Ava'] after the assignment?
options: Both 95 and 97 (kept together)
A KeyError
items.explanation: Assigning to an existing key overwrites its previous value rather than adding a second entry. This matches the idea: grades['Ava'] = 97 overwrites the old value (95), so grades['Ava'] becomes 97.

items.stem: A student says: “I can put two values in a dictionary under the same key and both will be kept.” For grades = {'Ava': 95}, after you run grades['Ava'] = 97, what is true?
options: Both 95 and 97 are kept because the key is the same
The dictionary now has two separate entries for 'Ava'
The value under key 'Ava' becomes 97 (the old value is overwritten)
A KeyError is raised because the key already exists
items.explanation: Confronting the misconception: “Students assign two values to the same key and expect both to be kept.” Keys are unique; assigning to an existing key overwrites its previous value rather than adding a second entry. So grades['Ava'] becomes 97.

items.stem: You want a recursive function to compute factorial. Which option correctly includes both a base case and a recursive step that shrinks the input?
options: def factorial(n): return factorial(n - 1)  # no base case
def factorial(n): return 1 if n == 1 else n * factorial(n + 1)  # grows
def factorial(n): return 1 if n == 0 else n * factorial(n - 1)  # shrinks to base
def factorial(n): return n * factorial(n)  # repeats same n
items.explanation: Correct: the base case is n == 0, and the recursive call uses n - 1 so the recursion shrinks the problem until the base case is reached. This matches the idea that recursion calls itself on a smaller input and stops when the solution is known or can easily be found.

items.stem: Consider this recursive pattern: f(n) calls itself with the same value n (no change). What is the main problem?
options: It will always reach the base case immediately, because the base case is implied
It shrinks the problem automatically because recursion repeats until stable
It may never reach the base case, because the problem isn’t getting smaller
It converts the recursion into an iterative loop, so it can’t overflow
items.explanation: The issue is that each recursive call must move toward the base case by shrinking the problem (e.g. n - 1). As the corrective states: “Each recursive call must move toward the base case by shrinking the problem (e.g. n - 1), or the base case is never reached.”

items.stem: You see: class Dog: ...; a = Dog(); b = Dog(). If you later do a.name = 'Rex', what is the most accurate prediction about b.name?
options: b.name also becomes 'Rex' because instances of the same class share attribute values
b.name stays whatever it was before; changing one Dog's name does not change another Dog's name
b.name becomes 'Rex' only if methods are shared
b.name becomes an error because attributes can only be set on the class
items.explanation: Each instance has its own attributes, so changing one Dog's name does not change another Dog's name; only the methods are shared.

items.stem: Consider this belief: “Students treat the class itself as an object and expect to store data on it, confusing the blueprint with the things built from it.” If a student followed that belief, where would they incorrectly store per-dog data?
options: On each instance created from the class (e.g., a = Dog(), b = Dog())
On the class itself (e.g., Dog.name) when they intend it to be per object
Only inside the methods, so attributes cannot be stored anywhere else
Nowhere; attributes are only temporary during a function call
items.explanation: Corrective: “A class is the blueprint; you create instances from it (e.g. d = Dog()), and per-object data lives on each instance, not on the class.” Storing per-object data on Dog itself is the confusion.

items.stem: A student says: “The first element is position 1, so lst[1] is the first item.” Which option fixes that misunderstanding?
options: “The first element is at index 0, so lst[0] is the first item and lst[1] is the second.”
“The first element is at index 1, so lst[1] is the first item.”
“Index numbers are arbitrary, so lst[1] could be any element.”
“Lists don’t have indices; you must use a loop.”
items.explanation: The first element is at index 0, so lst[0] is the first item and lst[1] is the second. Indexing does not start at 1 in Python lists.

items.stem: Let s = 'Python'. What is the result of s[0:3]?
options: 'Pyth' (four characters, including index 3)
'Pyt' (three characters)
'Python' (full string)
'Py' (two characters)
items.explanation: The end index of a slice is exclusive, so s[0:3] returns characters at indices 0, 1, and 2 — three characters, stopping before index 3.

items.stem: You call the following twice in a row (without reopening the file): f = open('data.txt'); a = f.read(); b = f.read(). What is the value of b assuming the file is not modified in between?
options: b is the entire file again because read() always starts at the beginning
b is '' (empty string) because the file position is already at the end
b is a list of lines because read() returns lines
b raises an error because you cannot call read() twice
items.explanation: Reading advances a position marker through the file; once read() reaches the end, a second read() returns '' until the file is reopened or the position is reset.

items.stem: Why is this recommended in beginner code: with open('data.txt') as f: text = f.read() ?
options: It automatically converts the file into a Python list
It ensures Python closes the file automatically even if an error occurs
It prevents read() from returning a single string
It keeps the file open so later reads are always faster
items.explanation: Always close the file when done, or open it in a with statement so Python closes it automatically even if an error occurs.

items.stem:
Which statement best fixes this misconception?

“Students write a recursive function with no base case, so it recurses forever and raises a RecursionError.”
options: Add a return statement inside the recursive call, but you can still skip the base case
The function should stop by itself once n becomes small enough, even without a base case
Add a base case that solves the simplest input directly (so the self-calls eventually stop)
Replace the recursion with a loop, but don’t worry about base cases
items.explanation: Confronting the misconception: “Students write a recursive function with no base case, so it recurses forever.” The corrective is: “Every recursion needs a base case — a simplest input solved directly without another call — so the chain of self-calls eventually stops.”

items.stem: Which expression will produce the whole-number quotient 3 (not 3.5)?
options: 7 / 2 to give 3 (integer division) because the operands look like whole numbers.
int(7) / int(2)
float(7) // 2
items.explanation: In Python 3, the / operator always returns a float, so 7 / 2 is 3.5; use // for whole-number floor division, which gives 3.

items.stem: A student says: "Students forget to update the variable in the loop condition, so the condition stays true forever and the program hangs." Which small change fixes that issue for a counter loop?
options: Add an update like n = n - 1 (or n += 1) inside the body so the condition eventually becomes false
Remove the colon after the while condition and put it after the assignment instead
Change while n > 0 to while true: so it keeps checking faster
Move the update outside the loop so it happens only once
items.explanation: Fixing the hang means making progress toward ending the condition. “Every while loop must change something the condition depends on; a counter loop needs n = n - 1 (or += 1) inside the body so the condition eventually becomes false.”

items.stem:
What does this print?

for i in range(5):
    print(i)

Pick the option that matches the exact output.
options: Range(5) produces 1 through 5, so their loop runs one time too few or accesses the wrong indices.
items.explanation: range(5) yields 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 — it starts at 0 and stops before the endpoint, giving exactly five values. So the loop prints those five integers in order.

items.stem:
Students claim: “range(5) produces 1 through 5.” If a student writes:

for i in range(5):
    print(i)

after believing that claim, what actual behavior would happen?
options: They would print five numbers, but starting at 1 instead of 0.
They would print 1, 2, 3, 4, 5.
They would print 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 (five values, but the index is shifted).
The loop would run one extra time and print 0 through 5.
items.explanation: The belief “range(5) produces 1 through 5” is off by one. range(5) yields 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 — it starts at 0 and stops before the endpoint, giving exactly five values.

items.stem:
Consider this code:

vals = [10, 20, 30]
for x in vals:
    x = x + 1
print(vals)

What is printed?
options: Reassigning the loop variable inside a for loop changes the underlying list it came from.
It causes an error because x can’t be reassigned.
items.explanation: The loop variable is a fresh binding to each element in turn; assigning to it does not edit the container. To change list contents, index into the list directly.

items.stem:
A student writes:

def greet():
    print('hi')

After that, they expect the output 'hi' to appear immediately—without calling greet(). What is the correct behavior?
options: The function body runs immediately when Python sees the def statement
Nothing prints until you call greet(), such as greet()
Python prints 'hi' when the file is saved
Python prints 'hi' the next time any variable is assigned
items.explanation: Defining a function only stores it; the body runs when the function is called by name, such as greet(). The def keyword creates the reusable block, but it does not execute the indented body right away.

items.stem: Misconception check: A student says, “I can store two different numbers in a dictionary by assigning to the same key twice; both values will be kept.” Which choice matches the actual behavior?
options: Both values are kept as a list automatically
The first value remains and the second assignment is ignored
The second assignment overwrites the previous value for that key
A new key is created automatically with a different position
items.explanation: That belief is incorrect. “Keys are unique; assigning to an existing key overwrites its previous value rather than adding a second entry.” So only the most recent value for that key remains.

items.stem: A student claims: "Recursion is like a loop; if I write a recursive function that calls itself, it will eventually stop by itself even without a base case." What’s the best response?
options: That’s fine—Python automatically stops recursion when it gets “close enough.”
That’s fine—recursion always stops even with no base case.
Every recursion needs a base case so the self-calls eventually stops.
Recursion stops when the program reaches the end of the file.
items.explanation: This directly conflicts with the required stopping condition: "Every recursion needs a base case — a simplest input solved directly without another call — so the chain of self-calls eventually stops." Without it, self-calls never end and the call stack overflows.

items.stem: You create two objects from the same class: a = Dog() and b = Dog(). After creation, you run a.name = 'Rex'. Which outcome is correct?
options: b.name also becomes 'Rex' because the class shares attribute values
b.name stays whatever it was before because each instance carries its own copy of the attributes
b.name becomes None because attribute updates always reset other instances
Both a.name and b.name become the same value only if a method is called on the class
items.explanation: “Each instance carries its own copy of the attributes,” so changing one Dog’s name does not change another Dog’s name; only the methods defined by the class are shared.

items.stem: A student says, 'As soon as count becomes 0 inside the loop, Python should stop the current pass right there.' What is the best reply?
options: Yes, the loop ends in the middle of the body.
No, the rest of the current pass still runs before the condition is checked again.
The condition is checked before every statement in the body.
The loop only checks the condition after it has already ended.
items.explanation: The loop expression is tested only at the top of each iteration; the rest of the current pass still runs before the condition is checked again. If count changes in the body, Python finishes that pass and then checks the condition at the top of the next pass.

items.stem: A student writes a function that creates a value inside the body, then tries to print that value on the next line outside the function. What fix matches the problem?
options: Rename the variable outside the function so Python can see it
Move the print statement into the function body
Return the value from the function and store the returned value in the caller
Use range() so the local variable becomes global
items.explanation: Local variables exist only during the call that created them; to use a result outside, the function must return it and the caller must capture the returned value. In this case, the outside code needs the function’s result, not the local name itself.

items.stem: A learner types def greet(): then expects the greeting to appear right away. What actually happens?
options: The body runs immediately because def means execute
The function is stored, and the body runs only when greet() is called
The function runs once for each variable in scope
Python waits until the next for loop starts
items.explanation: Defining a function only stores it; the body runs when the function is called by name, such as greet(). Here, greet() is the step that triggers the code inside the function.

items.stem: A student writes a function to compute a value, then plans to use that value later in the program. Which version of the plan matches how scope works?
options: Create the value inside the function and read it later from outside the function
Create the value inside the function, return it, and save the return value in a variable outside
Create the value outside the function so every local variable becomes visible
Use a for loop so the value becomes global
items.explanation: Local variables exist only during the call that created them; to use a result outside, the function must return it and the caller must capture the returned value. The outside variable gets the returned result, not direct access to the local name.

items.stem: You run this code: profile = {'name': 'Mina'}; profile['name'] = 'Mina Patel'. What should you expect?
options: Both values stay under the same key
The key 'name' now stores 'Mina Patel'
A second 'name' key is added
The dictionary turns into a list
items.explanation: Keys are unique; assigning to an existing key overwrites its previous value rather than adding a second entry. After the update, 'name' points to the new value.

items.stem: You open a text file and call read() once. Then you call read() again on the same file object. What should you expect?
options: The second call returns the same contents again.
The second call returns an empty string until the file is reopened or reset.
The second call returns a list of lines.
The second call skips to the next file.
items.explanation: Reading advances a position marker through the file; once read() reaches the end, a second read() returns '' until the file is reopened or the position is reset. In this case, the file object is already at the end, so there is nothing left to return.

items.stem: A recursive function has a base case, but the recursive call uses the same input size each time. What will most likely happen?
options: The function returns immediately
The base case is reached sooner
The function keeps calling itself without getting closer to the stop condition
The function becomes an iterative loop
items.explanation: The recursive call has to shrink the problem so it moves toward the base case. If the input size stays the same, the function does not progress and the base case is never reached.

items.stem: A student writes Dog = 'Milo' and expects every dog object to show that name. What is the best correction?
options: Put the name on the class so all instances share it.
Create a Dog instance and store the name on that instance.
Use the same method name for every Dog object.
Make the class itself the pet and skip instances.
items.explanation: A class is the blueprint; you create instances from it (e.g. d = Dog()), and per-object data lives on each instance, not on the class. In this case, 'Milo' belongs on one dog object, not on the Dog class.

items.stem: You are writing a program to split 7 cookies equally among 2 friends and want the exact Python result of the division. What does `7 / 2` produce in Python 3?
options: An error because the operands are integers
items.explanation: Python 3 uses true division with `/`, so the result is a float. In Python 3 the / operator always returns a float, so 7 / 2 is 3.5; use // for whole-number floor division, which gives 3. Here, `7 / 2` is `3.5`.

items.stem: In this code, x starts at 1: while x < 3: print(x); x = x + 1. Which statement is true?
options: The loop stops immediately after x becomes 3 in the middle of the body
The loop prints 1 and 2, then stops when the condition is checked again
The loop never prints 2 because the condition is checked after print(x)
The loop is infinite because x increases
items.explanation: The loop expression is tested only at the top of each iteration; the rest of the current pass still runs before the condition is checked again. So print(x) runs, x changes, and only then does the next top-of-loop check decide whether to continue.

items.stem: A student writes `def greet(): print('hi')` and then immediately expects `hi` to appear. What is the best explanation?
options: The function body runs as soon as Python sees `def`.
Defining a function only stores it; the body runs when the function is called by name, such as greet().
The print statement cannot be used inside a function.
The function is missing a return statement, so it will not print.
items.explanation: The definition creates the function, but it does not execute the body. Defining a function only stores it; the body runs when the function is called by name, such as greet().

items.stem: A student writes a recursive function for countdown from n, but the function keeps calling countdown(n) with the same n. What is the main problem?
options: The function needs a global variable instead of a parameter.
The recursive call is not getting closer to a base case.
The function should be defined with parentheses after the name.
The base case should be placed inside a different file.
items.explanation: The problem is that the call is not shrinking the input, so the recursion never reaches a stopping point. Each recursive call must move toward the base case by shrinking the problem (e.g. n - 1), or the base case is never reached.

items.stem: Which version of a recursive function is safest for stopping correctly?
options: A function that calls itself on the same input until Python stops it.
A function with no return statement but many print statements.
A function that calls itself on a smaller input and has a base case for the simplest input.
A function that is defined with def but never called.
items.explanation: A recursive solution needs a stopping rule and progress toward that stop. Every recursion needs a base case — a simplest input solved directly without another call — so the chain of self-calls eventually stops.

items.stem: You want to store a pet's name and age, and also give it a bark() behavior. Which code idea matches the reading best?
options: Put name and age on the class itself, then create no instances.
Create a class as the blueprint, then make each pet as an instance with its own data.
Use only a function, because objects cannot have behavior.
Put all pet names in one shared variable so every pet uses the same values.
items.explanation: The class is the blueprint, and the pet you build from it is the instance. Attributes belong to each instance, while the class supplies shared methods. A class is the blueprint; you create instances from it (e.g. d = Dog()), and per-object data lives on each instance, not on the class.

items.stem: Two Dog objects were created from the same class. You change one dog's name attribute. What should you expect?
options: Both dogs change name because they came from the same class.
Only the dog you changed updates; each instance has its own attributes.
Nothing changes until the class definition is edited.
The method names change, but the attributes stay shared.
items.explanation: Instances do not share their attribute values. Each object keeps its own data, so editing one does not edit the other. Each instance has its own attributes, so changing one Dog's name does not change another Dog's name; only the methods are shared.

items.stem: A classmate says: "The condition is re-checked in the middle of the body the instant the variable changes." Which response is best?
options: Yes; Python checks after every assignment inside the loop.
No; the loop expression is tested only at the top of each iteration.
Yes; that is why `while` loops can stop halfway through a line.
No; the condition is never checked again after the first time.
items.explanation: The check happens at the top of each pass, not in the middle of the body. So the loop expression is tested only at the top of each iteration, and the rest of the current pass still runs before the condition is checked again.

items.stem:
Consider this code:

 def make_message():
     text = "hello"

 print(text)

What happens, and why?
options: It prints `hello` because `text` was created inside the function.
It prints nothing because `text` is local to `make_message()` and cannot be accessed outside the function.
It prints `hello` only if you call `make_message()` twice.
It changes `text` into a global variable automatically.

items.stem: You have `names = ['Ava', 'Ben', 'Cy', 'Dee', 'Eli']`. Which index gives the last element, and what happens with `names[5]`?
options: Index 5 gives the last element; `names[5]` is `Eli`.
Index 4 gives the last element; `names[5]` is out of range.
Index 1 gives the last element; `names[5]` is the first element.
Index 0 gives the last element; `names[5]` returns an empty value.
items.explanation: The last position in a 5-item list is index 4, not 5. “Indexes begin at 0 and end at one less than the length of the sequence,” so a 5-item list's last index is 4; `names[5]` is out of range and raises an error.

items.stem: A student says, “The first element is at position 1, so `scores[1]` is the first score.” Which response is correct?
options: Yes. Python counts the first element as 1.
No. The first element is at index 0, so `scores[0]` is the first score.
No. The first element is always at index -1.
Yes. `scores[1]` is the first score if the list has four items.
items.explanation: No—the first element is at index 0, not 1. The corrective is: “The first element is at index 0, so `lst[0]` is the first item and `lst[1]` is the second.” So `scores[0]` is first and `scores[1]` is second.

items.stem: Given `names = ['Ava', 'Ben', 'Cy']`, what does `names[2]` return?
options: `'Ava'`
`'Ben'`
It raises an IndexError because the first index is 1.
items.explanation: `names[2]` returns the third element because indexes start at 0. In this list, `names[0]` is `'Ava'`, `names[1]` is `'Ben'`, and `names[2]` is `'Cy'`. The wrong belief that the first index is 1 is incorrect: the first element is at index 0, so `lst[0]` is the first item and `lst[1]` is the second.

items.stem: A student writes `d = {'Ava': 95, 'Ben': 88}` and then says `d[0]` should give the first entry. Which fix is correct?
options: Use `d[0]` because dictionaries are ordered like lists.
Use `d['Ava']` or another key, because dictionaries are accessed by key, not position.
Convert the dictionary to a string first, then index it.
Add a second zero key so `d[0]` will work.
items.explanation: Dictionaries are accessed by key, not position; use `d['name']` to get the value stored under the key `'name'`, not `d[0]`. If you want Ava's score, ask for the key `'Ava'` directly.

items.stem: You open a file and run `text = f.read()`. A few lines later, you run `f.read()` again without reopening the file or moving the file position. What happens?
options: It returns the same contents again as a new string.
It returns an empty string `''` because the file position is already at the end.
It returns a list of the remaining lines.
It raises a dictionary key error.
items.explanation: The second call is empty because reading advances through the file. As the corrective says, “Reading advances a position marker through the file; once read() reaches the end, a second read() returns '' until the file is reopened or the position is reset.”

items.stem: You need to read all of `data.txt` and make sure the file is closed even if an error happens while you process the text. Which pattern should you use?
options: `f = open('data.txt'); text = f.read()` and never close it
`with open('data.txt') as f: text = f.read()`
`text = read('data.txt')`
`data = f.readlines('data.txt')`
items.explanation: Use the `with` statement. It matches the lesson example: `with open('data.txt') as f: text = f.read()` opens the file, reads all of it, and closes it automatically. Put differently, “Always close the file when done, or open it in a with statement so Python closes it automatically even if an error occurs.”

items.stem: A student writes `countdown(n)` like this: it prints `n`, then calls `countdown(n-1)`, and stops when `n == 0`. What is the role of `n == 0`?
options: It is the base case that stops the self-calls.
It is the recursive call that makes the function repeat.
It is the call stack overflow point.
It is the same-size input that keeps the function going.
items.explanation: `n == 0` is the base case: the simplest input solved directly without another call. Every recursion needs a base case — a simplest input solved directly without another call — so the chain of self-calls eventually stops.

items.stem: A function `sum_to(n)` is supposed to compute `1 + 2 + ... + n`. One student writes: `return n + sum_to(n)`. What is the best diagnosis?
options: It has a base case, but it uses the wrong variable name.
It never moves toward the base case because the recursive call uses the same-size input.
It solves a simpler version of the problem correctly.
It will always stop after one call because Python prevents repeats.
items.explanation: The problem is that `sum_to(n)` calls itself with the same value of `n`, so the input is not shrinking. Each recursive call must move toward the base case by shrinking the problem (e.g. `n - 1`), or the base case is never reached.

items.stem: Two `Dog()` objects are created, `a` and `b`. You set `a.name = 'Mochi'`. What should you expect about `b.name`?
options: `b.name` also becomes `Mochi` because the class shares the attribute value.
`b.name` changes only if the class has a method called `name`.

Every recursion needs a base case — a simplest input solved directly without another call — so the chain of self-calls eventually stops.

items.stem: A file was opened with open('notes.txt') and assigned to f. Which choice best matches good file handling?
options: Leave f open after the last read, because Python closes it only when the program ends.
Use a with block or close the file when done, so the resource is released.
Call read() twice to force the file to close itself.
Use recursion to close the file by calling the function again on a smaller input.
items.explanation: File I/O means opening, using, and closing the file; a with statement closes it automatically. Leaving it open is the mistake, and read() or recursion do not close the resource. Each recursive call must move toward the base case by shrinking the problem (e.g. n - 1), or the base case is never reached. Reading advances a position marker through the file; once read() reaches the end, a second read() returns '' until the file is reopened or the position is reset.

items.stem: You write `class Dog:` and then `Dog.name = 'Milo'` before making any objects. Later you create `a = Dog()` and `b = Dog()`. What should you expect when you set `a.name = 'Rex'`?
options: `b.name` also becomes `'Rex'`, because the class itself stores the data for every Dog built from it.
`a.name` becomes `'Rex'`, and `b.name` stays whatever it was, because each instance has its own attributes.
`a.name` stays `'Milo'`, because a class is a blueprint and cannot hold any attributes at all.
`a.name` and `b.name` both become `'Rex'`, because methods are shared by every instance.
items.explanation: `a` and `b` are separate instances, so each carries its own copy of the attributes. The tempting class-level idea is the misconception: a class is the blueprint; per-object data lives on each instance, not on the class.

items.stem: In this worked example, `class Dog:` defines the blueprint; `a = Dog()` and `b = Dog()` are two instances, each with its own `name` attribute. If you assign `a.name = 'Luna'`, which statement is true?
options: `b.name` automatically becomes `'Luna'`, because two instances of the same class share their attribute values.
`a.name` is `'Luna'`, and `b.name` is unchanged unless you set it too.
`a.name` cannot be set, because only the class can store names.
`a.name` and `b.name` both point to the same attribute storage, so changing one changes the other.
items.explanation: Each instance has its own attributes, so setting `a.name` does not change `b.name`. The shared part is the methods defined by the class, not the attribute values. A class is the blueprint; you create instances from it (e.g. d = Dog()), and per-object data lives on each instance, not on the class.

options: Put `count` on the class itself so every Counter object reads the same stored value.
Put `count` on each instance so one Counter's count can change without changing another's.
