items.explanation: The system x + y = 1 and x + y = 3 is inconsistent because the equations are parallel lines that never meet. Separate from that, vectors are defined by the vector-space axioms—anything satisfying them is a vector (polynomials, matrices, and functions included)—and if a real linear system has two distinct solutions then it has infinitely many since the whole line through them solves the system.

items.stem: Which statement best describes a solution to a system of linear equations?
options: Every system of equations has a solution.
A solution assigns a value to each variable so that every equation holds simultaneously
A solution is any subset of R^n that is closed under addition
A solution is the same thing as a nonzero vector with an additive inverse
items.explanation: A system like x + y = 1 and x + y = 3 is inconsistent, because it represents parallel lines that never meet. And over the real numbers, if a linear system has two distinct solutions, then it has infinitely many since every point on the line through them solves the system.

options: [[3, 2], [0, -2]] because multiplication works entrywise, like addition
items.explanation: Use row-by-column dot products: the first row of A with each column of B gives 11 and 5, and the second row gives -4 and -2. The entrywise option is the wrong operation; “the product AB combines rows of A with columns of B via dot products.”

items.stem: Which statement about pivots is correct?
options: The columns with the largest numbers become pivot columns
Pivot positions are determined by echelon structure during elimination, not by the size of the entries
Pivot columns are exactly the columns with the smallest entries
Any column can be chosen as a pivot column if it has a nonzero entry
items.explanation: Pivot positions come from the echelon form: the first nonzero entry in a row is the pivot, not the largest numbers. The idea “largest numbers” confuses arithmetic size with elimination structure. And in matrix products, order matters, so AB = BA only in special cases (e.g., one factor is the identity or both are powers of the same matrix).

items.stem: A 2×2 matrix has columns [1, 2] and [2, 4]. What can you conclude about invertibility?
options: It is invertible because every nonzero matrix has an inverse.
It is not invertible because its columns are linearly dependent, so it has no inverse.
It is invertible because it is square and has two columns.
It is not invertible because matrix products are not commutative.
items.explanation: The columns are multiples, so they are linearly dependent and the matrix cannot have an inverse. The tempting choice repeats the wrong belief that every nonzero matrix has an inverse; a square matrix with a zero determinant can still be nonzero yet have no inverse.

items.stem: Let A and B be invertible. Which formula gives the inverse of AB?
options: (AB)⁻¹ = A⁻¹B⁻¹, because the inverse of a product keeps the same order.
(AB)⁻¹ = B⁻¹A⁻¹, because undoing two composed operations requires reversing their order.
Every nonzero matrix has an inverse.
(AB)⁻¹ does not exist, because a product of matrices is never invertible.
items.explanation: A square matrix with a zero determinant—for example one with two equal rows—can be nonzero yet has no inverse. When undoing a product, you must reverse the order: (AB)⁻¹ = B⁻¹A⁻¹, not A⁻¹B⁻¹.

items.stem: Solve Ax = b when A is invertible. Which statement is always true?
options: Every nonzero matrix has an inverse.
The unique solution is x = A⁻¹b.
The unique solution is x = bA⁻¹.
No solution is possible unless b = 0.
items.explanation: A square matrix with a zero determinant—for example one with two equal rows—can be nonzero yet has no inverse. If A were invertible, you could use x = A⁻¹b to get a unique solution for every b, which is why claiming otherwise is wrong.

items.stem: A matrix has entries all between -2 and 2, but its determinant is 18. Which statement is consistent with the lesson facts?
options: This can happen, because the determinant measures invertibility and volume scaling, not entry size
This cannot happen, because a matrix with small entries has a small determinant
This means the matrix is automatically a 'big' matrix in the geometric sense
This must be false, because large determinant values only come from large entries
items.explanation: The determinant tracks invertibility and volume scaling, so small entries do not force a small determinant. The mistaken belief that a matrix with small entries has a small determinant, and a large determinant means a 'big' matrix, confuses entry size with what the determinant actually measures; a matrix of large numbers can have determinant zero.

items.stem: Which statement is true about invertibility?
options: A square matrix is invertible exactly when its determinant is nonzero
Every nonzero matrix has an inverse
Only matrices with large determinants are invertible
A matrix is invertible whenever its entries are all nonzero
items.explanation: The determinant measures invertibility and volume scaling, not entry size; a matrix of large numbers can have determinant zero. That’s why “every nonzero matrix has an inverse” is false: a matrix can be nonzero yet still not be invertible when det(A) = 0.

items.stem: If A and B are invertible, which formula gives the inverse of their product?
options: (AB)⁻¹ = B⁻¹A⁻¹, because undoing composed operations reverses the order
Vectors are always arrows in 2D or 3D space.
(AB)⁻¹ = A⁻¹ + B⁻¹, because inverses distribute over products
(AB)⁻¹ = (A + B)⁻¹, because products and sums have the same inverse rule
items.explanation: Undoing AB requires reversing order: first undo B, then undo A, giving (AB)⁻¹ = B⁻¹A⁻¹ rather than A⁻¹B⁻¹. Separately, anything satisfying the vector-space axioms is a vector—polynomials, matrices, and functions included—so geometry is only one model.

items.stem: Let U = { (x,y,0) : x,y in R } and W = { (x,0,z) : x,z in R }. What is U + W?
options: The xy-plane, because the span of two vectors is always a plane.
All of R^3, because any vector in R^3 can be written as (x,y,0) + (0,0,z).
The line x = y = 0, because sums of subspaces stay inside the smaller one.
A set that is not a subspace, because adding subspaces can leave the zero vector behind.
items.explanation: Anything satisfying the vector-space axioms is a vector—polynomials, matrices, and functions included—so geometry is one model, not the definition. In R³, this is why every (a,b,c) can be written as (a,b,0) + (0,0,c), making the sum span all of R³. If the two vectors are parallel (or one is zero), their span collapses to a line or a point; the span's dimension depends on independence.

items.stem: In R^2, consider v1=(1,0), v2=(0,1), and v3=(1,1). Which statement is correct?
options: They are independent because the vectors are different from each other.
They are dependent because v3 is a linear combination of v1 and v2.
They are independent because more vectors give more independence.
They are independent because each vector points in a different direction.
items.explanation: v3 = v1 + v2, so one vector is a linear combination of the others and the set is dependent. Distinct vectors can still be dependent — independence is about redundancy, not distinctness. Any set of more than n vectors in R^n is automatically dependent; adding vectors can only create dependence, never remove it.

items.stem: Which statement must be true for any set of 4 vectors in R^3?
options: The set is independent because the vectors are different from each other.
The set is independent because more vectors give more independence.
The set is dependent because any set of more than n vectors in R^n is automatically dependent.
The set is a basis because every spanning set of 4 vectors in R^3 is automatically independent.
items.explanation: In R^3, any set with more than 3 vectors is automatically dependent. Adding vectors can only create dependence, never remove it, so the first two choices miss the dimension limit. Distinct vectors can still be dependent — (1, 0), (0, 1), and (1, 1) are pairwise different yet dependent; independence is about redundancy, not distinctness.

items.stem: A student says a vector space has only one basis. Which example best refutes that claim?
options: R^2 has the standard basis {(1,0),(0,1)} and also {(1,1),(1,-1)}.
R^2 has only one basis because its dimension is 2.
R^2 has infinitely many vectors, so it has only one basis.
R^2 has one basis if the vectors are different from each other.
items.explanation: Spaces have infinitely many bases — R^2 is spanned by the standard basis but equally by (1, 1) and (1, -1). Only the SIZE of a basis is fixed, not the particular vectors. Distinct vectors can still be dependent — (1, 0), (0, 1), and (1, 1) are pairwise different yet dependent; independence is about redundancy, not distinctness.

items.conceptName: midterm exam covering systems through subspaces
items.stem: Consider the two vectors v = [1,2,3]^T and w = [2,4,6]^T. Which best describes span{v,w}?
options: It is always a plane, because the span of two vectors is always a plane.
It is a line through the origin, because the two vectors are parallel and their span collapses.
It is the whole of R^3, because two vectors in R^3 generate all of R^3.
It is not a subspace, because spans are not closed under scalar multiplication.
items.explanation: These vectors are parallel, so their span collapses to a line through the origin rather than a plane. The span is still a subspace, and its dimension depends on independence; two vectors do not automatically give a plane. Anything satisfying the vector-space axioms is a vector — polynomials, matrices, and functions included; geometry is one model, not the definition.

items.stem: A matrix A has columns [1,0,0]^T and [0,1,0]^T. Which set is Col(A)?
options: The xy-plane through the origin, because the columns span all linear combinations of [1,0,0]^T and [0,1,0]^T.
The line through [1,0,0]^T and [0,1,0]^T, because any line or plane in R^3 is a subspace.
All of R^3, because two vectors always generate every vector in three dimensions.
The zero vector only, because the span of two vectors is always a plane.
items.explanation: Those columns are independent, so their span is exactly the xy-plane through the origin. The “any line or plane in R^3 is a subspace” belief misses that only ones through the origin work, and “span of two vectors is always a plane” fails when the vectors are parallel or zero. Only lines and planes through the origin are subspaces; others miss the zero vector and are not closed under scaling.

items.stem: A 3-by-5 matrix R has rows [1,2,3,4,5], [2,4,6,8,10], and [0,0,0,0,0]. What is rank(R)?
options: 2, because the original matrix has two nonzero rows.
5, because the matrix is tall and has many rows.
1, because the rows are proportional after row reduction, so there is one pivot.
3, because rank counts the nonzero entries in the original matrix.
items.explanation: Only one row is independent: the second row is a multiple of the first, and the zero row adds nothing, so there is one pivot after row reduction. The wrong beliefs count nonzero rows or nonzero entries before reduction, but rank is about pivots, not raw appearance. Rank never exceeds the smaller of the row and column counts, and dependence among columns lowers it further.

items.stem: Which statement about a subset of R^n is enough to make it a vector space?
options: It is any subset of R^n, since subsets automatically inherit vector-space structure.
It contains the zero vector and is closed under addition and scalar multiplication.
It has more than one vector, so it must have a finite number of vectors.
It is a line not through the origin, because lines are always vector spaces.
items.explanation: A subset must contain the zero vector and stay closed under addition and scalar multiplication. A line not through the origin fails that test, so it is not a vector space in its own right. Over the real numbers, once a linear system has two distinct solutions it has infinitely many, because the whole line through the two solutions solves the system.

items.stem: Which matrix is singular but not the zero matrix?
options: [[1,1],[1,1]] because every entry matches so it must be zero matrix behavior
items.explanation: A zero eigenvalue means some nonzero vector is sent to zero, so the matrix is singular, not necessarily zero. The zero matrix is one example, but [[1,0],[0,0]] already shows a nonzero matrix with a zero eigenvalue. Eigenvectors are required to be nonzero — A0 = λ0 holds trivially and identifies nothing about the matrix.

items.stem: A matrix A has characteristic polynomial det(A−λI)=λ(λ−2). What must be true?
options: A is diagonalizable because every matrix with a zero eigenvalue is a zero matrix.
A has a zero eigenvalue, so A is not invertible.
A has eigenvalue 0, so the zero vector is an eigenvector for λ=0.
A must have two distinct eigenvectors even if they are the zero vector.
items.explanation: A zero eigenvalue means the matrix is not invertible, not that it is the zero matrix. The zero-vector belief fails because eigenvectors must be nonzero, so A0=0 does not count as an eigenvector statement. Eigenvectors are required to be nonzero — A0 = λ0 holds trivially and identifies nothing about the matrix. A zero eigenvalue only means some nonzero vector is sent to zero — the matrix is singular, not necessarily zero.

items.stem: For the matrix [[0,1],[0,0]], which claim is correct?
options: It has a zero eigenvalue, so it is a zero matrix.
It has a zero eigenvalue, so it is singular, not necessarily zero.
It cannot have any eigenvectors because the zero vector is the only candidate.
It must be diagonalizable because one eigenvalue is 0.
items.explanation: This matrix has a zero eigenvalue, which shows it is singular. The zero-matrix belief is too strong: a zero eigenvalue only means some nonzero vector is sent to zero, not that every entry is zero. Eigenvectors are required to be nonzero — A0 = λ0 holds trivially and identifies nothing about the matrix.

items.stem: A data scientist uses two basis functions in a model, and their dot product is 0. What does that tell you?
options: They are orthogonal, because their inner product is zero even if they are not pictured as arrows.
They are perpendicular lines in a picture, so the model must live in 2D.
They are the same direction, because zero dot product means the basis has changed.
They cannot be vectors, because only arrows in 2D or 3D can be orthogonal.
items.explanation: In linear algebra, anything satisfying the vector-space axioms is a vector, so polynomials, matrices, and functions count too. Geometry is just one model, not the definition. Orthogonality is defined by the inner product being zero, which extends to functions and high-dimensional data where no picture exists.

items.stem: The system Ax=b has no exact solution, but the least-squares solution x̂ is computed. What is true about Ax̂ and b?
options: Least squares finds an exact solution to the system, so Ax̂ = b.
It minimizes the residual; the fitted values Ax̂ generally differ from b.
It only works when the system already has infinitely many solutions.
It chooses x̂ so that every equation is satisfied exactly after row reduction.
items.explanation: Least squares minimizes the residual, so the fitted values Ax̂ are closest to b without needing to equal it. A system like x + y = 1 and x + y = 3 is inconsistent because the equations describe parallel lines that never meet, and two distinct real solutions would force infinitely many along the whole line through them.

items.stem: Points are (1,2), (2,1), and (3,0). Which statement about the least-squares line is correct?
options: A best-fit line must pass through the data points, so this line has to go through all three.
The least-squares line minimizes the sum of squared vertical gaps and can miss every single data point.
Because there are three points, the best-fit line is always one of the data lines between two points.
Orthogonal simply means the lines look perpendicular in a graph.
items.explanation: The least-squares line minimizes the sum of squared vertical gaps, so it need not pass through any data point. Orthogonality is defined by the inner product being zero, which extends to functions and high-dimensional data where no picture exists.

items.stem: After row reduction, a linear system in the real numbers has two distinct solutions listed. What must be true?
options: The system has exactly two solutions.
The system is inconsistent.
It actually has infinitely many solutions.
The two solutions mean the row reduction was invalid.
items.explanation: Over the real numbers, once a linear system has two distinct solutions it has infinitely many, because the whole line through the two solutions solves the system. So "exactly two" is not an option for a linear system.

items.stem: In an echelon form matrix, what determines the pivot positions?
options: The largest numbers in each column.
The number of variables in the system.
The echelon structure produced during elimination.
Whichever entries were nonzero in the original matrix.
items.explanation: Pivot positions are determined by echelon structure during elimination, not by the size of the entries. A large entry is not automatically a pivot; the row-reduction structure decides that.

items.stem: A student says the span of (1, 2) and (2, 4) in R^2 must be all of R^2 because there are two vectors. What is the best response?
options: Correct: two vectors always span a plane
Incorrect: parallel vectors can span only a line
Correct only if the vectors are unit vectors
Incorrect: any two vectors span only the zero vector
items.explanation: The number of vectors does not control the dimension of the span; independence does. Since the vectors are parallel, the span collapses to a line, not all of R^2. That is exactly the corrective: "If the two vectors are parallel (or one is zero), their span collapses to a line or a point; the span's dimension depends on independence."

items.stem: Suppose Av = 3v and Aw = 5w, with v and w both nonzero. What can you conclude?
options: v and w must be scalar multiples of each other
v and w are automatically linearly independent
A must be the zero matrix
3 and 5 cannot both be eigenvalues
items.explanation: Eigenvectors belonging to distinct eigenvalues are automatically linearly independent. Here 3 and 5 are distinct eigenvalues, so v and w cannot collapse onto the same line.

items.stem: You’re building a label for an integer score. What code will correctly produce the string "Score: 19" without a TypeError?
options: 'Score: ' + 19
'Score: ' + str(19)
7 / 2 to give 3 (integer division) because the operands look like whole numbers.
19 + 'Score: '
items.explanation: Use explicit type conversion before joining: Convert the number with str() before adding it to text. The corrected idea is: 'Age: ' + str(19) builds 'Age: 19', while 'Age: ' + 19 raises a TypeError because a str and an int cannot be added.

items.stem:
You run this code: 

for i in range(4):
    print(i)

What is the exact output (the printed numbers, in order)?
options: Range(5) produces 1 through 5, so their loop runs one time too few or accesses the wrong indices.
items.explanation: range(n) yields values from 0 up to n-1. So range(4) produces 0, 1, 2, 3. The code prints i for each element in that sequence.

items.stem: Two instances of the same class should share what, according to the core idea?
options: Only the methods; each instance has its own copy of the attributes
Only the attributes; each instance has its own copy of methods
Both attributes and methods, since they come from the same class
Nothing is shared; instances are completely independent of class definitions
items.explanation: Kernel fact: “Each instance carries its own copy of the attributes, while the methods defined by the class are shared by every instance.” So methods are shared; attributes are per-instance.

items.stem: A class uses perfect-competition predictions for a market dominated by one firm. What is the most accurate judgment?
options: The model may be misleading because a key assumption breaks in that market.
The model must be correct because all economic models are literally true.
The model is useful only if the market has zero firms.
The model works best when it ignores all assumptions.
items.explanation: In this case the problem is not that the model is useless in every setting; it is that one of its key assumptions breaks. The chapter’s rule is that a model is useful when its assumptions are close enough for the question at hand, and misleading when a key assumption breaks.

items.stem: A student says, “A model is literally true, so if reality disagrees, reality must be wrong.” Which option is the best reply?
options: A model is a simplified representation of reality, so it can be useful even when it is not literally true.
A model is only useful when it includes every detail of reality.
A model never uses assumptions, so disagreement is impossible.
A model is mainly a way to prove that perfect competition always holds.
items.explanation: That belief confuses the model with the world. A model is a simplified representation of reality, and it is useful when its assumptions are close enough for the question at hand; it can be misleading when a key assumption breaks.

items.stem: A student skips a paid shift to attend a free concert ticket. What is the opportunity cost of attending the concert?
options: Zero, because the ticket was free
Only the gas money to get there
The value of the next best alternative use of that time, such as the wage from the shift
The price of the concert ticket plus any snacks bought there
items.explanation: The right answer is the forgone shift value. As the course note says, "the opportunity cost of a choice is the value of the next best alternative that must be given up"; a free ticket is not free if it uses time or resources that could have produced something else.

items.stem: A lawyer types faster than her assistant and also earns more per hour from legal work. What should the firm conclude?
options: The lawyer should type everything because she has absolute advantage in both tasks.
The assistant should type because the lawyer’s opportunity cost of typing is higher.
No one should type because typing has no cost if the software is free.
The lawyer should stop doing legal work whenever typing needs to be done.
items.explanation: Gains from trade come from differences in opportunity cost, not from absolute skill. Even if the lawyer types faster, the lawyer’s time has a higher-value legal use. So the assistant types and the lawyer does legal work.

items.stem: Which choice is most consistent with the consumer-choice model?
options: Pick the bundle you want most, even if it is above the budget, because utility matters more than feasibility.
Pick any bundle inside the budget, because all affordable bundles are equally good.
Pick the affordable bundle that yields the highest satisfaction.
Pick the bundle with the highest price, because it must signal higher utility.
items.explanation: The model is explicit: the consumer maximizes utility subject to a budget constraint. So the right choice is the affordable bundle with the highest satisfaction, not the most expensive bundle or just any feasible one.

items.stem: Which formula gives price elasticity of demand?
options: Change in price divided by change in quantity demanded
Percentage change in quantity demanded divided by percentage change in price
Quantity demanded divided by price
Percentage change in price divided by percentage change in quantity demanded
items.explanation: The correct formula is **percentage change in quantity demanded divided by percentage change in price**. That is the definition used in the lesson, and the absolute value tells us whether demand is elastic or inelastic.

items.stem: Which statement best matches the law of supply?
options: A higher price raises the quantity producers are willing to supply, so the supply curve slopes upward
A higher price lowers the quantity producers are willing to supply, so the supply curve slopes downward
A higher price always shifts the supply curve to the right
Supply is a fixed stock that does not vary over time
items.explanation: The law of supply says higher price means higher quantity supplied, so the curve slopes upward. The phrase to keep in mind is that 'a higher price raises the quantity that producers are willing to supply.'

items.stem: At a price above equilibrium, what is the market pressure on price?
options: A shortage pushes price up.
A surplus pushes price down.
Demand equals supply, so there is no pressure.
The price cannot change because equilibrium has already been reached.
items.explanation: Above equilibrium, sellers have more to offer than buyers want to buy, so a surplus forms and pushes the price down.

items.stem: A price ceiling keeps the price below equilibrium. What happens according to the reading's example?
options: The shortage disappears because the market immediately reaches equilibrium.
The shortage persists because the restoring rise is blocked.
A surplus persists because price is held down.
Demand shifts left until the shortage ends.
items.explanation: The example says that if a price ceiling holds the price below equilibrium, the resulting shortage persists because the restoring rise is blocked. That is why the market cannot move back to equilibrium on its own.

items.stem: A country’s gross investment is 120 and depreciation is 150. What happens to the capital stock over this period?
options: It rises because gross investment is positive.
It stays the same because investment and depreciation are both large.
It falls because net investment is negative.
It doubles because investment exceeded zero.
items.explanation: Net investment is gross investment minus depreciation. Here that is 120 - 150 = -30, so the capital stock falls. The stock grows only when net investment is positive.

items.stem: A factory has strong gross investment this year, but its capital stock still does not grow. Which explanation is most plausible?
options: Depreciation must have been at least as large as gross investment.
Gross investment always creates growth in the stock.
Saving disappeared from the economy.
The capital stock is a flow, so it cannot be measured over time.
items.explanation: Because net investment equals gross investment minus depreciation, strong gross investment can still leave no growth if depreciation is just as large or larger. The stock grows only when net investment is positive.

items.stem: Hematite can look silvery or red. What is the best mineral ID test from the lesson when specimen color changes like that?
options: Surface color
Streak
Weight alone
Shape only
items.explanation: The worked example leads to streak: hematite can look silvery or red, but its streak is always reddish-brown, so the powder color gives it away when the specimen color does not.

items.stem: Which statement about luster is correct?
options: It is the color of a mineral's powder
It describes how a mineral's surface reflects light
It measures scratch resistance
It tells whether a mineral breaks along flat planes
items.explanation: Luster is about reflected light. The lesson defines it as how a mineral's surface reflects light — metallic, glassy, or dull.

items.stem: A volcano has runny basaltic magma and a broad gentle slope. What eruptive style should you expect?
options: Violent explosive eruptions are most likely because all volcanoes build pressure the same way.
Gentle lava flows are most likely because low-silica basaltic magma is low-viscosity and oozes easily.
A pyroclastic flow is most likely because basalt is the deadliest type of magma.
The magma will not erupt because runny magma cannot reach the surface.
items.explanation: Eruptive style depends on viscosity: low-silica basaltic volcanoes ooze lava gently, while only high-silica, high-viscosity volcanoes build the pressure that drives explosive eruptions. Runny basalt is the gentle end of the spectrum.

items.stem: A rock has ripple marks, well-sorted sand-sized grains, and no fossils. What environment is most consistent with those features?
options: A sandy, current-swept setting
A deep, quiet marine setting
A lava flow that cooled quickly
A place where rock cooled directly from magma
items.explanation: Ripple marks and sand-sized grains fit a moving-water setting. The reading’s worked example links sandstone with ripple marks to a sandy, current-swept environment, so that is the best match here.

items.stem: A mineral specimen is silvery on the outside, but its powder is reddish-brown. What property is most dependable for identification here?
options: Color of the whole specimen
Streak
Surface shine alone
Its sedimentary layers
items.explanation: Streak is the color of the powder and is more reliable than the color of the whole specimen. Hematite is the model example: it can look silvery or red, but its streak is reddish-brown.

items.stem: A rock contains minerals lined up in planes. It formed after an older rock was changed by heat and directed pressure, but the crystals never melted. What is the best interpretation?
options: It is a foliated metamorphic rock
It is an extrusive igneous rock
It is a sedimentary rock formed by cementation
It is magma that cooled underground
items.explanation: Minerals lined up in planes is foliation. That matches metamorphism in the solid state, not melting, so the rock is a foliated metamorphic rock.

items.stem: A sample is a rock that formed when loose sediment was deposited, compacted, and cemented near the surface. What kind of rock is it?
options: Metamorphic rock
Sedimentary rock
Igneous rock
Magma
items.explanation: This is sedimentary rock, not a cooled melt. The corrective says: “Sedimentary rock does not cool from a melt; it forms when loose sediment is deposited, compacted, and cemented (lithified) at low temperatures near the surface.”

items.stem: A volcano is fed by low-silica basaltic magma that moves like syrup. Which hazard pattern best fits this volcano?
options: Gentle lava flows are more likely than explosive blasts
A fast cloud of hot ash and gas is the main hazard
It will always erupt explosively because all volcanoes do
The magma will trap gas most efficiently because it is runny
items.explanation: Because low-viscosity, low-silica basaltic magma flows easily, it usually erupts effusively. The key contrast is in the reading: “Low viscosity magma flows easily more like syrup” and the eruptive style depends on viscosity, not on the fact that it is a volcano.

items.stem: A sandstone cliff breaks into fragments during freezing nights, but the pieces stay piled at the base of the cliff all winter. Which statement is best?
options: That is erosion, because the rock was broken apart.
That is weathering, and no erosion has happened yet because nothing transported the pieces.
That is chemical weathering because the rock changed into clay.
That is sedimentary rock forming by cooling from a melt.
items.explanation: This is the clearest way to separate the terms: weathering breaks rock down in place; erosion is the separate step that carries the broken material away. Here, the cliff weathers, but because the pieces stay put, there is no erosion yet.

items.stem: A research note says, 'We emailed a satisfaction survey to our most loyal customers because we wanted quick feedback.' Which inference is safest?
options: The results may be limited by the purpose and method of collection.
The results prove all customers are satisfied.
The dataset is objective fact, so purpose is irrelevant.
The survey must be wrong because it was emailed.
items.explanation: Since the survey was sent to the most loyal customers for quick feedback, the method and purpose matter. The collection method and its purpose can bias what the data can support, so the safest inference is that the results may be limited.

items.stem: Two studies use the same null hypothesis. Study A has p = 0.20 and Study B has p = 0.01. Which conclusion is most justified from the p-values alone?
options: Study B’s data are more unusual under the null than Study A’s data.
Study B must have a larger effect size.
Study A proves the null is true.
Study A and Study B have the same evidence against the null.
items.explanation: A smaller p-value means the observed data would be less likely under the null, so Study B’s data are more unusual under that same null. Do not read p-values as effect sizes; the text says the p-value “does not measure the size of an effect.”

items.stem: Which description best matches a statistical model?
options: A perfect copy of the data with no simplifications.
A simplified mathematical representation of how data are generated.
A rule that is valid only when the sample size is large.
A graph that is useful only when R-squared is high.
items.explanation: A model is not a mirror image of the data. The anchor quote is direct: “a simplified mathematical representation of how data are generated.”

items.stem: A regression model keeps a few structural features and discards others. What is the best reason for doing that?
options: To make the model look more complicated
To simplify the data-generation story while keeping the important structure
To avoid needing any assumptions at all
To guarantee the conclusions are never misleading
items.explanation: This is the point of a statistical model: it is a simplified representation, so it keeps important structure and discards the rest. But that simplicity only works when the assumptions fit the situation; otherwise the conclusions can be misleading.

items.conceptName: data collection bias and survey design
items.stem: A classmate says, “I do not need to know who collected the data, because the conclusion is already written in the chart.” What is the best reply?
options: Charts remove bias, so provenance is unnecessary.
The purpose of the collection can matter only in science classes.
You can trust the conclusion if the chart has a title.
Conclusions are only as trustworthy as the provenance of the data behind them.
items.explanation: Confront the chart-first assumption directly: “Conclusions are only as trustworthy as the provenance of the data behind them.” If you do not know who collected it, how, and why, you do not know what the numbers can really support.

items.stem:
Suppose you write:

x = 5
while x > 0:
    print(x)
    x = x - 1

What will this loop print, in order?
options: 5, 4, 3, 2, 1, then stops
5, 4, 3, 2, then stops
Nothing, because the condition is false at the start
It never stops because x > 0 stays true
items.explanation: This while loop re-checks the loop expression before each iteration, and the body updates the condition variable: x = x - 1. Starting at x = 5, it prints 5, then 4, then 3, then 2, then 1, and stops when x reaches 0 (so x > 0 becomes false).

items.stem:
A student writes:

def square(n):
    result = n * n
    return result

Then they try to do this outside the function: print(result)
What is the most likely outcome?
options: It prints n * n successfully because result is a global variable
It raises a NameError because result is not defined outside the function
It prints the function object for square
It causes a RecursionError because result is recursive
items.explanation: Variables created inside a function have local scope. The corrective rule is: “Local variables exist only during the call that created them; to use a result outside, the function must return it and the caller must capture the returned value.”

items.stem: Pick the best recursive structure for factorial(n) that matches the worked example and guarantees termination.
options: if n == 0: return 1; else: return n * factorial(n - 1)
if n == 1: return 1; else: return n * factorial(n + 1)
return n * factorial(n - 1) with no base case
if n == 0: return factorial(n - 1); else: return n
items.explanation: This matches the provided pattern: factorial(n) returns 1 when n is 0 (base case) and otherwise returns n * factorial(n - 1), shrinking n each call until it’s small enough to solve directly.

items.stem: Which option correctly matches the roles in a Python class?
options: Class = built object; instance = blueprint
Class = blueprint; instance = individual object built from it
Class = local variables created when a function is called
Instance = code block that runs only when called
items.explanation: You’re looking for the blueprint relationship: “A class is a blueprint for creating objects.” Then, “Individual objects created of the class type are called instances.”

items.stem:
Which statement about variable access is correct in this program?

def make_total(a, b):
    total = a + b
    return total

outside = make_total(2, 3)
print(outside)

(Assume indentation is correct.)
options: total is global, so it can be accessed anywhere; outside is unnecessary.
total is local to the function call, and outside holds the returned value.
outside is a local variable inside make_total, so print(outside) fails.
The function must be called twice for outside to exist.
items.explanation: A variable created inside a function has local scope and cannot be accessed outside the function. To use it outside, the function returns it, and the caller captures the returned value (outside = make_total(2, 3)).

items.stem: A student says: "I call f.read() and it returns one line at a time, so if I want a list of lines I can keep calling read()." What is the best correction?
options: That’s correct: read() returns the next line each time
That’s incorrect: read() reads the entire contents of a file and returns a single string
That’s incorrect: readline() returns a list, but read() returns one line
That’s incorrect: read() returns an integer count of lines
items.explanation: The read() function reads the contents of a file and returns a string (not one line at a time). If you want lines, use readline() or readlines().

items.stem: A student says: “Students think writing def greet(): runs the function body immediately.” What is the correct interpretation of what def does?
options: Writing def greet(): runs the function body right away
Defining a function only stores it; the body runs when the function is called by name, such as greet()
Python runs the body when the file is imported, not when greet() is called
Python runs the body every time the interpreter reaches the def line, even without a call
items.explanation: Correct: the corrective matches exactly—“Defining a function only stores it; the body runs when the function is called by name, such as greet().”

items.stem:
You write:

x = 3

def f():
    x = x + 1
    return x

What is the most accurate expectation when you call f()?
options: It returns 4 because x becomes global inside f
It raises UnboundLocalError because x is treated as local in f
It returns 3 because return cancels the update
It raises NameError because x wasn’t defined inside f
items.explanation: Inside the function, assigning to x makes x a local variable for that call; then x = x + 1 tries to use the local x before it’s defined. This is the same core scope idea: local variables exist only during the call, and local scope changes where a name can be accessed.

items.stem: Consider: `if temp > 100: print('boiling') else: print('not boiling')`. If temp is 100, what prints?
options: boiling
not boiling
If age > 13 and < 19 is valid, chaining the second comparison without repeating the variable.
Nothing prints
items.explanation: The else branch runs only when the if condition is false. Since temp > 100 is false when temp is 100, it prints `not boiling`.

items.stem: Misconception check (strings): A student says, “Strings are mutable; I can change one character by doing s[0] = 'X'.” What is the best correction?
options: It works like a list, so s[0] = 'X' is allowed
It raises an error; instead convert to a list, mutate, then join back, or build a new string
It automatically expands the string and keeps the old character too
Use s.insert(0, 'X') to modify the original string in place
items.explanation: The correction is that `str` is immutable. To change characters, use a new value: convert to a list of characters for mutation (chars=list(s)), then convert back to a string (s=''.join(chars)), or build a new string using slicing.

items.stem:
Students say: “Students try to read a dictionary value with a numeric index like d[0], expecting list-style positions.”

Given d = {'name': 'Mina', 'age': 12}, what happens with d[0]?
options: It returns 'Mina' because 'name' is the first item
It returns 12 because it's the second item
It fails because dictionaries are not indexed by numeric position
It returns an empty string ''
items.explanation: Dictionaries are accessed by key, not position; use d['name'] to get the value stored under the key 'name', not d[0].

items.stem: A loop starts with n = 5 and the body never changes n. What is the most likely outcome if the condition is n > 0?
options: It stops after one pass.
It runs forever.
It changes n automatically.
It only checks the condition after the body changes n.
items.explanation: Because n never changes, the condition stays true. Every while loop must change something the condition depends on; a counter loop needs n = n - 1 (or += 1) inside the body so the condition eventually becomes false. In this case, the loop has no path to false, so it becomes an infinite loop.

items.stem: Consider `n = 2` and `while n > 0: n = n - 1; print(n)`. What happens on the first pass?
options: The loop stops before `print(n)` runs.
`print(n)` runs with the old value of `n`, then the condition is checked again.
The condition is checked after each line, so the loop ends as soon as `n` becomes 1.
The body runs only if `n` becomes negative.
items.explanation: The loop expression is tested only at the top of each iteration; the rest of the current pass still runs before the condition is checked again. So the subtraction happens, then `print(n)` still runs, and only after that does the next condition check happen.

items.stem: A loop needs to process every item in a list from left to right. Which structure matches that need best?
options: A for loop over the list
An if statement on the list name
A function definition with no call
A single index that skips to the last item
items.explanation: A for loop can iterate through a list, visiting each element in order. That matches the goal of handling every item from left to right.

items.stem: A nested record stores a user's city inside a dictionary value. What is the safest way to read the city?
options: Use a numeric index because nested data always behaves like a list
Read the outer key first, then use the inner key on the nested dictionary
Assign a second city to the same key so both stay available
Call lower() on the dictionary before reading it
items.explanation: Work from the outside in: get the nested dictionary with its outer key, then use the inner key to read the city. Dictionaries are labeled lookup structures, so the key names guide both steps.

items.stem: A student says, 'I read the file, so I do not need to close it.' What is the best fix?
options: Close the file when done, or use a with statement.
Call read() again so Python closes it.
Convert the file object into a dictionary.
Use readlines() instead of read().
items.explanation: Always close the file when done, or open it in a with statement so Python closes it automatically even if an error occurs. That habit matters any time the program is finished with the file, even if the last line of code ran successfully.

items.stem: A data set is naturally labeled with names, not ordered by position. Which structure fits that need best?
options: A dictionary written with curly braces and key: value pairs
A list accessed only by numeric position
A single string from read()
A file object returned by open()
items.explanation: A dictionary stores key-value pairs and is ideal when data is naturally labeled rather than ordered. The key gives the lookup label, which is the point of the structure.

items.stem: You are tracing a recursive function on paper. Which step should you identify first?
options: The final returned value
The base case
The variable that changes type
The last recursive call
items.explanation: Start with the base case because it is the stopping point that makes the rest of the trace make sense. After that, you can follow the smaller calls and then the returns.

items.stem: You want a recursive solution to stop when the input is already simple enough. Which code idea fits that purpose?
options: Call the function with the same input until it works.
Add a base case that solves the simplest input directly.
Put the data on the class so every call shares it.
Skip the stopping point and rely on the stack.
items.explanation: The recursive pattern needs a direct answer for the simplest input. That base case is what stops the self-calls.

items.stem: What happens when Python executes def greet(): print('hi') but the program never uses greet()?
options: The body runs once because the function is defined.
Python treats greet() as a global variable.
The function body runs only when greet() is called by name.
The print statement runs only if there is a base case.
items.explanation: Defining a function does not run its body. Defining a function only stores it; the body runs when the function is called by name, such as greet().

items.stem: A function creates a variable total inside the function and then ends. Later, code outside the function tries to print(total). What is the result most likely to be?
options: It prints the local value because all variables become global after return.
It causes a NameError because total is local to that call.
It calls the function again automatically.
It works only if the function has a base case.
items.explanation: The variable was created inside the function call, so it does not exist outside that call. Local variables exist only during the call that created them; to use a result outside, the function must return it and the caller must capture the returned value.

items.stem: A programmer says, 'I wrote a function with def, so it should already be available to use inside its own body.' Which fix is best if the goal is to use the result outside the function?
options: Replace def with global.
Have the function return the result and store it in a variable outside the function.
Remove the function name so it becomes anonymous.
Add a base case to the function body.
items.explanation: The outer code cannot read a local variable directly. Local variables exist only during the call that created them; to use a result outside, the function must return it and the caller must capture the returned value.

items.stem: Which line best matches the lesson’s description of `readlines()`?
options: `lines = f.readlines()` because it returns a list with every line of the file
`lines = f.read()` because it returns one line at a time
`lines = f.readline()` because it returns the whole file as a string
`lines = open('data.txt')` because `open()` returns the file contents
items.explanation: `readlines()` returns a list containing all the lines in order, which is exactly what the lesson states and what the anchored quote says: “The readlines() function reads the individual lines of a file and returns a string list containing all the lines of the file in order.”

items.stem: Which statement best matches how `readline()` and `readlines()` differ?
options: `readline()` returns the whole file as a string; `readlines()` returns one line at a time
`readline()` returns the next single line; `readlines()` returns a list with every line of the file
Both return the same type of result
`readlines()` only works after `read()`
items.explanation: The key distinction is that `readline()` returns the next single line, while `readlines()` returns a list with every line of the file. If you need one line, use `readline()`; if you need all lines collected, use `readlines()`.

items.stem: You are tracing a recursive function and want to know when the calls stop. Which condition must be present?
options: A loop that runs exactly once.
A base case that solves the simplest input directly.
A print statement before every recursive call.
A larger input on every call so the final answer is bigger.
items.explanation: The stopping point is the base case. Every recursion needs a base case — a simplest input solved directly without another call — so the chain of self-calls eventually stops.

items.stem:
You run this code:
score = 10
score = score + 5
What does score hold after the second line, and why?
options: 20, because = means mathematical equality and forces the result to match the left side
15, because the right side (score + 5) is evaluated and the result is stored back into score
10, because variables store the expression score + 5 and keep it symbolic
15, because Python always uses integer division so score + 5 is computed as 10/2 + 5
items.explanation: In Python 3, the / operator always returns a float, so 7 / 2 is 3.5; if you want whole-number floor division, use //, which gives 3. This is about choosing the correct operator, not about balancing anything like an equation.

items.stem: Which statement would the author most likely reject?
options: Classic works should be respected, but not treated as untouchable objects.
Specialization can narrow how people view literature.
Literature should be made easier to approach for ordinary readers.
Only esoteric approaches count as legitimate ways to read literature.
items.explanation: What the reading rejects is the idea that only “esoteric” approaches count. It says specialization can narrow how people view literature, but that is a warning about exclusion, not a defense of it.

items.stem: Which label best fits a prose narrative with implausible characters, far-away imaginative settings, extravagant action, and supernatural interventions?
options: Novel, because any long prose narrative counts as realism.
Romance, because those features match the chapter’s contrast with the novel.
Historical realism, because supernatural interventions prove the events really happened.
Lyric prose, because the setting is imaginative.
items.explanation: Those traits line up with romance in the chapter’s distinction. The novel is tied to realistic people and situations; romance is the form with implausible characters, imaginative settings, extravagant action, and supernatural interventions.

items.stem: Students claim: “I read x = x + 1 as a mathematical equation, so it should mean x equals x+1, which is impossible.” Which response is correct?
options: Correct: it’s a math equation, so Python should reject it
Correct: it updates x by increasing it by one, because = is assignment
Incorrect: assignment makes x become the string "x + 1"
Incorrect: x = x + 1 means x stores the expression itself and updates later
items.explanation: In Python `=` is assignment, not equality: the right side is evaluated first and the result is bound to the name on the left, so `x = x + 1` simply increases x by one.

items.stem: A student claims: "If I change the loop variable inside a for loop, it edits the original list because the loop variable is the list." Which is correct?
options: Yes—assigning to the loop variable edits the list
No—the loop variable is a fresh binding; assigning it does not edit the container
It edits the list only when the loop variable is an integer
It edits the list only when the list is inside range()
items.explanation: Confronting the claim: assigning to the loop variable does not edit the container. The loop variable is a fresh binding to each element in turn; assigning to it does not change the underlying list. To change list contents, index into the list directly.

items.stem: You want to compute factorial(n) recursively. Which pair of statements best matches the recursion structure?
options: Base case: n == 0, Recursive case: return n * factorial(n - 1) (and n - 1 shrinks).
Base case: n == 1, Recursive case: return n * factorial(n + 1) (and n + 1 shrinks).
Base case: n == 0, Recursive case: return n + factorial(n - 1) (and n - 1 grows).
Base case: n == -1, Recursive case: return factorial(n) (so it’s simpler each time).
items.explanation: This is the worked-example structure: factorial(n) returns 1 when n is 0 (base case) and otherwise returns n * factorial(n - 1), shrinking n each call. That shrink is what ensures you eventually reach the base case.

items.stem: You want to reuse behavior for every pet you model. Where should the behavior (methods) go so all instances can use it?
options: In the class definition, because methods are shared by every instance
In each instance only, because classes can’t define behavior
Only in global variables, so instances can access it
In a list of instances, because lists share behavior with their elements
items.explanation: Methods belong in the class definition: “Each instance carries its own copy of the attributes, while the methods defined by the class are shared by every instance.” So behavior is defined once on the class and used by all instances.

items.stem: Pavlov's dogs salivate when meat powder is placed in front of them. What is meat powder in this example?
options: Conditioned stimulus
Unconditioned stimulus
Conditioned response
Extinction
items.explanation: Meat powder is the unconditioned stimulus because it directly elicits the reflexive response without learning. In other words, 'an unconditioned stimulus (UCS): a stimulus that elicits a reflexive response in an organism'—the learning comes later when something neutral is paired with it.

items.stem: After many pairings, a bell makes a dog salivate. If the bell is rung over and over but food no longer appears, what happens to the salivation?
options: It becomes an unconditioned response
It increases because of spontaneous recovery
It decreases; this is extinction
It becomes a new conditioned stimulus
items.explanation: This is extinction: the conditioned response decreases when the unconditioned stimulus stops accompanying the conditioned stimulus. If the response later returns after a rest period, that is spontaneous recovery, which is different from extinction.

items.stem: A parent takes away a teenager's phone for breaking curfew, and curfew-breaking goes down. Which statement is best?
options: Negative reinforcement because something is removed
Punishment because the behavior decreases
Positive reinforcement because something is added
Conditioned stimulus because the phone predicts curfew
items.explanation: Because the behavior goes down, this is punishment. Don't let the sign mislead you: in operant conditioning positive means adding something and negative means taking something away; either operation can serve reinforcement or punishment.

items.stem: A parent takes away screen time after a child hits a sibling. What is this?
options: Negative punishment
Positive punishment
Negative reinforcement
Positive reinforcement
items.explanation: In operant conditioning positive means adding something and negative means taking something away; either operation can serve reinforcement or punishment. Here, the parent adds an unpleasant consequence to decrease the behavior, so it is positive punishment.

items.stem: A student studies harder after the teacher announces that the weekly quiz will be dropped if everyone finishes the review sheet on time. What process is this?
options: Negative punishment
Positive punishment
Negative reinforcement
Positive reinforcement
items.explanation: The quiz is not being added; it is being removed if the behavior happens. The target behavior increases because an undesirable stimulus is removed, which is exactly negative reinforcement.

items.stem: Which statement best captures why the models children see matter?
options: Observational learning only affects aggressive behavior, not helpful behavior.
Observational learning can have both prosocial and antisocial effects.
Children imitate only adults, never peers.
Children imitate only when they are directly rewarded first.
items.explanation: The reading makes this broad point directly: "this learning can have both prosocial and antisocial effects." So the models children see matter because they can encourage helpful actions or harmful ones.

items.stem: Which study move is most likely to improve memory for a new psychology term?
options: Recopy the term ten times exactly as it appears.
Say the term once and then stop thinking about it.
Explain the term in your own words and connect it to an example.
Look at the term for a few seconds and rely on sensory memory.
items.explanation: Explaining a new term in your own words is semantic encoding, and the reading says words encoded semantically are remembered better than words encoded visually or acoustically. Meaning-based processing is the deeper route into storage.

items.stem: A professor flashes a list of words on the screen for a split second. Most students can report only a few items and then the words are gone. Which stage best explains that very brief hold?
options: Long-term memory
Working memory
Sensory memory
Retrieval
items.explanation: That brief hold is sensory memory. It stores brief sensory events, such as sights and sounds, for only up to a couple of seconds before they fade or move on.

items.stem: Which pair is the best match for explicit memory?
options: Procedural memory and balance corrections
Episodic memory and semantic memory
Sensory memory and short-term memory
Implicit memory and unconscious skill
items.explanation: Explicit memory divides into episodic memory, which is events you have personally experienced, and semantic memory, which is knowledge about words, concepts, and facts.

items.stem: A teacher asks students to explain a new term in their own words instead of copying it ten times. Why is this a better study move?
options: Because visual encoding always beats all other encoding
Because semantic encoding is a deeper route into storage than visual or acoustic encoding
Because retrieval only works after sensory memory
Because long-term memory cannot store meaning
items.explanation: Explaining the term in your own words uses semantic encoding. The lesson fact says words encoded semantically are remembered better than words encoded visually or acoustically.

items.stem: A student believes memory works like a single container where information simply sits once it is seen. Which correction is best?
options: Memory is only retrieval, not storage
Memory is a set of processes, not a place
Memory begins in long-term storage and then moves backward
Everything is stored in sensory memory
items.explanation: Memory is a set of processes, not a place: information must be encoded, pass through sensory and short-term stages into long-term storage, and then be retrieved — and it can be lost at every step. That is why the “single container” picture is wrong.

items.stem: Leah learned a new phone number last week. Now she keeps recalling her old number instead of the new one. What is happening?
options: Proactive interference, because old information hinders recall of newly learned information
Retroactive interference, because newer information hinders recall of older information
Encoding failure, because she never stored either number
Storage decay, because all memories disappear after 24 hours
items.explanation: This is proactive interference: old information hinders the recall of newly learned information. The old number is getting in the way of the new one.

items.stem: Which statement best matches Ebbinghaus’s forgetting curve?
options: Forgetting is slow at first and then speeds up after a day.
Forgetting is fast at first, then the curve levels out.
Forgetting happens only when old memories are overwritten.
Forgetting is caused mainly by encoding failure, not storage decay.
items.explanation: The curve is steep early and then flattens: an average person loses about 50% after 20 minutes and 70% after 24 hours. That pattern shows storage decay is fastest at first, then levels out.

items.stem: A teacher wants reluctant students to start reading more. Which plan fits the lesson best?
options: Offer a pizza reward to get them started, since extrinsic motivation can help begin a behavior.
Avoid any outside reward because extrinsic motivation never affects behavior.
Tell students reading should only be done for personal satisfaction, even if they hate reading right now.
Assume rewards always strengthen motivation, so more prizes will keep increasing reading.
items.explanation: A reading-for-pizza program can work as an entry point for reluctant readers. Real motivation is often a mix of intrinsic and extrinsic factors, so an outside incentive can help start behavior even if it is not the whole story.

items.stem: Which statement best matches the lesson's view of motivation?
options: Motivation is usually a mix of intrinsic and extrinsic factors, and the mix can change over time.
People are either intrinsically motivated or extrinsically motivated, but not both.
Extrinsic motivation is always bad because it destroys all enjoyment.
Intrinsic motivation only matters when no reward is possible.
items.explanation: The lesson does not treat people as locked into one type. It says our motivations are often a mix of both intrinsic and extrinsic factors, and that mix can change over time.

items.stem: A student writes x = 4, then later writes x = x + 1. What happens to x?
options: x becomes 5
x stays 4 because 4 + 1 is not equal to 4
x stores the expression x + 1
Python treats = as equality and rejects the line
items.explanation: The right side is evaluated first, then the result is bound to x. That makes x = x + 1 an update, not a math sentence to judge true or false. The common mistake is to read = as equality; in Python here it is assignment.

items.stem: A program uses total and Total in two different lines. What should you assume?
options: They are the same variable because they look alike
Python ignores capitalization in names
They are different variables
Only one of them can be assigned a value
items.explanation: Variable names are case-sensitive, so total and Total are different names. The visual similarity is misleading; Python treats the capitalization as part of the name.

items.stem: A loop should keep asking for input until the user types `done`. Which change makes the loop able to stop?
options: Print `done` inside the body
Add a variable update that makes the condition false
Move the condition check to the middle of the body
Use `or` instead of `and`
items.explanation: A while loop must change something the condition depends on. If the body never moves the program toward a false condition, the loop can never stop.

items.stem: A for loop is written to visit each item in a list. Inside the loop, the code assigns a new value to the loop variable. What happens to the list?
options: The list changes because the loop variable points into the list.
Only the loop variable changes; the list stays the same.
The list is erased.
Every item in the list changes to the new value.
items.explanation: The loop variable is a fresh binding to each element in turn. Assigning to that variable does not edit the container. To change the list, index into the list directly.

items.stem: A variable is created inside a function. Where can it be accessed?
options: Anywhere in the program
Only inside that function call
Only after the function ends
Only if the function was defined with a name
items.explanation: A variable created inside a function has local scope. It cannot be accessed outside the function because it belongs to that call.

items.stem: A program has x = 7 outside any function. A function reads x without redefining it inside. What is true about x?
options: It has local scope inside the function
It has global scope and can be accessed anywhere in the program
It only exists after the function is called
It cannot be used after the line where it appears
items.explanation: A variable created outside any function has global scope and can be accessed anywhere in the program.

items.stem: You want to print every element in a list in order. What is the best tool?
options: A for loop
The index 0 only
The last index only
Square brackets by themselves
items.explanation: A for loop visits each element in order. Direct indexing gives one item, not the whole list.

items.stem: You need to store a shopping cart with item names and counts. Which structure fits best?
options: A list, because the items are labeled
A dictionary, because each item name can map to a count
A string, because it keeps the items in order
A list, because dictionaries use numeric positions
items.explanation: A dictionary is a good fit when data is naturally labeled. Item names work well as keys, and counts can be the values.

items.stem: Which piece is the base case in a recursive solution?
options: The first call the program ever makes.
The simplest input solved directly without another call.
Any call that uses a smaller input.
The line where the function name appears again.
items.explanation: The base case is the simplest input handled directly. It is the part that stops the chain of self-calls.

items.stem: Which description matches recursion best?
options: A function that solves a problem by reducing it to a simpler version of the same problem.
A function that uses only one call and no base case.
A function that always works on the same input size.
A function that stops because the call stack runs out first.
items.explanation: Recursion is problem reduction: the function calls itself on a smaller input until it reaches a base case.

items.stem: A learner says, 'I changed the class, so all existing objects should now have the new attribute value.' What is the better response?
options: Yes, all instances always share attribute values.
No, each instance has its own attributes, so one object's data can stay different.
Yes, because the first instance controls the rest.
No, because methods are the only part a class can have.
items.explanation: The corrective is simple: instances do not share their attribute values. The class is the blueprint, and the per-object data lives on each instance.

items.stem: Which pairing is correct?
options: Class = finished object; instance = blueprint
Class = blueprint; instance = object built from it
Class = method; instance = attribute
Class = index; instance = list element
items.explanation: A class is the blueprint, and each object built from it is an instance.

items.stem: A student says, 'Heuristics are sloppy, so I should always use an algorithm instead.' Which reply fits the course idea best?
options: Yes. Heuristics are never useful
No. Heuristics are general frameworks that fit situations with limited time or too much information
Yes. Algorithms always exist for every problem
No. Heuristics are just random guesses
items.explanation: That claim misses the point of heuristics. They are deliberate general frameworks used when the problem is too large, too messy, or too time-limited for a full step-by-step formula.

items.stem: A loop is meant to count down from 4 to 1. Which update belongs in the body so the loop eventually ends?
options: No update is needed if the condition is `n > 0`
items.explanation: A while loop must make progress toward false. If the condition is `n > 0`, subtracting 1 each pass moves `n` toward 0 and lets the loop stop.

items.stem: Which statement correctly describes the scope of a variable created inside a function?
options: It has global scope and can be used anywhere.
It exists only during the call that created it.
It is available only inside loops, not functions.
It becomes a list element automatically.
items.explanation: A variable created inside a function has local scope and cannot be accessed outside the function. If you need the value later, return it and save the result.

items.stem: Which statement best describes the relationship between a class and an instance?
options: An instance is the blueprint, and the class is one object made from it.
A class is the blueprint for creating objects, and objects made from it are instances.
A class and an instance are the same thing with different names.
An instance stores methods, while the class stores only data.
items.explanation: A class is the blueprint for creating objects. Individual objects created from a class are called instances, and each instance carries its own copy of the attributes while the methods are shared by every instance.

items.stem: A student writes 'Age: ' + 19 to label an age in a string. What happens?
options: It becomes 'Age: 19' because Python automatically turns 19 into text inside +.
It raises a TypeError because a str and an int cannot be added directly.
It becomes 'Age: 19' only if you first run int('19').
It raises a TypeError because Python always refuses to join any text with numbers.
items.explanation: 'Age: ' + 19 raises a TypeError because Python will not silently turn an int into a string inside a + with a str. Convert the number with str() first, or use formatting: 'Age: ' + str(19) builds 'Age: 19'.

options: 'not boiling', because the else branch runs when the if condition is false.
'boiling', because if-else takes exactly one branch and 100 is close to 100.
Nothing prints, because a false if condition skips both branches.
'boiling' and 'not boiling', because the condition is checked again in the middle of the body.
items.explanation: When temp is 100, temp > 100 is false, so the if body is skipped and the else body runs. An if-else statement takes one branch or the other, and the else clause is the one executed when the if condition is false.

items.stem: Suppose you assign `grades['Ava'] = 95` and then later assign `grades['Ava'] = 97`. What happens in the dictionary?
options: The old value is overwritten, so 'Ava' maps to 97.
Both values are kept because dictionaries allow duplicate keys.
The second assignment is ignored because keys are read-only.
The dictionary turns 'Ava' into a numeric index and stores both values.
items.explanation: Keys are unique; assigning to an existing key overwrites its previous value rather than adding a second entry.

items.stem: Look at this code: def greet(): print('hello') Which statement is true when Python reads the def line?
options: It only stores the function; the body runs when greet() is called by name.
It runs the function body immediately, because writing def greet(): executes the code inside right away.
It makes the variable greet local to the function body, so greet() cannot be called later.
It calls itself on a smaller input, because every def statement is recursive.
items.explanation: Defining a function only stores it. The body runs when the function is called by name, such as greet(). The def line itself does not execute the printed line.

items.stem: A function creates x inside its body and then returns. What happens if you try to use x outside that function without returning it?
options: You get a NameError, because x has local scope and exists only during that function call.
You can use x anywhere in the program, because every variable created in a function becomes global.
x is automatically printed after the function ends, because local variables persist forever.
Python turns x into a recursive base case, so the outer code can read it later.
items.explanation: Local variables exist only during the call that created them. To use a result outside, the function must return it and the caller must capture the returned value.

items.stem: You want two `Dog` objects to keep separate names. Which design matches the course idea of instances best?
options: Store the name on `Dog` itself so every dog instance can read the same value.
Create each dog with its own name attribute, because each instance carries its own copy of the attributes.
Put the name inside a method so it is shared by every dog and never changes.
Use `def Dog():` so the class body runs each time you need a new name.
items.explanation: A class is the blueprint, and each object built from it is an instance. Each instance carries its own copy of the attributes, so separate dogs should store separate names on their own objects.

items.stem: Which statement about a class is the best match for the lesson?
options: A class is the object that stores all data for every instance that will ever be created.
A class is a blueprint for creating objects, and the objects created from it are instances.
A class is a function that runs only when you call it with parentheses.
A class is the local scope of a program, where variables cannot be accessed outside.
items.explanation: A class is a blueprint for creating objects. Individual objects created from the class are instances.

items.stem: Which statement best matches the definition of a trade-off in this unit?
options: A trade-off is when you can have any outcome you want because choices are independent
A trade-off is an unavoidable choice among mutually exclusive alternatives when resources are limited
A trade-off is the same as paying explicit out-of-pocket costs
A trade-off occurs only when money changes hands
items.explanation: Trade-off is defined as: “an unavoidable choice among mutually exclusive alternatives when resources are limited.” It’s not limited to explicit spending. If options are mutually exclusive due to scarcity, choosing more of one means giving up some of another.

items.stem: A teacher asks students to compute opportunity cost. One student reports: “I listed my explicit costs (money paid) and treated that as the cost.” Which feedback most directly fixes the reasoning?
options: “That’s fine—opportunity cost equals explicit out-of-pocket spending.”
“Always ask what the next best use of the time or money was; that foregone value is the real cost.”
“Opportunity cost is only relevant when there is a shortage of goods, not for trade.”
“Comparative advantage never depends on opportunity cost—only on absolute advantage.”
items.explanation: This directly confronts the misconception that costs are only explicit out-of-pocket spending. The fix is to list both the money paid and the next-best forgone option, then compute opportunity cost using the value of the alternative, not just the money paid. Always ask what the next best use of the time or money was; that foregone value is the real cost.

items.stem: Suppose in a simple economy there are two producers. After specialization according to comparative advantage and trading, what must be true?
options: Each producer’s total output must rise, so both produce more than before even without trading.
Total output rises and both can consume beyond what they could produce alone.
Trade reduces output because specialization concentrates resources on fewer tasks.
Trade can only increase consumption if one producer has absolute advantage in both goods.
items.explanation: When each producer specializes according to comparative advantage and then trades, total output rises and both can consume beyond what they could produce alone. The key is differences in opportunity cost, not absolute skill. Trade can raise consumption even when one producer is better at everything.

items.stem: A student writes: “Necessities like insulin have inelastic demand because patients have no close substitute.” Is the reasoning aligned with the core elasticity determinants?
options: Yes. Necessities tend to have inelastic demand because consumers have few substitutes
No. Necessities tend to have elastic demand because demand responds strongly to price
No. Inelastic demand happens only because the demand curve has a steep slope
Yes, but only because the demand curve shifts when price changes
items.explanation: Yes—this matches both kernel ideas and the anchor. The course states: “Necessities tend to have inelastic demand because consumers have few substitutes,” and also “The availability of close substitutes is a primary determinant of elasticity.” That’s exactly the insulin logic in the worked example.

items.stem: Which statement best describes the difference between a movement along the demand curve and a shift of the demand curve?
options: A change in price causes a movement along the demand curve; a change in income or tastes shifts the curve
A change in income causes a movement along the demand curve; a change in price shifts the curve
Any change automatically shifts the curve because the law of demand never holds
Elasticity determines whether price causes movement or shifting
items.explanation: Demand curve meaning: it shows quantity willing and able at each price, holding other factors constant. The kernel fact says: “A change in price causes a movement along the demand curve, while a change in income or tastes shifts the curve.” Elasticity is about responsiveness to price changes, not whether the graph moves vs shifts.

items.stem: In a market, the equilibrium price is $10. The market price is currently $14. Which outcome best matches what happens next?
options: Buyers face a shortage, so sellers are pushed to raise the price toward $10.
There is a surplus, so the price is pushed downward toward $10.
The market is in equilibrium, so the price has no tendency to change.
A shortage forms, so the price is pushed upward even though the price is already above equilibrium.
items.explanation: When the price is above equilibrium, the market has a surplus. The core idea is: “a surplus pushes it down, and when the price is below equilibrium a shortage pushes it up.” Since $14 is above $10, the surplus pushes the price downward toward $10.

items.stem: Suppose the price of coffee increases. Which statement correctly describes what happens on the supply curve?
options: The higher coffee price shifts the whole supply curve right because price is a non-price factor.
The higher coffee price causes a movement along the supply curve (a higher quantity supplied).
The higher coffee price shifts the demand curve right because consumers buy more at higher prices.
The higher coffee price moves the supply curve because technology changes.
items.explanation: Use the rule: “A change in the good's own price moves along the supply curve, while a change in input costs or technology shifts the whole curve.” So when coffee’s own price rises, that is movement along the supply curve (higher quantity supplied).

items.stem: Coffee demand is downward sloping. When coffee prices fall, what happens to quantity demanded (holding other factors constant)?
options: Quantity demanded decreases because the demand curve slopes downward.
Quantity demanded increases; this is movement down along the demand curve.
The entire demand curve shifts because price changes cause shifts, not movements.
Quantity demanded is unchanged because equilibrium ensures no tendency for price to change.
items.explanation: Apply the law of demand: “Demand curves typically slope downward, reflecting the law of demand.” Also, “A change in price causes a movement along the demand curve.” So if coffee prices fall, consumers buy more—movement down along the demand curve.

items.stem: In the circular flow, households earn income and decide to save some of it by depositing it in a bank. Which option correctly describes what happens next in the flow?
options: The saved money disappears permanently because saving is not part of the circular flow.
The saved money leaks out as saving, but banks lend it to firms as investment, re-injecting spending.
Households keep the saved money as spending by immediately buying imports, which balances the flow.
Investment happens only if households spend their income directly, not if they save.
