items.explanation: Your choice should match the worked example: “Household saving deposited in a bank is lent to firms as investment, re-injecting money that had leaked out of the flow.” So saving is a leakage, but investment re-injects the spending back into the circular flow.

items.stem: Which statement correctly links the capital stock, gross investment, and depreciation?
options: The capital stock rises when depreciation rises
The capital stock rises through gross investment and falls through depreciation
The capital stock changes only when net investment is zero
The capital stock is the flow of investment per year
items.explanation: This is directly tied to the definition: capital stock "rises through gross investment and falls through depreciation." Also, capital stock is a LEVEL (total equipment/structures/tools), not the flow of investment per year.

items.stem: In the circular flow, households save money. Students who get confused sometimes say: “Saving disappears from the economy, so it reduces spending and lowers national income permanently.” What is the best correction in balance?
options: That is correct: saving disappears, so it can never come back as spending
Saving is not destroyed; in balance it re-enters the flow as investment, government spending, or exports
Saving enters the flow only as government spending, never as investment
Saving and investment are unrelated in the circular flow
items.explanation: Confronting the misconception: "Saving is not destroyed; in balance it re-enters the flow as investment, government spending, or exports." In the circular flow, saving is a leakage, but it must be matched by injections like investment, government spending, and exports when the economy is in balance.

items.stem: You’re asked to describe Earth’s layered systems in one correct sequence and include a state-of-matter detail. Which answer is best?
options: Crust → core → mantle; the asthenosphere is molten magma.
Crust → mantle → core; the mantle’s asthenosphere is solid rock that flows slowly by convection.
Mantle → crust → core; the core is solid rock throughout.
Core → mantle → crust; the mantle is entirely liquid.
items.explanation: This matches the reading: Earth is layered into a thin outer crust, a thick rocky mantle, and a metallic core. It also correctly includes the detail that the upper mantle asthenosphere is “solid rock” that “flows slowly by convection.”

items.stem: A student sees a mineral that looks bright red, but after scratching and testing it leaves a reddish-brown powder. Which property should the student use most to identify the mineral?
options: A) The surface color of the whole specimen
B) The color of the mineral’s powder (streak)
C) Whether the mineral is metallic-looking
D) How smooth the surface appears under light
items.explanation: Use streak: "Streak examines the color of a powdered mineral." In the hematite example, hematite can look silvery or red, but its streak is always reddish-brown—"the powder color gives it away when the specimen color does not."

items.stem: You compare two crystals with a Mohs hardness test. Mineral A scratches Mineral B, but Mineral C cannot be scratched by Mineral A. Which statement best matches Mohs hardness?
options: A) Hardness measures resistance to being scratched, on the Mohs scale
B) Hardness measures resistance to cracking (toughness)
C) Hardness describes luster (how light reflects from the surface)
D) Hardness is determined by the color of the mineral powder (streak)
items.explanation: Hardness on the Mohs scale is about scratch resistance. It does not directly measure toughness/cracking resistance—so you should not treat Mohs hardness as “toughness.”

items.stem: A student says, “I think the mineral is a sheet silicate because it breaks into thin flakes along smooth surfaces.” Which silicate linkage best matches that claim?
options: The silica tetrahedron is a flat triangle because it is often drawn as a triangle on paper.
Sheets of linked tetrahedra
Single chains of linked tetrahedra
A full 3‑D framework with no cleavage
items.explanation: Sheets form from tetrahedra linked together so there are preferred planes to break. In the worked examples, micas “form sheets that cleave into thin flakes,” which is the behavior you described.

items.stem: You identify a sedimentary clastic rock as made of pieces of preexisting weathered rock. Which term best matches this description?
options: Bioclastic (formed only from living shells)
Clastic (detrital) sedimentary rock
Igneous (formed by cooling magma)
Metamorphic rock (formed by heat and pressure)
items.explanation: Corrective target idea from the reading logic: “Detrital or clastic sedimentary rocks consist of preexisting sediment pieces that comes from weathered bedrock.” Those preexisting fragments become part of the deposit that later lithifies.

items.stem: Which statement correctly describes the motion at a transform boundary?
options: Two plates move toward each other and lithosphere is destroyed
Plates move away from each other and new lithosphere is created
Plates slide horizontally past each other in the horizontal plane
Plates float on a liquid magma layer that carries them
items.explanation: Use the boundary definition: “A transform boundary is where the lithospheric plates slide past each other in the horizontal plane.” The key idea is horizontal sliding past.

items.stem: A report says the volcano’s magma is “runny” and low in silica. Which hazard outcome is most likely?
options: Most likely hazard is a pyroclastic flow, because runny magma traps gas
Most likely hazard is gentle lava flows, because low-silica magma flows easily like syrup
Most likely hazard is mudflows caused by high-silica magma trapping gas
Most likely hazard is an earthquake, because plate motion controls volcanic explosions
items.explanation: Low-silica (basaltic) magma is low-viscosity and “flows easily like syrup,” which produces gentle eruptions and lava flows rather than the deadliest pyroclastic flows typical of explosive high-silica volcanoes.

items.stem: A cliff face develops cracks, and chunks loosen but stay put at the base. Which process best matches what’s happening right now?
options: Erosion, because the rock is breaking into sediment
Weathering, because bedrock is being broken down into sediment in place
Chemical weathering only, because cracks form
No process yet, because erosion must occur first
items.explanation: Weathering breaks rock down in place; erosion is the separate step that carries the broken material away. A rock can weather without eroding if nothing transports the pieces.

items.stem: A river carries sand and gravel away from where it formed. Which statement correctly describes erosion?
options: Erosion is a mechanical process that transports sediment, usually driven by water, wind, gravity, or ice
Erosion is chemical weathering that dissolves minerals into new substances
Erosion is the in-place breakdown of bedrock into sediment
Erosion changes minerals into new substances but does not transport them
items.explanation: Erosion is a mechanical process, usually driven by water, wind, gravity, or ice, which transports sediment. That’s the “transport away” step, not the in-place breakdown step.

items.stem: Which sequence correctly matches the worked example about a cliff and downstream fragments?
options: River erodes first; then frost wedging breaks bedrock
Frost wedging (mechanical) cracks the cliff; a river then erodes fragments downstream
Chemical weathering turns feldspar to clay before any fragments form
Erosion occurs before weathering because transport exposes fresh rock
items.explanation: The worked example states: “Frost wedging (mechanical) cracks a cliff into fragments; a river then erodes them downstream, where chemical weathering may turn feldspar to clay.” Frost wedging is weathering (mechanical) and the river’s transport is erosion.

items.stem: Which statement best captures the passage’s critique of guardians of the classics?
options: They made literature more accessible by keeping it in everyday life rather than in schools.
They pedestalized literature, taking life out of it and making it irrelevant to American life.
They argued that teachers should require music theory before listening to music.
They showed that only scholarly methods can generate enjoyment in reading.
items.explanation: The passage says the guardians of literature have “taken the life out of literature,” putting it “on a pedestal” and making it “an irrelevant aspect of American life.” This is a criticism of treating classics as objects to honor rather than texts to read.

items.stem: Which description best matches a while loop?
options: It runs its body as long as the loop condition stays true, checking again before each iteration.
It checks the condition once after the body finishes and then stops.
It always runs the body exactly one time.
It repeats only when the condition is false.
items.explanation: A while loop repeats based on a condition that is re-checked each time. That matches the reading: 'A while loop repeatedly runs its body as long as a loop condition stays true, re-checking the condition before each iteration.'

items.stem: A program has n = 4 and this loop: while n > 0: print(n). What change must be added so the loop eventually stops?
options: Add n = n - 1 somewhere in the body so the condition becomes false.
Add print(n) again so the condition gets checked more often.
Change while to for so the condition is ignored.
Put break at the top; then the loop will count down automatically.
items.explanation: The key is progress: “Every while loop must change something the condition depends on; a counter loop needs n = n - 1 (or += 1) inside the body so the condition eventually becomes false.” Printing does not affect the condition, and a for loop is a different structure entirely.

items.stem:
A program does this:

def make_message():
    msg = 'Hello'
    return msg

print(msg)

What is the best fix?
options: Remove the return statement because local variables are automatically visible outside.
Use msg = make_message() and then print(msg).
Rename msg to global_msg inside the function and print it outside.
Call make_message() twice so msg becomes global.
items.explanation: Local variables exist only during the call that created them; to use a result outside, the function must return it and the caller must capture the returned value. Here that means saving the returned string in msg before printing it.

items.stem: Which statement about classes and instances is correct?
options: Methods belong to the class, but each instance has its own attributes.
Attributes belong only to the class, and instances borrow them temporarily.
Instances are blueprints, and classes are the objects made from them.
Methods are copied separately into every instance, but attributes are shared.
items.explanation: A class defines a type of object with attributes and methods, and each instance carries its own copy of the attributes while the methods are shared by every instance. So the correct split is shared methods, per-instance data.

items.stem: A student wants to print each character in a string. Which idea matches the loop behavior?
options: A for loop can step through the string one character at a time.
A while loop must be used because strings cannot be iterated.
range() produces characters from the string.
The loop variable changes the string itself.
items.explanation: A for loop iterates over each element of a container, and a string is one of the container types here. Each pass binds the loop variable to one character.

items.stem: What does a for loop do with a list?
options: It jumps to the last item first.
It visits each element in order.
It changes every item to a string.
It starts counting indexes at 1.
items.explanation: A for loop can iterate through a list by visiting each element in order. That is the point of the loop: it handles the whole sequence one item at a time.

items.stem: A student says s[0] = 'H' should turn "cat" into "Hat". What is the best response?
options: That works only for strings that have at least four characters.
Strings are immutable, so you need to build a new string such as 'H' + s[1:].
Use s[0:1] = 'H' because slices can be reassigned.
Use str(s[0]) to convert the first character before assigning it.
items.explanation: Strings do not support changing one character in place. The fix is to create a new string, such as 'H' + s[1:], rather than trying to assign into s[0].

items.stem: A student writes code that opens a file and never closes it. Which fix matches Python practice?
options: Call read() again at the end.
Use a with statement so Python closes the file automatically.
Convert the file object to a string.
Use readline() instead of read().
items.explanation: Always close the file when done, or use a with statement so Python closes it automatically even if an error occurs. The issue is not which read method you choose; it is leaving the file open.

items.stem: You define `def greet():` and then do nothing else. What is true right after that line runs?
options: The body runs immediately
The function is only stored, not executed
A local variable is created outside the function
The base case has already been reached
items.explanation: Defining a function stores it. The body runs only when the function is called by name, such as `greet()`.

items.stem: You write Dog = 'friendly' before creating any dogs. What is the best reason this is a bad idea?
options: The class name should stay as a blueprint, and per-object data belongs on each instance.
A class cannot have methods if it has a name.
Instances cannot be created after a class is defined.
Attributes can only exist inside functions.
items.explanation: The class is the blueprint, not the finished object. Per-object data belongs on each instance, so storing dog-specific data on the class mixes up the blueprint with what gets built from it.

items.stem: Which result best matches `int(3.9)`?
options: 4, because int() rounds to the nearest whole number
3, because int() removes the fractional part
3.9, because int() leaves floats unchanged
An error, because int() only works on strings
items.explanation: int() converts a value to an integer and removes any fractional part, so int(3.9) is 3. Use it when you need the integer form of a numeric value, not when you want rounding.

items.stem: Which statement about if and else is correct?
options: if always runs both branches
else runs when the if condition is false
else only runs when the if condition is true
if and else both test the condition again
items.explanation: A conditional chooses which block of code to run based on whether a condition is true. An if statement runs its body only when the condition is true, and an else clause holds statements that run when the if condition is false. So else is the fallback branch.

items.stem: A while loop is meant to count down from 3 to 0, but it never ends. Which fix makes the condition eventually become false?
options: Add `n = n + 1` inside the body.
Remove the condition from the while loop.
Change the body so `n` is never mentioned again.
Move the update after the loop.
items.explanation: Every while loop must change something the condition depends on; a counter loop needs n = n - 1 (or += 1) inside the body so the condition eventually becomes false. In a countdown, increasing or decreasing the counter in the right direction is what lets the loop finish.

items.stem: A student thinks this loop will stop the instant `x` becomes 0 halfway through the body. What is the best correction?
options: The condition is checked only after the body finishes, so the rest of the pass still runs.
The condition is checked in the middle of the body every time a variable changes.
The body only runs once, so the condition never matters.
The loop variable is the same as the condition, so changing one changes the other immediately.
items.explanation: The loop expression is tested only at the top of each iteration; the rest of the current pass still runs before the condition is checked again. So if `x` becomes 0 in the middle of the body, the remaining statements in that pass still execute before the next check.

items.stem: A function computes a total inside its body, but the total is needed later in the program. What must happen?
options: The total will be visible everywhere after the function finishes.
The function must return the total, and the caller must capture it.
The total must be stored at index 0 of a list.
The function must be defined after the print statement.
items.explanation: Local variables exist only during the call that created them; to use a result outside, the function must return it and the caller must capture the returned value. If the value stays inside the function, code outside cannot read it.

items.stem: A program defines count inside a function and then tries to print count outside the function. What should you expect?
options: The variable is global, so it prints normally.
The variable is local to the function call and cannot be accessed outside.
The variable becomes the second item in a list.
The program changes the index of count to 0.
items.explanation: Local variables exist only during the call that created them; to use a result outside, the function must return it and the caller must capture the returned value. Here, count stays local unless it is returned and stored outside the function.

items.stem: A program stores a menu item and its price in a dictionary, then needs to print 'Tea costs $3'. Which approach best fits the course ideas?
options: Use a numeric index on the dictionary and concatenate the parts
Use the key for 'Tea' and format the text with the price value
Change the dictionary into a list first
Use slicing on the price value to get the dollar sign
items.explanation: Dictionaries store labeled data, so the key gives you the price value. String formatting lets programs combine text with values to produce readable output, which makes 'Tea costs $3' straightforward.

items.stem: You need every line from a file so you can loop over them one by one. Which method fits best?
options: `read()` because it gives one string containing the whole file
`readline()` because it returns the next single line
`readlines()` because it returns a list with every line of the file
`open()` because it returns the text directly
items.explanation: `readlines()` matches the job because it collects every line into a list. That makes it easy to loop through line by line.

items.stem: You want each pet in a game to have its own name, but all pets should share the same bark behavior. Which choice fits best?
options: Put the names on the class so every pet uses the same name.
Create a class for the pets, then make each pet an instance with its own name.
Store the names in one dictionary and use the dictionary as the pet.
Define the bark behavior only after you create the pet objects.
items.explanation: A class is the blueprint; you create instances from it (e.g. d = Dog()), and per-object data lives on each instance, not on the class. For this game, each pet object should carry its own name, while the bark method comes from the class.

items.stem: A function creates a total inside its body, then the code below the function definition tries to print that total directly. What is the problem?
options: The total is global, so the print works everywhere.
The total is local to the function call, so it is not available outside.
The function definition erased the print statement.
The value becomes a class attribute after the function ends.
items.explanation: Local variables exist only during the call that created them; to use a result outside, the function must return it and the caller must capture the returned value. If you need that total later, return it and store the returned value in a variable outside the function.

items.stem: A student reduces a system and gets the pair of equations x + y = 1 and x + y = 3. What should they conclude about the original system?
options: It is consistent with exactly two solutions.
It is inconsistent because the equations describe parallel lines that never meet.
It has infinitely many solutions because both equations involve the same variables.
The row reduction must have created a new answer set.
items.explanation: This is the inconsistency case: "A system like x + y = 1 and x + y = 3 is inconsistent: the equations describe parallel lines that never meet." So there is no solution to the original system.

items.stem: Which statement best explains why elimination is a legitimate method for solving a linear system?
options: Each elementary row operation is reversible and preserves the solution set.
Row operations always make the coefficients smaller.
The final matrix always has the same numbers as the original.
Only the first row matters in a system.
items.explanation: Each elementary row operation is reversible and preserves the solution set — that is exactly why elimination is a valid solving method. The point is not that the entries look nicer; it is that the solution set stays the same.

items.stem: A student says, “If a linear system has more than one solution, it must have a finite number of solutions.” What is the best response?
options: Correct, because solutions are counted one by one.
Incorrect; over the real numbers, two distinct solutions force infinitely many solutions.
Correct only when there are exactly three variables.
Incorrect only if the system has no pivots.
items.explanation: Over the real numbers, once a linear system has two distinct solutions it has infinitely many, because the whole line through the two solutions solves the system. So a finite count larger than one does not happen for linear systems.

items.stem: Which object can be a vector in a vector space even though it is not an arrow in 2D or 3D geometry?
options: Only a geometric arrow
Only a column of numbers
A polynomial, matrix, or function under the usual operations
Any object that can be drawn on a graph
items.explanation: The definition is algebraic, not pictorial: "Anything satisfying the vector-space axioms is a vector — polynomials, matrices, and functions included; geometry is one model, not the definition."

items.stem: What happens to the system x + y = 1 and x + y = 3?
options: It has exactly two solutions
It is inconsistent because the equations describe parallel lines that never meet
It has one solution at (1, 2)
It has infinitely many solutions because both equations involve the same variables
items.explanation: There is no shared point here. The corrective says: "A system like x + y = 1 and x + y = 3 is inconsistent: the equations describe parallel lines that never meet."

items.stem: A student row-reduces a matrix and says, 'The row operations changed the answers.' What is the best reply?
options: Yes, because row reduction changes the equations
No, because each elementary row operation is reversible and preserves the solution set
Yes, unless the matrix is already in echelon form
No, because only scaling rows is reversible
items.explanation: That objection is exactly what elimination avoids: "Each elementary row operation is reversible and preserves the solution set — that is exactly why elimination is a valid solving method."

items.stem: In an echelon form matrix, which columns are pivot columns?
options: The columns with the largest entries
The columns that appear first in the original system
The columns determined by echelon structure during elimination
The columns with nonzero entries in every row
items.explanation: Pivot columns are structural, not numerical. The rule is: "Pivot positions are determined by echelon structure during elimination, not by the size of the entries."

items.stem: You row-reduce an augmented matrix and replace one row by itself plus 3 times another row. Why is the new system still equivalent to the old one?
options: Because row operations are designed to make numbers smaller.
Because elementary row operations are reversible and preserve the solution set.
Because only row swaps preserve solutions.
Because the operation keeps the pivot columns unchanged.
items.explanation: A row operation is valid here because it does not invent or destroy solutions. Each elementary row operation is reversible and preserves the solution set — that is exactly why elimination is a valid solving method.

items.stem: During elimination, a pivot is the first nonzero entry in a row. Which feature determines pivot positions?
options: The size of the entries in the columns.
Which columns contain the most nonzero numbers.
The echelon structure created during elimination.
The original order of the variables only.
items.explanation: Look at the elimination pattern, not the magnitudes. Pivot positions are determined by echelon structure during elimination, not by the size of the entries.

items.stem: Which system is inconsistent?
options: x+y=1 and x+y=3
x+y=1 and 2x+2y=2
x+y=1 and y=1-x
x+y=1 and x-y=0
items.explanation: Two equations that force the same left-hand side to equal different constants cannot both be true. A system like x + y = 1 and x + y = 3 is inconsistent: the equations describe parallel lines that never meet.

items.stem: Suppose a linear system over the real numbers has two distinct solutions. What must be true?
options: It has exactly two solutions.
It has infinitely many solutions.
It has no solution because two solutions is impossible.
It has only one solution after row reduction.
items.explanation: A linear system cannot stop at two solutions. Over the real numbers, once a linear system has two distinct solutions it has infinitely many, because the whole line through the two solutions solves the system.

items.stem: If A and B are invertible, which expression equals the inverse of AB?
options: A⁻¹B⁻¹
B⁻¹A⁻¹
(A⁻¹)(B⁻¹) in the same order as AB
AB⁻¹
items.explanation: Undo the composition in reverse: "Undoing two composed operations requires reversing their order: (AB)⁻¹ = B⁻¹A⁻¹." The order is the whole point; copying the original order gives the wrong matrix.

items.stem: Suppose A is invertible. Which statement about the system Ax = b is correct for every right-hand side b?
options: It has at most one solution.
It has a unique solution x = A⁻¹b.
It has a solution only when b = 0.
It has infinitely many solutions for every b.
items.explanation: Because A is invertible, multiplication by A can be undone. That is why the system Ax = b has the unique solution x = A⁻¹b for every right-hand side b.

items.stem: Let A=[[1,2],[3,4]] and B=[[0,1],[1,0]]. Which description of AB is correct?
options: AB is formed by multiplying corresponding entries of A and B.
AB combines rows of A with columns of B via dot products.
AB is always equal to BA for square matrices.
AB is undefined because both matrices are 2×2.
items.explanation: The entry formula is the point: the product AB combines rows of A with columns of B via dot products; the entrywise product is a different, rarely used operation.

items.stem: A square matrix C is nonzero but has two equal rows. What must be true?
options: C has an inverse because it is nonzero.
C has a nonzero determinant because it is square.
C has zero determinant and no inverse.
C must be the zero matrix.
items.explanation: Two equal rows force a zero determinant, so the matrix is nonzero yet not invertible. A square matrix with a zero determinant — for example one with two equal rows — is nonzero yet has no inverse.

items.stem: If A and B are invertible, what is the inverse of AB?
options: AB itself
items.explanation: Undoing two composed operations requires reversing their order: (AB)^-1 = B^-1A^-1. The order flips because the second operation must be undone first.

items.stem: Which subset of R^3 is definitely a subspace?
options: The plane x + y + z = 1
The line through (1, 0, 0) and (1, 1, 0)
The span of (2, 1, 0) and (4, 2, 0)
The set of points with x > 0
items.explanation: A subspace must contain the zero vector and be closed under addition and scalar multiplication. The plane x + y + z = 1 and the line through (1,0,0) and (1,1,0) both fail because they do not pass through the origin; in fact, "Only lines and planes through the origin are subspaces; others miss the zero vector and are not closed under scaling." The span of two vectors is always a subspace, so option 3 is correct.

items.stem: A linear system over the real numbers has exactly two distinct solutions. What must be true?
options: The system is inconsistent
The system has exactly two solutions
The system has infinitely many solutions
The system must have no free variables
items.explanation: Once you have two different real solutions to a linear system, the whole line through them also satisfies the system. So you do not stop at two. Use this corrective as stated: "Over the real numbers, once a linear system has two distinct solutions it has infinitely many, because the whole line through the two solutions solves the system."

items.stem: Which statement about determinants is true?
options: det(A + B) = det(A) + det(B) for all square matrices
The determinant measures entry size more than anything else
det(AB) = det(A)det(B)
A matrix with large entries cannot have determinant zero
items.explanation: The product rule is the reliable one here. Determinants do not add the way scalars do, and large entries do not force a nonzero determinant. The corrective combines both ideas: "The determinant is multiplicative, not additive: det(AB) = det(A)det(B), but det(A + B) usually differs from det(A) + det(B)."

items.stem: In R^3, what can you conclude about any set of 4 vectors?
options: It is automatically independent because there are many directions in R^3.
It may be independent if no vector is zero.
It is automatically dependent.
It spans R^3 automatically.
items.explanation: Any set of more than 3 vectors in R^3 must be dependent. The key fact is exactly this: “Any set of more than n vectors in R^n is automatically dependent; adding vectors can only create dependence, never remove it.”

items.stem: Which statement is true about bases of R^2?
options: R^2 has only one basis, the standard basis.
R^2 has infinitely many bases, but every basis has 2 vectors.
R^2 has infinitely many bases, and every basis has 3 vectors.
R^2 has exactly two bases, one for each coordinate axis.
items.explanation: A basis is not unique. For R^2, the standard basis is one basis, but so is {(1,1),(1,-1)}. That is why we say, “Spaces have infinitely many bases ... only the SIZE of a basis is fixed.”

items.stem: Which set is a subspace of R^3?
options: {(x,y,1) : x,y in R}
{(x,y,0) : x,y in R}
items.explanation: The set {(x,y,0)} contains the zero vector and is closed under addition and scaling, so it is a subspace. The other options fail the subspace tests. In particular, “Only lines and planes through the origin are subspaces; others miss the zero vector and are not closed under scaling.”

items.stem: Suppose v and w are parallel nonzero vectors in R^3. What is span{v,w}?
options: A plane, because there are two vectors.
All of R^3, because two vectors always span a 3D space.
A line through the origin.
A single point not necessarily at the origin.
items.explanation: Parallel vectors do not give two independent directions. So the span collapses to one direction: a line through the origin. As the corrective states, “If the two vectors are parallel (or one is zero), their span collapses to a line or a point; the span's dimension depends on independence.”

items.stem: A matrix A has columns that span exactly the vectors b for which Ax = b can be solved. What is that span called?
options: Null space
Column space
Row space
Pivot set
items.explanation: That is the column space: by definition it is the span of the columns of A, and it consists of exactly those b for which Ax = b is consistent.

items.stem: A 5-by-2 matrix has two dependent columns. What can you say about its rank?
options: It must be 5
It is at most 2 and may be smaller
It must be 2
It is always 0
items.explanation: Rank cannot exceed the smaller dimension, and dependence lowers it further. So the correct bound is: "Rank never exceeds the smaller of the row and column counts, and dependence among columns lowers it further."

items.stem: For matrix multiplication, which statement is correct?
options: AB is computed entrywise, like addition
AB and BA are always equal
The (i,j) entry of AB is a dot product of row i of A with column j of B
Matrix multiplication is defined only for square matrices
items.explanation: The product is built from row-column dot products. That is why the corrective says: "The product AB combines rows of A with columns of B via dot products; the entrywise product is a different, rarely used operation."

items.stem: A student checks the system x + y = 1 and x + y = 3 and says it has one solution because there are two equations. What is the best correction?
options: It has exactly two solutions, one from each equation.
It is inconsistent: the equations describe parallel lines that never meet.
It has infinitely many solutions because both equations are linear.
It has no solution only if the coefficients are different.
items.explanation: The right correction is that this system is inconsistent. In the course wording, “A system like x + y = 1 and x + y = 3 is inconsistent: the equations describe parallel lines that never meet.”

items.stem: Which statement correctly describes the product AB?
options: Compute A and B entry-by-entry, then multiply matching entries.
AB is defined whenever A and B have the same number of rows.
The (i, j) entry of AB is the dot product of row i of A with column j of B.
AB is always the same size as A and B combined.
items.explanation: Remember the structure of matrix multiplication: the product AB combines rows of A with columns of B via dot products; the entrywise product is a different, rarely used operation. That is why the dimensions must match in the row-column way, not by matching entries.

items.stem: Which set is definitely a vector space under the usual operations?
options: The set of all arrows drawn in the plane
The set of all polynomials
The set of all points on the line y = 2
The set of all circles in the plane
items.explanation: Anything satisfying the vector-space axioms is a vector — polynomials, matrices, and functions included; geometry is one model, not the definition. So the polynomial set is a standard example, even though it is not made of arrows.

items.stem: Which subset of R^3 is a subspace?
options: A line not through the origin
A plane not through the origin
A line through the origin
A sphere centered at the origin
items.explanation: A subset must contain the zero vector and be closed under addition and scalar multiplication; a line not through the origin fails all three. Only lines and planes through the origin are subspaces; others miss the zero vector and are not closed under scaling.

items.stem: Which statement correctly identifies an eigenvector of a square matrix A?
options: Any vector x, including x = 0, such that Ax = λx
A nonzero vector x such that Ax is a scalar multiple of x
Any vector x such that Ax = 0
Any vector x such that det(A − xI) = 0
items.explanation: The definition requires a **nonzero** vector, and the image must be a scalar multiple of the same vector: Ax = λx. The zero vector does satisfy A0 = λ0 trivially, but that “identifies nothing about the matrix,” so it is not an eigenvector.

items.stem: If A and B are invertible, what is (AB)⁻¹?
options: A⁻¹B⁻¹
B⁻¹A⁻¹
(A⁻¹B⁻¹)⁻¹
AB
items.explanation: Undoing two composed operations requires reversing their order: (AB)⁻¹ = B⁻¹A⁻¹. Think of composition first, inversion last; the reverse order is what makes the product multiply back to I.

items.stem: Which equation is the right starting point for finding eigenvalues of a square matrix A?
options: Ax = λx for any vector x
det(A − λI) = 0
A − λI = 0
Ax = 0 only
items.explanation: det(A − λI) = 0 is the starting point because eigenvalues are roots of the characteristic polynomial det(A − λI). The other choices are either incomplete or not the eigenvalue test.

items.stem: A least-squares model gives fitted values Ax̂ that do not equal b. Which interpretation is right?
options: This means the method failed, because least squares always solves Ax=b exactly.
It minimizes the residual; the fitted values Ax̂ generally differ from b — being closest is not being equal.
It shows A has no column space.
It proves x̂ is not unique in every case.
items.explanation: It minimizes the residual; the fitted values Ax̂ generally differ from b — being closest is not being equal. In an inconsistent system, that difference is the whole point of least squares.

items.stem: A data set has a least-squares line that misses every observed point. What is the correct conclusion?
options: Impossible; a best-fit line must pass through at least one point.
That line is not a least-squares line.
The least-squares line minimizes the sum of squared vertical gaps and can miss every single data point.
The line must be horizontal.
items.explanation: The least-squares line minimizes the sum of squared vertical gaps and can miss every single data point. Best fit is about minimizing total squared error, not forcing the line through the data.

items.stem: Which set is definitely a subspace of R^3?
options: A plane shifted away from the origin.
Any line in R^3.
The set {(x,y,1): x,y∈R}.
A plane through the origin.
items.explanation: Only lines and planes through the origin are subspaces; others miss the zero vector and are not closed under scaling. The origin condition is not optional.

items.stem: A student claims: "7 / 2 will give 3 because 7 and 2 are whole numbers." Which expression correctly computes the whole-number quotient you’d expect from integer division?
options: floor(7 / 2)
items.explanation: In Python 3 the / operator always returns a float, so 7 / 2 is 3.5; use // for whole-number floor division, which gives 3.

items.stem: A student tries: 'Age: ' + 19 and gets an error. What is the best fix using the ideas from this week?
options: 'Age: ' + str(19)
'Age: ' + int(19)
'Age: ' + (19 as str)
items.explanation: Convert the number with str() before joining it to text, or use formatting; Python will not silently turn an int into a string inside a + with a str. So 'Age: ' + str(19) builds 'Age: 19'.

items.stem:
A student writes this:

n = 3
while n > 1:
    n = n - 1
    print(n)

How many times does print(n) run?
options: 2 times
3 times
1 time
It prints forever
items.explanation: It prints 3 times. The loop expression is checked only at the top of each iteration; the rest of the current pass still runs before the condition is checked again. So the body runs while n > 1 is true at the top, then n is reduced and printed during that pass. After the third pass, the next top-of-iteration check sees n is no longer > 1 and the loop ends.

items.stem: Which while-loop condition is written correctly to check whether age is between 13 and 19 (exclusive)?
options: age > 13 and < 19
age > 13 and age < 19
age = 13 and age = 19
items.explanation: Correct: age > 13 and age < 19. Each comparison needs its own operands joined by and. The bare < 19 has nothing on its left, so age > 13 and < 19 is not valid.

items.stem: A student says: “I can write if score = 100: because Python will compare score to 100 for me.” Which correction is correct?
options: Replace = with ==: if score == 100:
Keep = but add parentheses: if (score = 100):
Use assignment with no change: if score = 100 then run the body
Write: if score equals 100: (with the word equals)
items.explanation: The correction is: comparison uses == (two equals signs); a single = is assignment. A condition that asks whether two values are equal must be written score == 100.

items.stem: You want a condition that is true only when age is between 14 and 18 inclusive. Which condition is properly formed in Python?
options: if age > 13 and < 19:
if age > 13 and age < 19:
if < 19 and age > 13:
if age > 13 or age < 19:
items.explanation: Each comparison needs its own operands joined by and: age > 13 and age < 19. The bare < 19 has nothing on its left.

items.stem:
Consider this code:

nums = [3, 1, 4]
count = 0
for n in nums:
    if n == 4:
        count = count + 1

What is the final value of count?
items.explanation: The for loop iterates over each element of the list nums. The if condition uses == to compare n to 4; only n equals 4 once (the element 4), so count increases once.

items.stem:
Misconception check: A student writes:

def square(n):
    inside = n * n

square(5)
print(inside)

They say, "A variable defined inside a function should be accessible outside the function." What is the most likely result?
options: It prints 25
It prints 5
It raises a NameError
It raises a TypeError
items.explanation: “Local variables exist only during the call that created them; to use a result outside, the function must return it and the caller must capture the returned value.” Since inside is local to square(5), print(inside) causes a NameError.

items.stem: Consider: info = {'student': {'name': 'Ava', 'score': 95}}. What is the result of info['student']['score'] ?
options: The string 'Ava'
The number 95
A KeyError because 'score' is nested
A TypeError because dictionaries can’t be nested
items.explanation: Because the value stored at info['student'] is itself a dictionary, you can look up the nested key 'score' using bracket key lookup: info['student']['score'] returns 95.

items.stem:
You have:

grades = {'Ava': 95, 'Ben': 88}

A student tries: grades[0]

What is the best explanation of what should happen?

(Consider what dictionaries are keyed by.)
options: It returns the value stored at the first item (95)
It raises an error because dictionaries are accessed by key, not position
It returns 'Ava' because index 0 maps to the first key
It returns a list of values because dictionaries store ordered items
items.explanation: Dictionaries are accessed by key, not position; use d['name'] to get the value stored under the key 'name', not d[0].

items.stem: You’re given the recursive rule: f(n) calls f(n - 1) until n becomes 0, and you’re told f(0) is directly returned as 1. What value is returned by f(3) assuming each call returns n * (result of f(n - 1))?
items.explanation: This recursion shrinks toward the base case because each call uses n - 1, and it stops when n is 0 (the base case is solved directly). Trace: f(3)=3*f(2), f(2)=2*f(1), f(1)=1*f(0), and f(0)=1, so f(3)=3*2*1=6.

items.stem: Trace the first three calls for factorial(2). You only need to list the sequence of inputs passed to factorial.
options: factorial(2) → factorial(1) → factorial(0)
factorial(2) → factorial(3) → factorial(4)
factorial(2) → factorial(0) → factorial(1)
factorial(2) → factorial(1) → factorial(1)
items.explanation: Using the worked example rule: factorial(n)=1 when n is 0 (base case), otherwise factorial(n)=n*factorial(n-1), shrinking n each call. So factorial(2) calls factorial(1), which calls factorial(0).

items.stem: Which recursive function structure matches the core requirement for termination?
options: Always call the function on the same input size, and never include a base case
Always call the function on a smaller input, but stop only when the call stack overflows
Include a base case for the simplest input, and otherwise call itself on a smaller input
Omit the base case and rely on Python to stop recursion when it reaches the target output
items.explanation: Correct pattern: “Every recursion needs a base case — a simplest input solved directly without another call — so the chain of self-calls eventually stops,” and the recursive call must reduce the problem (smaller input).

items.stem: Which example best shows when a model becomes misleading?
options: Using perfect-competition predictions in a market dominated by one firm.
Using a simplified model to focus on the features relevant to a question.
Leaving out details that do not matter for the question.
Choosing assumptions that are close enough for the question at hand.
items.explanation: Perfect-competition predictions can mislead when one firm dominates the market because the key assumption of perfect competition breaks. The other choices describe how models are supposed to work when they are useful.

items.stem: A market is dominated by one firm, but a student applies perfect-competition predictions anyway. What is the best diagnosis?
options: The model is always true, so the prediction should still hold
The model is being used where its assumptions clearly fail
The student needs more math, not a different model
The market must be efficient by definition
items.explanation: A model is a tool whose conclusions hold only while its assumptions approximately hold. The text also says models are useful when their assumptions are close enough for the question at hand, and misleading when a key assumption breaks; monopoly-like dominance is exactly the kind of case that can break the assumption.

items.stem: Which statement best fits an economic model?
options: A literal copy of the real world
A simplified representation of reality that keeps the features relevant to a question and discards the rest
A claim that every assumption is exactly true
A list of facts with no assumptions
items.explanation: Models simplify on purpose. The anchor quote says they are "a simplified representation of reality that keeps the features relevant to a question and discards the rest." That is why they can help for one question and mislead for another.

items.stem: A factory can produce either more cars or more bikes with its fixed resources. If it produces more cars, what must happen to bikes?
options: Bikes can also rise because of better planning
Bikes must fall because the scarce resource is being used on cars
Nothing, because trade-offs are only about prices
Bikes fall only if the cars are expensive
items.explanation: This is the core trade-off logic: limited resources create feasible choices, and more of one good means less of another. The corrective is to identify the scarce resource(s) and the alternatives that cannot simultaneously be achieved; a PPF makes that sacrifice visible.

items.stem: Two roommates split chores. Maya can cook dinner faster than Luis, and Luis can clean the kitchen faster than Maya. Which assignment best uses comparative advantage?
options: Maya should do both chores because she is faster at both time-saving tasks.
Maya should cook dinner and Luis should clean the kitchen.
Luis should cook dinner and Maya should clean the kitchen.
They should each do half of both chores so the work is perfectly equal.
items.explanation: Compare opportunity costs, not absolute skill; specialize where your opportunity cost is lowest. Here Maya cooks and Luis cleans, so each does the task with the lower opportunity cost. That is exactly the logic behind comparative advantage.

items.stem: A student says, ‘I bought the concert ticket, so going to the concert is free tonight.’ What is the best response?
options: Yes, it is free because the ticket is already paid for.
No, the opportunity cost includes the wage and study time given up to attend.
Only the travel cost counts; time does not matter.
It is free unless the concert sells out.
items.explanation: Always ask what the next best use of the time or money was; that foregone value is the real cost. A ‘free’ ticket still uses scarce time, so the concert has an opportunity cost even after the ticket is bought.

items.stem: Which statement best captures why trade can make both parties better off?
options: Trade helps only when one person is better at everything.
Trade works because each person specializes according to comparative advantage and then trades.
Trade always increases total output even if both sides produce the same mix as before.
Trade eliminates scarcity, so no one faces trade-offs anymore.
items.explanation: When each producer specializes according to comparative advantage and then trades, total output rises. That extra output is what makes it possible for both sides to consume beyond what they could produce alone.

items.stem: Which example best shows opportunity cost, not just price?
options: A pencil costs $1 at the store.
A student spends an hour studying instead of working a paid shift.
A bus ride has a printed fare on the ticket.
A shirt is on sale for 20% off.
items.explanation: The opportunity cost of a choice is the value of the next best alternative that must be given up. Studying instead of the paid shift captures that foregone value directly, while the other options only list prices.

items.stem: Maya has a fixed budget for Friday night. If she buys one more concert ticket, what must happen according to the consumer-choice model?
options: She must buy fewer meals out, because the affordable bundle changes when one good rises.
She can always buy the same number of meals out if she wants the ticket enough.
Her utility rises with no tradeoff because the ticket is a better experience.
The opportunity cost is zero because she already paid for the budget.
items.explanation: This is the tradeoff idea in the reading: with a fixed budget, buying more concert tickets means buying fewer meals out. At the optimal choice, utility cannot be increased without exceeding the budget, so more of one good requires less of another.

items.stem: A student says, “The opportunity cost of attending the free campus event is zero because I paid nothing.” What is the best response?
options: Correct; free means no cost at all.
Incorrect; always ask what the next best use of the time or money was; that foregone value is the real cost.
Correct if the event is enjoyable.
Incorrect only if there was a ticket price.
items.explanation: That mixes up price with cost. The concept says the opportunity cost of a choice is the value of the next best alternative that must be given up, and a decision that looks free still has an opportunity cost if it uses time or resources that could have produced something else. Always ask what the next best use of the time or money was; that foregone value is the real cost.

items.stem: A clinic raises the price of a drug that patients need daily. There are no close substitutes. Which outcome best describes the demand for the drug?
options: Elastic, because necessities always have many substitutes
Inelastic, because patients have few substitutes
Elastic, because the price is high
Unit elastic, because all medical goods are unit elastic
items.explanation: In this situation the best choice is **Inelastic, because patients have few substitutes**. The kernel fact says necessities tend to have inelastic demand because consumers have few substitutes, and the insulin example points the same way: insulin has highly inelastic demand because patients have no close substitute.

items.stem: On a straight-line demand curve, what happens to elasticity as you move from the top-left toward the bottom-right?
options: It stays constant because the slope is constant
It rises because the slope gets steeper
It falls because price changes are smaller at the bottom-right
It stays constant because percentage changes do not matter
items.explanation: It **falls because price changes are smaller at the bottom-right** is the best answer. More important, the lesson’s corrective is explicit: **Elasticity compares percentage changes, so it varies along a straight-line demand curve even though the slope is constant.** That is why constant slope does not mean constant elasticity.

items.stem: A student says, “Elastic demand means there is a lot of demand.” Which response best fixes the mistake?
options: Yes; elastic and high demand mean the same thing
No; elasticity measures responsiveness to price changes, not the level of demand
Yes; elastic demand always means the good is expensive
No; elasticity only matters for necessities
items.explanation: No: **elasticity (responsiveness to price changes)** is not the same as the level of demand. A good can have the same quantity demanded as another good and still have a different elasticity depending on slope and substitutes/time horizons. So the student’s statement confuses responsiveness with how much people buy.

items.stem: Coffee prices fall, and consumers buy more coffee. Which description is correct?
options: This is a shift in demand because quantity demanded changed
This is a movement along the demand curve caused by a change in price
This is a shift in supply because price changed
This proves demand is elastic
items.explanation: Because the price changed, this is **a movement along the demand curve**. The demand-curve preview says a change in price causes a movement along the demand curve, while changes in income or tastes shift the curve. The coffee example uses exactly that logic: when coffee prices fall, consumers buy more coffee, moving down the demand curve.

items.stem: Coffee prices fall from $8 to $6. According to the law of demand, what happens to quantity demanded?
options: It increases, moving down the demand curve.
It decreases, shifting the demand curve left.
It stays the same because demand curves cannot move.
It increases because tastes changed.
items.explanation: This is a price change, so it causes a movement along the demand curve. The coffee example says that when coffee prices fall, consumers buy more coffee, moving down the demand curve.

items.stem: A store notices that more people buy coffee after the price falls, while income and tastes stay the same. Which description is best?
options: A shift of the demand curve caused by income.
A movement along the demand curve caused by price.
A change in the law of demand caused by tastes.
No change in quantity demanded.
items.explanation: Because price changed and other factors were held constant, the correct description is movement along the demand curve. The anchor quote is direct: “A change in price causes a movement along the demand curve.”

items.stem: A student says, “An economic model is literally true, so I should use it even when its assumptions clearly fail.” What is the best response?
options: Yes, because models are exact copies of reality.
No; a model is a tool whose conclusions hold only while its assumptions approximately hold.
Yes, because assumptions do not matter if the model is simple.
No; models should never be used for any market.
items.explanation: That belief is the misconception we want to avoid. A model is a tool whose conclusions hold only while its assumptions approximately hold, and the chapter also says models are useful when their assumptions are close enough for the question at hand.

items.stem: A market is dominated by one firm, but a student uses perfect-competition predictions as if nothing matters. What is the problem?
options: The student is applying a model where a key assumption breaks.
The student is correctly using the law of demand.
The student is describing a movement along the demand curve.
The student is proving that demand curves slope upward.
items.explanation: Perfect-competition predictions mislead in a market dominated by one firm. That is exactly what it means for a model to stop working well: a key assumption breaks, so the model’s conclusions are not reliable there.

items.stem: Which change would shift the demand curve rather than cause movement along it?
options: A change in the good’s own price.
A change in income.
A change from $6 to $5 coffee.
A lower quantity purchased because the price fell.
items.explanation: Income is one of the factors held constant when we read a demand curve, so a change in income shifts the curve. A price change, by contrast, causes movement along the demand curve.

items.stem: Which example is the best use of the supply model?
options: Using perfect competition to predict behavior in a market dominated by one firm
Using the supply curve to describe a market where its assumptions are close enough for the question at hand
Treating every model as literally true in every market
Ignoring assumptions because models are always exact
items.explanation: The point of a model is that it is a tool, not literal reality. A model is useful when its assumptions are close enough for the question at hand, and misleading when a key assumption breaks.

items.stem: Why can a perfect-competition model mislead in a market dominated by one firm?
options: Because all models are useless in business
Because the model is a tool whose conclusions hold only while its assumptions approximately hold
Because higher prices no longer affect quantity supplied
Because supply curves never slope upward in such markets
items.explanation: Perfect competition is an assumption built into the model. A model is a tool whose conclusions hold only while its assumptions approximately hold, so if a key assumption breaks, the result can mislead.

items.stem: A local market has the same amount buyers want to purchase and sellers want to sell. What is the best description of that price?
options: It is equilibrium because quantity demanded equals quantity supplied.
It is a shortage because buyers still purchase the good.
It is a surplus because sellers are active in the market.
It must be a price ceiling.
items.explanation: That is market equilibrium: it is the price where the quantity demanded by buyers equals the quantity supplied by sellers.

items.stem: Coffee prices fall. What happens to quantity demanded?
options: It increases, which is a movement along the demand curve.
It decreases, which shifts the whole demand curve left.
It increases, which shifts the whole demand curve right.
It does not change because demand curves are vertical.
items.explanation: When price changes, consumers move along the demand curve. The reading’s coffee example says that when coffee prices fall, consumers buy more coffee, moving down the demand curve.

items.stem: The price of coffee rises, and coffee growers offer more beans. Later, a frost kills plants. Which statement is correct?
options: Both events shift the supply curve.
The price rise shifts supply, and the frost is a movement along the supply curve.
The price rise is a movement along the supply curve, and the frost shifts the supply curve.
Both events are movements along the supply curve.
items.explanation: A price change moves along the supply curve; a non-price factor like frost shifts the whole curve. The kernel says, “A change in the good's own price moves along the curve; only non-price factors shift the curve.”

items.stem: A city has one seller of a product with no close substitutes, and barriers to entry keep competitors out. What is the best conclusion?
options: The market is in equilibrium because there is only one seller.
The market is a monopoly, and the seller has market power.
The seller is a price taker because buyers can always force the price down to cost.
The market must produce the same output as a competitive market.
items.explanation: The defining facts point to a monopoly: "a market with a single seller of a product that has no close substitutes, protected by barriers to entry." That structure gives market power, not price-taking behavior.

items.stem: Which outcome best follows from a monopoly producing less and charging more than a competitive market?
options: A larger surplus because fewer units are sold.
Deadweight loss because some mutually beneficial trades do not happen.
No effect on efficiency because only the price changes.
An automatic shortage that always lasts forever.
items.explanation: Because monopoly output is lower and price is higher than in competition, some trades that would have been worthwhile do not occur. That is why the reading states that "a monopoly creates deadweight loss."

items.stem: A student says, 'Market equilibrium means nothing is happening in the market.' Which reply is best?
options: Yes, equilibrium is a frozen market with no buying or selling.
No, equilibrium is a balance of ongoing opposing pressures, not a frozen market.
Yes, because quantity demanded and quantity supplied both become zero.
No, equilibrium only means the government has set the price.
items.explanation: Not so: equilibrium is when "the opposing pressures of demand and supply are balanced and there is no tendency for the price to change." That is a stable price, not a frozen market.

items.stem: Suppose a price is set above equilibrium in a market. What happens next if nothing blocks adjustment?
options: A shortage pushes the price up further.
A surplus pushes the price down.
The market becomes a monopoly.
The price stays above equilibrium forever.
items.explanation: Above equilibrium, quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded, so a surplus appears. As the reading says, "a surplus pushes it down"; the price falls toward equilibrium.

items.stem: Which set lists only leakages from the circular flow of income?
options: Investment, government spending, exports
Saving, taxes, imports
Saving, investment, exports
Taxes, government spending, imports
items.explanation: Leakages are the outflows: saving, taxes, and spending on imports. The other choices mix leakages with injections.

items.stem: If total leakages equal total injections, what happens to national income?
options: It must rise.
It must fall.
It neither rises nor falls.
It becomes zero.
items.explanation: When total leakages equal total injections, the circular flow is in balance and national income neither rises nor falls.

items.stem: Which statement best describes an economic model?
options: A literal copy of reality that is always true.
A simplified representation of reality that keeps the features relevant to a question and discards the rest.
A theory that works only in perfect competition.
A graph that is useful even when its assumptions fail completely.
items.explanation: A model is built to leave out what is not relevant. As the reading says, it is 'a simplified representation of reality that keeps the features relevant to a question and discards the rest.'

items.stem: A supply-and-demand model is used in a market dominated by one firm, and the predictions do not fit well. What is the best conclusion?
options: The model is always wrong in every market.
The model is a tool whose conclusions hold only while its assumptions approximately hold.
The model proves monopoly cannot exist.
The market must be perfectly competitive after all.
items.explanation: This is the point of model use: 'A model is a tool whose conclusions hold only while its assumptions approximately hold.' When a key assumption breaks, the model can mislead.

items.stem: Which statement correctly defines net investment?
options: Gross investment plus depreciation.
Gross investment minus depreciation, and it is the change in the capital stock over a period.
The total quantity of equipment, structures, and tools available for production.
Saving that households do not spend.
items.explanation: Net investment is “gross investment minus depreciation, is the change in the capital stock over a period.” That is the key relationship to use when deciding whether the stock rises or falls.

items.stem: Households save more this month. Which statement best fits the circular flow of income?
options: Saving is destroyed and leaves the economy forever.
Saving is not destroyed; in balance it re-enters the flow as investment, government spending, or exports.
Saving automatically becomes depreciation.
Saving always makes national income rise.
items.explanation: The circular flow says money returns to firms as spending unless it leaks out as saving, taxes, or imports. But leakages are balanced by injections such as investment, government spending, and exports. Saving is not destroyed; in balance it re-enters the flow as investment, government spending, or exports.

items.stem: A person stopped searching after months of rejection and is no longer looking for work. In the official labor statistics, how is this person counted?
options: Employed
Unemployed
Out of the labor force
Frictionally unemployed
items.explanation: People who have given up looking are classified as out of the labor force, not unemployed. That is why “recount the rate including discouraged workers and ask whose situation each definition makes visible” matters: the measured unemployment rate can look lower when discouraged workers are excluded.

items.stem: Households save more, so spending falls at first. Which statement is most accurate in the circular flow model?
options: Saving disappears from the economy and cannot return
Saving is only a loss, so income must always fall
Saving is not destroyed; in balance it re-enters the flow as investment, government spending, or exports
Only taxes can bring money back into the circular flow
items.explanation: Saving is a leakage, but it is not destroyed. The corrective is exactly that: “Saving is not destroyed; in balance it re-enters the flow as investment, government spending, or exports.” The circular flow stays balanced when leakages are matched by injections.

items.stem: Which person is unemployed rather than out of the labor force?
options: A retiree who is not looking for work
A parent on leave who says they are not searching and are unavailable
A student who wants a job but is not actively searching
A worker who is available, actively seeking work, and not employed
items.explanation: Unemployment is typically measured as the fraction of the labor force that is not employed but is actively seeking work and available for work. The other options describe people outside that count because they are not actively searching or not available.

items.stem: A city raises the minimum wage, while a nearby city does not. Employment falls in the treated city, and a student says, 'That proves the minimum wage caused the drop.' What is the best response?
options: Yes, because any before-and-after difference is a causal effect.
Only if the two cities were comparable apart from the policy change.
No, because policies never affect employment.
Yes, because observational data are always enough for causation.
items.explanation: The comparison is useful only when the groups are alike except for the policy. The corrective here is exactly: "The causal claim holds only if the groups differ just in the policy, not in confounders." If other things changed too, the observed difference may come from those confounders instead of the minimum wage.

items.stem: A student says, 'Economic models are literally true, so if a model predicts one thing, we should use it even when the real market has one dominant firm.' What is the best correction?
options: Models are valuable only when every assumption is exactly true.
A model is a tool whose conclusions hold only while its assumptions approximately hold.
Models should be ignored because they are never realistic.
A model is just a graph, not a way to reason.
items.explanation: A model is not literal reality; it is a simplified representation built for a question. Here is the corrective in plain terms: 'A model is a tool whose conclusions hold only while its assumptions approximately hold.' Once a key assumption breaks, the prediction can mislead, which is why a perfect-competition model can fail in a market dominated by one firm.

items.stem: Which statement best describes market equilibrium?
options: A market where buyers and sellers stop trading once the price is set.
A price above which there is always a shortage.
A balance of ongoing opposing pressures, not a frozen market.
Any point where the government sets a legal price.
items.explanation: Equilibrium is not motionless; buying and selling continue. What is balanced is the pressure on price, not activity itself. In course language: 'Equilibrium is a balance of ongoing opposing pressures, not a frozen market.'

items.stem: A policy analyst says, 'We can trust this natural experiment because the treated and comparison groups are not identical.' What is the best assessment?
options: That is enough; the groups should be different in many ways.
That is a problem, because the causal claim depends on comparability apart from the policy.
That proves the policy had no effect.
That means the result is automatically unbiased.
items.explanation: Not being identical is not the point; being comparable on everything relevant except the policy is the point. If the groups differ in confounders, the causal claim weakens. The fix is the same standard stated in the course: the groups must differ only in the policy, not in confounders.

items.stem: Which statement best describes the Earth’s main internal layers?
options: A thin crust, a thick rocky mantle, and a metallic core
A thick crust, a watery mantle, and a rocky core
A crust, a magma ocean, and a gas-filled center
A thin mantle, a thick crust, and an iron shell only
items.explanation: Earth is layered into a thin outer crust, a thick rocky mantle, and a metallic core. The mantle sits below the crust and above the core, so the ordering matters.

items.stem: A diagram shows a layer below the crust and above the core. Which label should you choose?
options: Asthenosphere
Outer crust
Mantle
Inner core
items.explanation: The mantle sits below the crust and above the core. The asthenosphere is part of the upper mantle, not the name for the whole layer.

items.stem: Which pair is correctly matched?
options: Mantle — mostly iron and nickel
Core — mostly iron and nickel
Crust — liquid outer layer and solid inner layer
Asthenosphere — the outermost chemical layer you live on
items.explanation: The core is made mostly of iron and nickel, and it has both liquid and solid layers. The crust is the outermost layer, and the asthenosphere is part of the mantle.

items.stem: A student finds a shiny red mineral that scratches glass, and says, 'It must be diamond because it's so hard.' What is the best response?
options: Yes, if it scratches glass it must be diamond.
No; hardness measures scratch resistance, not toughness, and diamond can still have perfect cleavage.
No; only luster matters for mineral identification.
Yes; diamond is always red and shiny.
items.explanation: Hardness does not mean unbreakable. The corrective is: "Hardness measures scratch resistance, not toughness; diamond tops the Mohs scale yet has perfect cleavage and can be split by a sharp blow along those planes."

items.stem: A mineral looks black in hand sample, but its powder is reddish-brown. Which property is giving the more dependable identification here?
options: Color of the whole specimen
Luster
Streak
Cleavage
items.explanation: Streak is the powder color, and that is what matters here. Color is unreliable; streak (the color of the powder) and properties like hardness and cleavage identify a mineral far more dependably.

items.stem: Which description best matches a mineral?
options: A naturally occurring, inorganic solid with definite chemical composition and ordered crystal structure
Any hard rock that forms underground
Any shiny material found in Earth
Any solid made of one element
items.explanation: That full description is the mineral definition used in this lesson: naturally occurring, inorganic, solid, definite chemical composition, and ordered crystal structure.

items.stem: A hand sample breaks into repeated flat surfaces instead of irregular chunks. Which property is most directly shown?
options: Luster
Cleavage
Streak
Hardness
items.explanation: Flat breakage points to cleavage, the tendency of a mineral to break along flat planes of weak bonding. Minerals without those planes fracture irregularly.

items.stem: Which silicate arrangement best matches quartz?
options: Isolated tetrahedra
Single chains
Sheets
A fully linked three-dimensional framework
items.explanation: Quartz belongs in the most interconnected category. More shared corner oxygens means a more interconnected framework; quartz, a fully linked framework silicate, is among the harder, more durable minerals.

items.stem: Why are micas easy to split into thin flakes?
options: They have no crystal structure.
They are a framework silicate with no weak planes.
They form sheets, so they cleave along flat planes.
They are identified only by surface color.
items.explanation: Micas are the sheet example from the lesson. Because they form sheets, they cleave along flat planes and split into thin flakes; that cleavage reflects the weak bonding between layers.

items.stem: A mineral leaves a red-brown powder even when the hand specimen looks metallic gray. What test is most useful here?
options: Color
Streak
Luster
Cleavage
items.explanation: This is the hematite example in action: the specimen color can mislead, but the streak reveals the powder color. Color is unreliable; streak (the color of the powder) and properties like hardness and cleavage identify a mineral far more dependably.

items.stem: Two minerals have the same surface color, but one has a reliable powder color and clear cleavage while the other does not. Which statement best fits mineral identification?
options: Color is enough if the sample is fresh.
Color is unreliable; streak and properties like hardness and cleavage identify a mineral far more dependably.
Only luster matters in mineral ID.
The specimen with the darker color must be the harder mineral.
items.explanation: Do not trust surface color alone. Color is unreliable; streak (the color of the powder) and properties like hardness and cleavage identify a mineral far more dependably.

items.stem: Which hazard is most closely associated with an explosive, high-silica volcano?
options: A slow lava flow that you can easily outwalk
A pyroclastic flow of hot ash and gas
A cool sheet of groundwater moving through cracks
A gentle stream of basaltic lava that barely moves
items.explanation: It is the opposite: cooler, silica-rich, high-viscosity magma traps gas and produces the deadliest pyroclastic eruptions, whereas runny basalt usually erupts effusively. That explosive setting points straight to pyroclastic flow.

items.stem: Two silicate minerals differ in how many corner oxygens they share. Which sample is more likely to be hard and durable?
options: The one with fewer shared corner oxygens, because less linkage makes stronger minerals.
The one with more shared corner oxygens, because it forms a more interconnected framework.
They should have the same durability because oxygen sharing does not affect mineral strength.
Only minerals with isolated tetrahedra are hard, because they are less connected.
items.explanation: More shared corner oxygens means a more interconnected framework; quartz, a fully linked framework silicate, is among the harder, more durable minerals. Greater linkage strengthens the framework instead of weakening it.

items.stem: Which statement best describes lithification?
options: It is the process of melting sediment into magma.
It is the process of weathering solid rock into loose fragments.
It is compaction and cementation together, turning sediment into rock.
It is the process of changing a mineral’s color at the surface.
items.explanation: Lithification is the combined effect of compaction and cementation. As more material accumulates on top, grains are squeezed together, and minerals glue them into stone.

items.stem: Which parent-rock pair best fits the protolith constraint described in the reading?
options: Shale to marble
Limestone to marble
Granite to slate
Basalt to coal
items.explanation: The protolith matters: limestone becomes marble, while shale commonly metamorphoses toward slate and then schist. The parent rock's composition is inherited.

items.stem: Two igneous rocks have similar chemistry. One has large crystals and the other has tiny crystals. What explains the difference best?
options: The large-crystal rock cooled fast at the surface
The tiny-crystal rock cooled slowly at depth
The large-crystal rock cooled slowly at depth
Crystal size only depends on whether the rock is sedimentary
items.explanation: Slow cooling at depth gives crystals time to grow large (coarse, intrusive); fast cooling at the surface freezes tiny crystals (fine, extrusive).

items.stem: A sample is molten rock underground. Later the same material erupts and cools at the surface. Which terms are correct?
options: It is lava underground and magma at the surface
It is magma underground and lava at the surface
It is sediment underground and lava at the surface
It is metamorphic underground and igneous at the surface
items.explanation: Magma is molten rock below the surface; once it erupts onto the surface it is called lava, and the two cool at very different rates.

items.stem: A layer contains rounded sand grains, is well sorted, and has ripple marks. What is the best conclusion?
options: It is decoration with no geologic meaning
It records a specific past environment such as a sandy, current-swept setting
It must be a metamorphic layer formed by pressure
It cooled from lava at the surface
items.explanation: Each layer's grain size, sorting, and fossils record a specific past environment — a river, beach, or deep sea — so layers are evidence, not decoration. In this case the ripple marks and sorting point to a sandy, current-swept setting.

items.stem: A volcano produces lava that cools almost instantly at the surface. What texture should you expect, and why?
options: Coarse crystals, because fast cooling gives minerals time to grow
Fine crystals, because fast cooling freezes tiny crystals
Coarse crystals, because lava is always coarse-grained
No crystals, because only magma makes crystals
items.explanation: Fast cooling at the surface makes tiny crystals. The corrective sentence is: “Slow cooling at depth gives crystals time to grow large (coarse, intrusive); fast cooling at the surface freezes tiny crystals (fine, extrusive).”

items.stem: Which boundary description matches the San Andreas Fault?
options: Divergent: plates move apart and new crust forms
Convergent: plates move together and crust is destroyed
Transform: plates slide horizontally past each other
No boundary: the plates are fixed in place
items.explanation: The San Andreas Fault is a transform boundary. The corrective says: “There are three distinct types: divergent (plates apart, new crust), convergent (plates together, crust destroyed), and transform (plates sliding past), each with its own landforms and hazards.”

items.stem: At the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, the plates are moving apart. What kind of boundary is this, and what is happening to crust there?
options: Convergent; crust is destroyed
Transform; crust is neither created nor destroyed
Divergent; new crust is created
Divergent; crust is destroyed
items.explanation: The Mid-Atlantic Ridge is the classic divergent example. At divergent boundaries, plates move away from each other and new lithosphere is created.

items.stem: An earthquake is recorded on a fault where the rocks had been bending for years before the sudden slip. Which process best explains the event?
options: Elastic rebound after stored elastic energy is released
P-wave refraction through the outer core
Transform motion creating new crust
S-wave motion through liquid rock
items.explanation: That is the earthquake cycle described by elastic rebound. The energy is stored over years as rock bends elastically along a locked fault; the quake releases it suddenly when the fault slips.

items.stem: Which boundary type best matches plates sliding horizontally past each other, like the San Andreas Fault?
options: Convergent
Divergent
Transform
Subducting
items.explanation: Transform boundaries are where plates slide past each other. The San Andreas Fault is the worked example for that motion.

items.stem: Which description best matches the magma most associated with pyroclastic flow hazard?
