options: Cooler, silica-rich, high-viscosity magma that traps gas
Hot, runny basalt that erupts gently
Any magma that moves like syrup
Magma that cannot erupt because it is too thick
items.explanation: The deadliest hazard here is linked to sticky magma, not runny magma. The corrective is explicit: “It is the opposite: cooler, silica-rich, high-viscosity magma traps gas and produces the deadliest pyroclastic eruptions, whereas runny basalt usually erupts effusively.”

items.stem: A news clip shows a volcano sending out a lethal blast of hot ash and gas. Which magma property most likely led to that hazard?
options: Low silica, low viscosity, easy lava flow
High silica, high viscosity, gas trapped until eruption
Low viscosity because it lets gas escape slowly
Basaltic magma because it always produces gentle eruptions
items.explanation: A pyroclastic flow is described in the reading as the most dangerous volcanic hazard and is typical of explosive high-silica volcanoes. High viscosity traps gas, builds pressure, and can produce that violent ash-and-gas cloud.

items.stem: Which volcano example from the reading best shows an effusive eruption rather than an explosive one?
options: Mount St. Helens
Kilauea
A volcano producing a pyroclastic blast
A volcano with trapped gas and sticky magma
items.explanation: Kilauea is the example of runny basalt and gentle lava flows. The worked example says, “Kilauea's runny basalt produces lava flows you can sometimes outwalk,” which is the effusive side of the contrast.

items.stem: You are choosing a volcano to monitor for the highest risk of pyroclastic flow. Which one should get the most urgent attention?
options: A basaltic shield volcano with runny lava
A low-silica volcano with gentle lava flows
A felsic volcano with thick, sticky magma
A volcano whose magma is described as syrup-like
items.explanation: Pyroclastic flow is the fast cloud of hot ash and gas tied to explosive high-silica volcanoes. A felsic, thick, sticky magma traps gas, so it is the scenario that raises the most concern.

items.stem: A student says, “Weathering is just erosion starting.” Which reply is most accurate?
options: Correct; the two words mean the same thing.
Not quite; weathering breaks rock down in place, while erosion transports the broken sediment away.
No; erosion only happens underground.
Yes; weathering is only chemical weathering.
items.explanation: Not quite—weathering breaks rock down in place; erosion is the separate step that carries the broken material away. A rock can weather without eroding if nothing transports the pieces, so the two are related but not synonyms.

items.stem: A warm, humid forest floor has abundant dissolved minerals and altered rock fragments. Which process is most favored there?
options: Chemical weathering
Only erosion
No weathering at all
Sedimentary rock cooling from magma
items.explanation: Warm, humid conditions favor chemical weathering. That process dissolves or alters minerals into new substances, rather than just breaking rock into smaller pieces.

items.stem: A tilted set of sedimentary layers is exposed in a road-cut. What is the best interpretation?
options: The layers were originally deposited horizontally and were disturbed later.
The layers were originally deposited at the same tilt they show now.
The bottom layer must be younger because it is closer to the center of Earth.
The tilt proves the rock was formed by absolute dating.
items.explanation: Start with the principle of original horizontality: sediments and lava flows are "are originally laid down horizontally." If they are tilted now, the layers were disturbed after deposition.

items.stem: In an undisturbed sequence, which layer is oldest?
options: The top layer
The middle layer
The bottom layer
All layers are the same age
items.explanation: By superposition, "the layers on the bottom are the oldest, and the layers above them are younger." That rule applies when the sequence has not been disturbed.

items.stem: Which pathway is allowed by the rock cycle?
options: Igneous rock can only become sedimentary rock and never anything else.
Metamorphic rock can erode to sediment or melt to magma and re-crystallize as igneous rock.
Sedimentary rock cannot change once lithified.
Rocks do not cycle; each type stays fixed forever.
items.explanation: The cycle has many paths: any rock type can become any other; metamorphic rock can erode to sediment, or melt to magma and re-crystallize as igneous rock. Over geologic time the same atoms cycle repeatedly through igneous, sedimentary, and metamorphic forms as conditions change.

items.stem: A granite body weathers into sand, the sand lithifies into sandstone, and later the sandstone turns into quartzite. What sequence of rock families is this?
options: Sedimentary → igneous → metamorphic
Igneous → sedimentary → metamorphic
Metamorphic → sedimentary → igneous
Sedimentary → metamorphic → igneous
items.explanation: Granite starts as igneous rock, sand that lithifies becomes sedimentary rock, and heat and pressure turn it into metamorphic rock. The worked example follows that same path.

items.stem: A city reports that most residents support a new parking rule. You later learn the survey was texted only to people who had already paid parking tickets online. What is the best statistical reaction?
options: Accept the result because the sample size was large.
Treat the result cautiously because the collection method may bias what the data can support.
Assume the rule is unpopular because tickets were involved.
Ignore how the data were collected; only the percentages matter.
items.explanation: The key issue is provenance: the data came from a selective collection method. That means the collection method and its purpose can bias what the data can support. In other words, you should ask who collected the data, how, and why before trusting what the numbers say.

items.stem: Which description best matches data provenance?
options: The number of rows in a dataset.
The record of where a dataset came from: who collected it, by what method, and for what purpose.
A graph that summarizes the data.
The average value in the dataset.
items.explanation: Data provenance is not a table or a summary; it is the record of where a dataset came from: who collected it, by what method, and for what purpose. That is why conclusions are only as trustworthy as the provenance of the data behind them.

items.stem: A student says, 'The numbers are the numbers; once data are collected, they speak for themselves.' What is the best reply?
options: Yes, numbers never depend on collection choices.
Only qualitative data need to worry about provenance.
Not quite—the collection method and purpose can bias what the data can support.
That is true only for very small datasets.
items.explanation: That belief ignores provenance. The collection method and purpose can bias what the data can support, so numbers do not speak for themselves. You have to ask who collected the data, how, and why before trusting what the numbers say.

items.stem: Which question is most useful first when checking whether a dataset is trustworthy?
options: What color is the graph?
How many decimals are reported?
Who collected the data, how, and why?
Does the conclusion sound persuasive?
items.explanation: The first check is provenance: who collected the data, by what method, and for what purpose. That is the fastest way to judge whether the conclusions are only as trustworthy as the provenance behind them.

items.stem: Ice-cream sales and drowning both rise in July. Which explanation fits the course example best?
options: Ice-cream sales cause drowning.
Drowning causes ice-cream sales.
Summer heat is the confounder behind the association.
The two variables are unrelated and the pattern is random.
items.explanation: Summer heat is the hidden third variable in the example. It influences both the supposed cause and the supposed effect, creating a spurious association rather than showing a causal link.

items.stem: In Python, x is 3. What does x = x + 1 do?
options: It tests whether x equals x + 1 and returns True.
It is impossible because x cannot equal x + 1.
It evaluates x + 1 first and then binds that result to x, so x increases by one.
It creates a new variable named x + 1.
items.explanation: Remember the programming rule here: '= is assignment, not equality.' The right side is evaluated first and the result is bound to the name on the left, so x = x + 1 simply increases x by one.

items.stem: Suppose x is 3 and you run y = x + 2. Later x becomes 10. What is y?
options: 12, because y updates when x changes.
5, because assignment stores the value computed at that moment.
3, because y always matches x.
10, because y takes the new value of x.
items.explanation: Once the statement runs, y holds the value computed then. Assignment stores the value computed at that moment; if y = x + 2 runs when x is 3, y is 5 and stays 5 even if x changes afterward.

items.stem: A company emails a satisfaction survey only to customers who bought again last month. Which question should you ask first before trusting the results?
options: Who collected the data, how, and why?
What is the median of the responses?
Is the survey answer a causal variable?
Can the survey be converted into a randomized experiment immediately?
items.explanation: That is the provenance check you want. Ask who collected the data, how, and why before trusting what the numbers say, because the collection method and purpose can bias what the data can support.

items.stem: A researcher finds that students who sit closer to the front have higher grades and concludes that moving everyone to the front will raise grades. What is the main problem?
options: The grades are not numerical.
The study is observational, so the association may be due to a confounder rather than a causal effect.
There is no association because grades are unrelated to seating.
The conclusion is fine if the researcher collected the data carefully.
items.explanation: Careful collection is not enough to rescue a causal claim from an observational study. The core issue is still that an association may be due to a confounding variable rather than a causal effect, so causation is not established.

items.stem: A class says, “These survey numbers must be objective fact, so we can trust the conclusion without looking further.” What is the best reply?
options: Trust it if the sample size is large enough, no matter who collected it
Ignore the method and focus only on the arithmetic mean
Ask who collected the data, how, and why before trusting what the numbers say
Treat any dataset as equally reliable because all numbers are factual
items.explanation: Ask who collected the data, how, and why before trusting what the numbers say. Data provenance is the record of where a dataset came from, and the collection method and purpose can bias what the data can support.

items.conceptName: sampling distribution of the sample mean
items.stem: You are told that the standard deviation of a sampling distribution of the mean got smaller when the sample size increased. Which statement matches the kernel fact?
options: It equals the population standard deviation divided by the square root of the sample size
It equals the population standard deviation times the sample size
It equals the sample standard deviation divided by the population size
It stays exactly the same for all sample sizes
items.explanation: This follows directly from the kernel fact: the standard deviation of the sampling distribution of the mean equals the population standard deviation divided by the square root of the sample size.

items.stem: Which choice best describes data provenance?
options: The numerical value of a sample mean
The record of where a dataset came from: who collected it, by what method, and for what purpose
The way a sampling distribution becomes normal
The square root in the standard deviation formula
items.explanation: Data provenance is the record of where a dataset came from: who collected it, by what method, and for what purpose. That provenance matters because the collection method and its purpose can bias what the data can support.

items.stem: A teacher repeatedly takes samples of size 40 from a population of dice rolls and computes each sample mean. What should the distribution of those sample means look like as the number of samples grows?
options: Uniform, because a single die roll is uniform
Near-normal, even though a single die roll is uniform
Exactly the same shape as the population, always
Skewed right, because averages always inherit the population shape
items.explanation: This is the worked-example idea: averaging many samples of size 40 produces a near-normal sampling distribution of the mean even when the population itself is uniform.

items.stem: Which statement best defines a sampling distribution?
options: The probability distribution of a statistic obtained from many samples drawn from a population
The list of all values in the population
The distribution of a single observation from one sample
The probability that a statistic equals the true parameter
items.explanation: This matches the anchor definition: a sampling distribution is the probability distribution of a statistic obtained from a large number of samples drawn from a specific population.

items.stem: A population has standard deviation 24. If the sample size increases from 9 to 36, what happens to the standard deviation of the sampling distribution of the sample mean?
options: It stays 24
It becomes 12
It becomes 6
It becomes 48
items.explanation: Use the rule: standard deviation of the sampling distribution of the mean equals population standard deviation divided by the square root of n. So 24/√36 = 24/6 = 4? Wait—check the arithmetic carefully: for n=36, the standard deviation is 24/6 = 4.

items.stem: Which formula gives the standard deviation of the sampling distribution of the sample mean?
options: Population standard deviation multiplied by the square root of the sample size
Population standard deviation divided by the square root of the sample size
Sample standard deviation divided by the sample size
Population standard deviation plus the sample size
items.explanation: The anchor quote states the spread is the population standard deviation divided by the square root of the sample size.

items.stem: A student says, “The p-value is the probability that the null hypothesis is true.” What is the best reply?
options: No; it is a probability about the data given the null, not about the hypothesis given the data.
Yes, if the p-value is small enough.
Only when the sample size is large.
Yes, because a p-value measures effect size.
items.explanation: No: the p-value is not the probability that the null hypothesis is true. It is the probability of obtaining a statistic at least as extreme as the one observed, assuming the null hypothesis is true. So the direction is data given null, not hypothesis given data.

items.stem: A student sees a model with a good fit and says, “That means the conclusions are definitely correct.” What is wrong with that reasoning?
options: Nothing; a good fit always makes the conclusions correct.
The model can still be misleading even if it fits the sample well.
The model is no longer simplified if the fit is good.
A good fit only matters for hypothesis testing, not for models.
items.explanation: The lesson says exactly that the model’s conclusions can be misleading even if it fits the sample well. So the fit does not protect you from assumption failures.

items.stem: A researcher is deciding whether to trust regression conclusions. Which question is most important first?
options: Did the model keep a few structural features and discard others appropriately?
Is the p-value smaller than 0.05?
Does the sample have the largest possible R-squared?
Can the model be treated as a perfect copy of the data?
items.explanation: The model is supposed to be simplified, not perfect. The lesson frames the key issue as whether the model keeps the right structural features while relying on assumptions like linearity and independent errors.

items.stem: A regression line has a high R-squared on the sample. What should you check before trusting the conclusions from the model?
options: Only whether the line passes close to most points
Whether the assumptions like linearity and independent errors are reasonable
Whether the sample size is the largest possible
Whether the x-values are evenly spaced
items.explanation: A high R-squared tells you the sample fit looks strong, but it does not prove the model is valid. The key check is whether the assumptions like linearity and independent errors are reasonable, because 'Good fit does not guarantee valid assumptions; check the assumptions, not just the fit.'

items.stem: Which feature is named in the lesson as one of the assumptions a linear regression relies on?
options: Independent errors
Equal sample sizes in each group
A random scatterplot shape
A median that equals the mean
items.explanation: The lesson says a linear regression keeps a few structural features and discards others, 'relying on assumptions like linearity and independent errors.' Independent errors is one of the named assumptions.

items.stem: A regression has a strong sample fit, but the errors are not independent. What is the most accurate conclusion?
options: The model is trustworthy because the fit is strong
The model may still be misleading because assumptions fail
The model is valid only if the line is steep
The model cannot be a statistical model
items.explanation: This is the worked-example idea in one sentence: 'A regression with strong R-squared can still mislead if the errors are not independent.' Strong fit does not rescue broken assumptions, so the conclusions may still be wrong.

items.conceptName: data collection bias and survey design
items.stem: A school posts results from an online poll about cafeteria food. The poll was sent only to students who already follow the school newsletter. What is the best first question to ask before trusting the result?
options: Who collected the data, how, and why did they collect it?
How large is the sample size, regardless of who answered?
What is the most convenient way to graph the percentages?
Can we assume the poll is objective because it is numerical?
items.explanation: Start with provenance: “who collected the data, by what method, and for what purpose.” That is the check that tells you whether the result can be trusted, instead of treating the numbers as objective fact.

items.conceptName: data collection bias and survey design
items.stem: A company emails a satisfaction survey only to repeat buyers. Which conclusion is most justified?
options: The survey may overstate satisfaction because unhappy customers who already left were excluded.
The survey is unbiased because it uses customer email addresses.
The survey must represent all customers because it has real responses.
The purpose of the survey does not matter if the questions are short.
items.explanation: This is the same problem as the textbook example: a survey emailed only to repeat buyers can overstate satisfaction because its provenance excludes the unhappy customers who already left. The collection method and purpose can bias what the data can support.

items.conceptName: data collection bias and survey design
items.stem: Which statement best describes data provenance?
options: The record of where a dataset came from: who collected it, by what method, and for what purpose
The number of observations in a dataset
A graph that makes the data look easier to read
The average value of the data after it is summarized
items.explanation: Data provenance is not just a citation or a graph label. It is “the record of where a dataset came from: who collected it, by what method, and for what purpose.”

items.conceptName: data collection bias and survey design
items.stem: A student says, “The spreadsheet is objective, so the numbers speak for themselves.” Which response best corrects that claim?
options: Only if the data are large enough do we need to ask about the source.
Ask who collected the data, how, and why before trusting what the numbers say.
If the numbers are rounded, the source no longer matters.
Objective spreadsheets cannot contain bias.
items.explanation: That belief treats the dataset as objective fact and ignores collection method and purpose. Ask who collected the data, how, and why before trusting what the numbers say.

items.conceptName: data collection bias and survey design
items.stem: A researcher wants a survey about campus dining habits to support decisions for all students. Which plan is strongest?
options: Email only students who already use the dining app, because they are easiest to reach.
Ask only students in one dining hall, because that is the smallest group to survey.
Collect responses using a method that reaches the intended student group and matches the purpose of the study.
Use whatever method gives the largest number of responses, since more responses always means better data.
items.explanation: A good design matches the collection method to the purpose. If the study is meant to support decisions for all students, the method has to reach the intended group rather than a narrow slice of it.

items.stem:
You write:
score = 10
score = score + 5
What will be printed by print(score)?
options: It causes an error because score is already assigned
items.explanation: The second statement reads the old value of score, computes score + 5, and then stores the result back into score. So score becomes 15 and print(score) outputs 15. This matches the worked example: “score = 10; score = score + 5 leaves score holding 15” and shows that assignment updates the name to the new value.

items.stem:
Students run this code:
x = 3
y = x + 2
x = 10
What is the value of y?
options: y becomes 12
items.explanation: Assignment stores the value computed at that moment; if y = x + 2 runs when x is 3, y is 5 and stays 5 even if x changes afterward. The variable does not keep a live expression that updates when x changes later.

items.stem: Which line correctly builds the text 'Age: 19' without causing a TypeError?
options: 'Age: ' + str(19)
'Age: ' + float(19)
str('Age: ') + 19 + str(19)
items.explanation: Use explicit conversion: Convert the number with str() before joining it to text. The worked example states: “‘Age: ' + str(19) builds 'Age: 19', while 'Age: ' + 19 raises a TypeError because a str and an int cannot be added.”

items.stem: Your program reads a number as text using input(). Which is the safest way to turn it into an integer you can do arithmetic with?
options: n = input('n: ')
n = str(input('n: '))
n = int(input('n: '))
n = input('n: ') + 0
items.explanation: Have students explicitly convert the result (e.g., n = int(input('n: '))) and discuss how input() always returns a str. So int(...) converts the text to an integer.

items.stem: A student writes: "if age > 13 and < 19:" and says it means "age is between 13 and 19." Which option correctly fixes the condition?
options: if age > 13 and < 19:
if age > 13 and age < 19:
if age = 13 and age = 19:
if age > 13 or age < 19:
items.explanation: Each comparison needs its own operands joined by and: age > 13 and age < 19. The bare `< 19` has nothing on its left. This directly corrects the mistaken belief that `age > 13 and < 19` is valid.

items.stem: A student claims: “In Python, / does integer division, so 7 / 2 is 3.” Which result is correct in Python 3?
options: It depends on the types of 7 and 2, so both are possible
items.explanation: In Python 3 the / operator always returns a float, so 7 / 2 is 3.5; use // for whole-number floor division, which gives 3. This confronts the exact misconception that `/` does integer division because the operands look like whole numbers.

items.stem:
Choose the correct way to build a sentence like:
"Age: 19"
from the number 19.
options: 'Age: ' + str(19)
items.explanation: Convert the number with str() before joining it to text. The correct form is 'Age: ' + str(19). This directly addresses the misconception that Python will silently turn an int into a string inside a + with a str.

items.stem: Choose the correct while condition and update pair for counting down from 10 to 1. (You want to print 10, 9, ..., 1.)
options: while n >= 0: print(n); n = n + 1
while n > 0: print(n); n = n - 1
while n > 1: print(n); n = n + 1
while n > 0: print(n); (no update needed)
items.explanation: To print 10 down to 1, the loop should run while n > 0 and the update must move n toward 0: n = n - 1 inside the body. This makes the condition eventually become false and stops the loop.

items.stem: You want to print exactly five numbers starting at 0. Which loop matches that behavior?
options: for i in range(1, 6): print(i)
for i in range(5): print(i)
for i in range(0, 5): print(i)
for i in range(0, 4): print(i)
items.explanation: Correct: range(5) yields 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 — it starts at 0 and stops before the endpoint, giving exactly five values. So the body runs five times and prints those five numbers.

items.stem: Consider this code: for i in range(3): print(i). What are the outputs (in order)?
items.explanation: range(3) yields 0, 1, 2 — it starts at 0 and stops before the endpoint. So i takes 0 then 1 then 2, producing three lines: 0, 1, 2.

items.stem: A student claims: “If I write for x in some_list: x = 0, that edits the underlying list so every element becomes 0.” What happens?
options: It edits the underlying list; reassigning x changes the list
It only rebinds x; assigning to x does not edit the container
It edits only the first element then stops
It raises an error because x is read-only
items.explanation: Corrective: “The loop variable is a fresh binding to each element in turn; assigning to it does not edit the container. To change list contents, index into the list directly.” So x=0 changes x, not the list elements themselves.

items.stem:
You define:

def square(n):
    y = n * n
    return y

After calling square(5), which variable name is guaranteed to exist outside the function?
options: y
n
the return value (you must assign it)
None of the above
items.explanation: Local variables exist only during the call that created them; to use a result outside, the function must return it and the caller must capture the returned value. In this code, y is local to square(). The value from return y only becomes available outside if you store it (for example, result = square(5)).

items.stem:
Consider:

def f():
    x = 10

f()
print(x)

What should a student expect?
options: It prints 10
It prints None
It raises a NameError because x is not accessible outside f()
It raises a TypeError because x is local
items.explanation: A variable created within a function has local scope and only exists within the function. So x exists during the call to f(), but after f() finishes, print(x) tries to access a name that is not available outside. That is why this leads to a NameError.

items.stem: A student says, "def greet(): runs the function body immediately." Which response is correct?
options: Yes, because def always executes the body right away
No; defining a function only stores it, and the body runs when greet() is called
Yes, but only if the body contains print()
No; functions never run in Python
items.explanation: Defining a function only stores it; the body runs when the function is called by name, such as greet(). The statement def greet(): creates the function object but does not execute the indented code yet.

items.stem:
You run:

s = 'Age: ' + str(19)

What is s?
options: Age: 19
TypeError
Age:
items.explanation: Convert the number with str() before joining it to text, or use formatting; Python will not silently turn an int into a string inside a + with a str. So 'Age: ' + str(19) successfully builds the text 'Age: 19'.

items.stem: You have lst = ['red','green','blue','yellow','white'] . What is the result of lst[4]?
options: 'yellow'
'white'
IndexError
None of the above
items.explanation: In a list, indexes begin at 0 and end at one less than the length of the sequence. This 5-item list’s last valid index is 4, so lst[4] is 'white'. A 5-item list does not have index 5.

items.stem: You want to build a label like 'Age: 19' from age = 19. Which code produces the correct string?
options: label = 'Age: ' + 19
label = 'Age: ' + str(19)
label = 19 + 'Age: '
items.explanation: Convert the number before joining it to text: Python will not silently turn an int into a string inside a + with a str. So 'Age: ' + str(19) works, while 'Age: ' + 19 raises a TypeError.

items.stem: A student claims: “Since 7 and 2 are whole numbers, 7 / 2 should give 3.” What is the correct result of 7 / 2 in Python 3?
options: It raises an error
items.explanation: In Python 3 the / operator always returns a float, so 7 / 2 is 3.5. If you want the whole-number quotient, use //, which gives 3.

items.stem: Suppose s = 'banana'. You want s to become 'bbnana'. Which code does what you intend?
options: s.replace('a','b')
s = s.replace('a','b')
s = s.split('a').join('b') without assignment
s.replace('a','b') and then use old s unchanged
items.explanation: Require assignment to a new variable (e.g., `s = s.replace('a','b')`) and point out that strings are immutable.

items.stem: In Python 3, what is the value of 7 / 2?
options: It raises an error because ints can’t divide
items.explanation: In Python 3 the / operator always returns a float, so 7 / 2 is 3.5; use // for whole-number floor division, which gives 3.

items.stem: You want to build a sentence: 'Age: 19'. Which approach is correct?
options: 'Age: ' + str(19)
'Age: ' + int(19)
f'Age: ' + 19
items.explanation: Convert the number with str() before joining it to text, or use formatting; Python will not silently turn an int into a string inside a + with a str.

items.stem:
Consider the statement below that a student wrote. Is it correct or incorrect (choose the best option).

“Students expect the first element of a list to be at index 1, so lst[1] is the first item.”
options: Correct: lst[1] is the first item
Incorrect: the first element is at index 0, so lst[0] is the first item
Correct only if the list has length 2
Incorrect because lst[1] is always the last element
items.explanation: The first element is at index 0, so lst[0] is the first item and lst[1] is the second.

items.stem: Which option shows the wrong belief: trying to read a dictionary value with a numeric index like d[0] ?
options: Dictionaries are accessed by key, not position.
Use d['name'] to get the value under the key 'name'.
Dictionaries can be read with a numeric index like d[0], expecting list-style positions.
Dictionary values are looked up by key.
items.explanation: The incorrect statement is the distraction itself. Dictionaries are accessed by key, not position; use d['name'] to get the value stored under the key 'name', not d[0].

items.stem:
A student writes: `with open('data.txt') as f:
    a = f.read()
    b = f.read()`.
What value is `b` most likely to be right after `a` was read fully?
options: It will repeat the same full file contents as `a`.
It will be an empty string '' because the read position is already at end-of-file.
It will be a list of lines, one per newline.
It will raise an exception because read() can only be called once.
items.explanation: Correct: once read() reaches the end, a second read() returns '' until the file is reopened or the position is reset. So `a` gets the whole file as one string, and `b` becomes ''.

items.stem: Given `s = 'Python'`, what does `s[0:3]` return?
options: 'Python' (all characters)
'Pyt' (characters at indices 0, 1, and 2)
'Py' (indices 0 and 1 only)
'Pyth' (includes index 3)
items.explanation: The end index of a slice is exclusive, so s[0:3] returns characters at indices 0, 1, and 2 — three characters, stopping before index 3.

items.stem: You define a class Dog, then create a = Dog() and b = Dog(). Which change should NOT affect the other variable?
options: Changing a's name attribute should not affect b's name attribute.
Changing a's method should affect b's method behavior.
Changing b's name attribute should also change a's name attribute.
Changing the class Dog's name field should change both a and b immediately.
items.explanation: Correct: “Each instance has its own attributes, so changing one Dog's name does not change another Dog's name; only the methods are shared.” a and b are two instances, each with its own attributes copy.

items.stem: A function is defined as def square(n): return n * n. What happens when your program reaches the line containing def square(...) ?
options: The body runs immediately and computes square of some unknown number.
The function definition is stored, and nothing in the body executes until square(...) is called.
The return value 25 is printed automatically once during def.
Variables inside square become global immediately.
items.explanation: Fix this misconception: “Defining a function only stores it; the body runs when the function is called by name, such as greet().”

items.stem: You want the whole-number quotient of 7 divided by 2. Which expression matches that goal in Python 3?
options: 7 / 2 to give 3 (integer division) because the operands look like whole numbers.
items.explanation: In Python 3, “the / operator always returns a float, so 7 / 2 is 3.5; use // for whole-number floor division, which gives 3.” So 7 // 2 is the whole-number quotient you want.

items.stem: Student statement: “x = x + 1 is a mathematical equation, so it can’t be true (x equals something larger than itself).” In Python, what should you conclude?
options: It’s impossible; Python rejects it
It’s assignment: compute x + 1 and store it back in x
It compares x to x + 1 and returns True/False
It makes no change to x
items.explanation: The student is applying math-equality thinking. The corrective is: “In Python = is assignment, not equality: the right side is evaluated first and the result is bound to the name on the left, so x = x + 1 simply increases x by one.”

items.stem: Student statement: “If I write y = x + 2, then y stores the expression x + 2, so if x changes later, y should update too.” Which response is correct?
options: Yes—y will automatically update whenever x changes
No—y stores the value computed then, so it won’t change when x changes later
It depends on whether x is an int or float
Only if you use // in the assignment
items.explanation: The belief is: “Students assume a variable stores the expression itself, so they expect it to update when the inputs later change.” The fix is: “Assignment stores the value computed at that moment; if y = x + 2 runs when x is 3, y is 5 and stays 5 even if x changes afterward.”

items.stem: Which statement correctly expresses a logical inversion for a single condition (so it becomes false when the original becomes true)?
options: if not (x > 5):
if not x > 5:
if x > not 5:
items.explanation: Use Python’s boolean operator not to invert a single condition: not inverts a single condition. So wrapping the condition like not (x > 5) expresses the inversion.

items.stem: You need to label a person with their age using text concatenation. Which line will work? (Assume age is an integer.)
options: label = 'Age: ' + age
label = 'Age: ' + str(age)
label = 'Age: ' + int(age)
label = 'Age: ' + float(age)
items.explanation: Convert the number with str() before joining it to text, or use formatting; Python will not silently turn an int into a string inside a + with a str. That’s why 'Age: ' + str(age) works.

items.stem: What is the result of 7 / 2 in Python 3?
items.explanation: In Python 3 the / operator always returns a float, so 7 / 2 is 3.5; use // for whole-number floor division, which gives 3.

items.stem: Which condition correctly checks whether age is between 13 and 19 (not including 19) for an if statement?
options: if age > 13 and < 19: ...
if age > 13 and age < 19: ...
if age < 19: ...
items.explanation: Use two comparisons joined by and: “Each comparison needs its own operands joined by and: age > 13 and age < 19. The bare < 19 has nothing on its left.” The option with “age > 13 and < 19” is missing the left operand for the second comparison.

items.stem: Which line correctly compares score to 100 inside a conditional?
options: if score = 100: ...
if score == 100: ...
if score eq 100: ...
if 100 = score: ...
items.explanation: Use equality comparison with two equals signs: “Comparison uses == (two equals signs); a single = is assignment. A condition that asks whether two values are equal must be written score == 100.” The “score = 100” version is the common wrong belief that it compares.

items.stem: You want a loop that prints the numbers 3, 2, 1 and stops. Which while-loop snippet is correct?
options: n = 3; while n >= 0: print(n); n = n - 1
n = 3; while n > 0: print(n); n = n - 1
n = 3; while n > 0: print(n)
n = 3; while n > 0: print(n); n = n + 1
items.explanation: Option 2 is correct because it both (a) uses the right loop expression (n > 0) and (b) updates the variable so the condition eventually becomes false: n = n - 1. This satisfies the while-loop requirement that the loop body make progress toward ending the condition.

items.stem: Consider: nums = [10, 20, 30]; for x in nums: x = 99. After the loop, what is nums?
options: It raises an error
items.explanation: The loop variable is a fresh binding to each element in turn; assigning to it does not edit the container. To change list contents, index into the list directly.

items.stem: Using the provided range logic, what values does i take in: for i in range(3): print(i)?
items.explanation: range(3) yields 0 through n-1, so i takes 0, 1, 2. This matches the worked example: for i in range(3): print(i) prints 0, 1, 2.

items.stem: You want square(5) to produce 25 and store it in a variable named ans. Which code does that correctly?
options:
def square(n): return n * n
ans = square
def square(n): return n * n
ans = square(5)
def square(n): n * n
ans = 25
def square(n): n * n
ans = n * n
items.explanation: In the reading’s form, def square(n): return n * n defines the reusable calculation, and square(5) runs the body and returns 25. Capturing that returned value with ans = square(5) makes it available outside the function call.

items.stem:
Students wrote the following and claimed it should update automatically:

def f(x):
    y = x + 2
    return y

value = f(3)
x = 10
print(value)

What will print?
options: 13, because y always equals x + 2 when x changes later.
5, because value stored the result computed when x was 3.
None, because y is local to f and can’t be returned.
An error, because changing x after calling f makes value invalid.
items.explanation: Assignment stores the value computed at that moment; if y = x + 2 runs when x is 3, y is 5 and stays 5 even if x changes afterward.

items.stem: A student says: "Students count the first element as position 1 instead of index 0." If lst = ['A', 'B', 'C'], what is lst[0] ?
options: A
B
C
IndexError
items.explanation: The first element is at index 0, so lst[0] is the first item and lst[1] is the second.

items.stem: For s = 'Python', what does s[0:3] return?
options: 'Pyt'
'Pyth'
'Pytho'
'Python'
items.explanation: The end index of a slice is exclusive, so s[0:3] returns characters at indices 0, 1, and 2 — three characters, stopping before index 3.

items.stem: Let s = 'Python'. What happens with the attempt s[0] = 'J' ?
options: It changes the first character in place and s becomes 'Jython'
It raises an error because strings are immutable
It does nothing and keeps s as 'Python'
It returns a new string automatically without assigning
items.explanation: Strings are immutable; you cannot assign to s[0]. Build a new string instead, e.g. 'H' + s[1:].

items.stem: You want to build the text 'Age: 19' using 'Age: ' and the number 19. Which expression is correct?
options: 'Age: ' + str(19)
items.explanation: Convert the number with str() before joining it to text, or use formatting; Python will not silently turn an int into a string inside a + with a str.

items.stem: You have names = ['Ava', 'Ben', 'Cy'] (a 3-item list). What is the value of names[1]?
options: 'Ava'
'Ben'
'Cy'
IndexError
items.explanation: The first element is at index 0, so lst[0] is the first item and lst[1] is the second. Therefore names[1] is 'Ben'.

items.stem: You have: lst = ['p', 'q', 'r', 's', 't'] (length 5). What happens with lst[5]?
options: It returns 't'
It returns the element after 't'
It raises an IndexError because lst[5] is out of range
It returns None
items.explanation: Confronting the misconception: "Students access the last element of a 5-item list with index 5 and get an IndexError." Indexes run from 0 to length minus 1, so a 5-item list's last index is 4; lst[5] is out of range.

items.stem: You write: s = 'Python'; s[0] = 'J' . What happens?
options: It changes the first character in place to 'Jython' and succeeds
It creates a new string automatically and rebinds s
It raises an error because strings are immutable
It truncates s to only one character
items.explanation: Strings are immutable; you cannot assign to s[0]. Build a new string instead, e.g. 'H' + s[1:].

items.stem: A student writes: “Every recursion needs a base case — a simplest input solved directly without another call — so the chain of self-calls eventually stops.” Which choice best describes what happens if you remove the base case from a recursive function?
options: It still finishes, because Python automatically detects repeating results
It can recurse forever and never reaches a point where the solution is known
It will run only once, because the function definition prevents self-calls
It will return None automatically, and recursion stops when it sees None
items.explanation: If you remove the base case, recursion has no stop point. The core corrective is: “Every recursion needs a base case — a simplest input solved directly without another call — so the chain of self-calls eventually stops.” Without it, the self-calls never end and can overflow the call stack.

items.stem: A function calculates a value and assigns it to a variable inside the function. A student then tries to use that variable name outside the function. Which outcome matches the correct scope behavior?
options: It works, because any variable created inside a function becomes global
It fails with NameError (or equivalent), because the local variable is not accessible outside the call
It works only if the function is called twice
It works only if you used def inside the main program block
items.explanation: Local variables exist only during the call that created them. The corrective is: “Local variables exist only during the call that created them; to use a result outside, the function must return it and the caller must capture the returned value.”

items.stem: You define square(n) as a reusable block and you write square(5) in your program. What should square(5) evaluate to?
items.explanation: From the worked example: def square(n): return n * n defines a reusable calculation; square(5) runs the body and returns 25.

items.stem: You define: def greet(): return 'Hi'. Which description matches when the function body runs?
options: It runs immediately when you write def greet():
It runs only when you call greet() by name
It never runs; functions only store the name, not behavior
It runs when the program starts, before any lines of code execute
items.explanation: Corrective: “Defining a function only stores it; the body runs when the function is called by name, such as greet().”

items.stem: You write: def f(): x = 10; return x. Which result is required so that x can be used outside the function?
options: Nothing—x is automatically global once it exists inside f
Call f() and capture the returned value in a variable outside, e.g., y = f()
Access x directly outside with x = f().x
You must declare x as global inside f for it to exist outside
items.explanation: Local variables exist only during the call that created them; to use a result outside, the function must return it and the caller must capture the returned value.

items.stem: You want whole-number division in Python 3. What should you use for 7 divided by 2 so the result is 3?
items.explanation: In Python 3, / always returns a float, so 7 / 2 is 3.5. Use // for floor division, which gives 3.

items.stem: You want the string 'Age: 19'. Which expression produces it without a TypeError?
options: 'Age: ' + str(19)
str('Age: ') + 19
items.explanation: Convert the number with str() before joining it to text, or use formatting. Python will not silently turn an int into a string inside a + with a str.

items.stem: Which command-line instruction is the most direct way to check which Python interpreter version you are running?
options: python -v
python --version
py version
check python in the IDE
items.explanation: Use the command line like `python --version` to confirm the interpreter version, then select the proper interpreter in your IDE and rerun a minimal script that prints output.

items.stem: Suppose x = [10, 20, 30]. You write: for v in x: v = 99 . After the loop, what is x?
options: [99, 99, 99] because changing v edits the list elements
[10, 20, 30] because assigning to v only changes the loop variable, not the container
[10, 20, 30, 99] because new values get appended
It becomes an error because v is read-only inside a for loop
items.explanation: The loop variable is a fresh binding to each element in turn; assigning to it does not edit the container. To change list contents, index into the list directly.

items.stem: A student says: “If I call s.strip(), it changes s in place, so s will automatically have the whitespace removed.” After running s = '  hi  ' and then s.strip(), what is the value of s?
options: 'hi' because s.strip() modifies s
'  hi  ' because you didn’t assign the returned value
'hi  ' because strip only removes left whitespace
An IndexError because strip() uses indexing
items.explanation: Run a short example and compare s before and after s.strip(): the string itself does not change. You must assign the returned result back, for example s = s.strip().

items.stem: Let lst = ['Ava', 'Ben', 'Cy', 'Dan', 'Eli'] (5 items). What happens if you evaluate lst[5]?
options: It returns the first element 'Ava' due to wrapping
It returns 'Eli' because 5 is the last index
It raises an IndexError because the index is out of range
It returns None because the list is full
items.explanation: Indexes run from 0 to length minus 1, so a 5-item list's last index is 4; lst[5] is out of range.

items.stem: A student says: “The first element of a list is position 1, so lst[1] is the first item.” If lst = ['Ava', 'Ben', 'Cy'], what is lst[1]?
options: 'Ava' because position 1 is index 1
'Ben' because index 1 is the second item
'Cy' because index 1 selects the last item
'Ava' because lists start counting at 1
items.explanation: The first element is at index 0, so lst[0] is the first item and lst[1] is the second.

items.stem:
Consider: 

def square(n):
    y = n * n
    return y

x = square(5)
What is the value of x?
options: The function object square
A NameError because y is local
None because return does nothing
items.explanation: Local variables exist only during the call that created them; to use a result outside, the function must return it and the caller must capture the returned value.

items.stem: A student writes `if score = 100 and score = 101: print('Perfect!')` thinking it’s a valid compound equality check. What is the best fix?
options: Replace both `=` with `==` and keep the `and`: `if score == 100 and score == 101:`
Keep `=` but change `and` to `or`: `if score = 100 or score = 101:`
Change `and` to `not`: `if score = 100 not score = 101:`
Remove comparisons and use booleans: `if score and score: print('Perfect!')`
items.explanation: Comparison uses == (two equals signs); a single = is assignment. A condition that asks whether two values are equal must be written score == 100. Here the compound condition must use `==` for each equality test.

items.stem: A student writes: if score = 100: print('win') else: print('no win'). What is the best correction to make the comparison work?
options: Change it to if score == 100: print('win') else: print('no win')
Change it to if score = 100: print('win') else if score = 100: print('no win')
Change it to if score > 100: print('win') else: print('no win')
Remove the else clause and keep if score = 100
items.explanation: Comparison uses == (two equals signs); a single = is assignment. A condition that asks whether two values are equal must be written score == 100.

items.stem: Which loop matches the idea: “run the body a fixed number of times using a numeric interval” and avoids manually tracking indices?
options:
for i in range(10):  # body executes 10 times
    pass

for i in 10:
    pass

while True:
    pass

for i in [0]:
    pass
items.explanation: A for loop can be paired with range() to repeat the body a fixed number of times. range(n) yields 0 through n-1, so the loop runs a predictable count (here, 10 times).

items.stem:
A student writes:

n = 3
while n > 0:
    print(n)

What is the most likely outcome, and why?
options: It prints 3, 2, 1 and then stops because the condition will become false automatically.
It prints 3 forever because the condition is evaluated only after the loop finishes.
It becomes an infinite loop because nothing changes the variable used in the condition.
It prints nothing because while loops need an else clause.
items.explanation: Every while loop must change something the condition depends on; a counter loop needs n = n - 1 (or += 1) inside the body so the condition eventually becomes false. Here, n never changes, so the condition stays true and the loop runs forever.

items.stem: A student says: "Writing def greet(): print('hi') runs the function body immediately." Which is the correct interpretation?
options: The body runs immediately when def greet() is executed.
The body runs only when greet() is called by name.
The body never runs because it must be returned.
The body runs only when an exception happens.
items.explanation: Defining a function only stores it; the body runs when the function is called by name, such as greet(). So merely writing def greet(): does not execute the print statement until greet() is called.

items.stem: Consider: d = {'first': {'x': 1}, 'second': {'x': 2}}. What expression correctly retrieves the value 2?
options: d['second']['x']
d['second'][2]
d['x']['second']
items.explanation: The outer dictionary lookup uses the key 'second', and the inner dictionary lookup uses the key 'x'. So d['second']['x'] correctly retrieves 2.

items.stem:
You run this twice on the same opened file object:

f = open('data.txt')
first = f.read()
second = f.read()

Which best describes what second will be?
options: It will contain the first half of the file again as a string
It will be '' (an empty string) because the position marker is at the end
It will throw an error because read() cannot be called more than once
It will return a list of lines like readlines()
items.explanation: Reading advances a position marker through the file; once read() reaches the end, a second read() returns '' until the file is reopened or the position is reset.

options: 'Mina'
A KeyError because 'name' is not numeric
items.explanation: Dictionaries are accessed by key, not position; use d['name'] to get the value stored under the key 'name', not d[0].

items.stem:
Consider:

grades = {'Ava': 95, 'Ben': 88}
grades['Ava'] = 97

What happens to the value stored for 'Ava'?
options: Both 95 and 97 are kept as separate entries under 'Ava'
The dictionary now has duplicate keys for 'Ava'
The value for 'Ava' becomes 97 (overwriting the old value)
A new key 'Ava 97' is created automatically
items.explanation: Keys are unique; assigning to an existing key overwrites its previous value rather than adding a second entry.

items.stem: You want the entire contents of 'data.txt' as one string. Which function matches that purpose?
options: readlines()
read()
readline()
open()
items.explanation: The read() function reads the contents of a file and returns a string.

items.stem: You’re writing factorial(n). Which recursive rule will correctly terminate and avoid a RecursionError?
options: def fact(n): return n*fact(n-1)
def fact(n): return 1 if n==0 else n*fact(n-1)
def fact(n): return n*fact(n)
def fact(n): return 1 if n==0 else fact(n+1)
items.explanation: Correct because it includes a base case and shrinks the input. The factorial kernel example is: factorial(n) returns 1 when n is 0 (base case) and otherwise returns n * factorial(n - 1), shrinking n each call.

items.stem:
You run:
with open('data.txt') as f:
    a = f.read()
    b = f.read()
If the file is not modified, what should b be?
options: A copy of a (same full text)
'' (empty string)
None
A list of lines
items.explanation: Reading advances a position marker through the file; once read() reaches the end, a second read() returns '' until the file is reopened or the position is reset.

items.stem: Choose the code strategy that matches correct resource handling for files.
options: open('data.txt') as f: text = f.read()
f = open('data.txt'); text = f.read()  # then never close it
with open('data.txt') as f: text = f.read()
with open('data.txt') as f: text = f.readlines(); keep f open
items.explanation: Use a with statement so Python closes it automatically even if an error occurs. The corrective is: "Always close the file when done, or open it in a with statement so Python closes it automatically even if an error occurs."

items.stem:
You call:
with open('data.txt') as f:
    lines = f.readlines()
What is the type/shape of lines?
options: A single string containing the whole file
A list of strings, one per line, in order
An integer count of lines
A dictionary mapping line numbers to text
items.explanation: The kernel fact says: "The readlines() function reads the individual lines of a file and returns a string list containing all the lines of the file in order."

items.stem: A student writes: def f(n): return 1 + f(n)  # no other changes. What is the most accurate prediction?
options: It terminates quickly because the return value becomes constant
It never reaches a base case, so the self-calls keep going until a recursion error
It always returns 1 because f(n) cancels itself
It terminates when n becomes negative
items.explanation: Corrective: “Every recursion needs a base case — a simplest input solved directly without another call — so the chain of self-calls eventually stops.” With none, the calls never stop.

items.stem: A student writes a recursive function call like factorial does, but their recursion step is f(n) -> f(n) (same n), not f(n-1). They claim, “It should still eventually reach the base case naturally.” What is the best response?
options: It’s fine: base case will still be reached because the function keeps calling itself
It fails because each recursive call must move toward the base case by shrinking the problem (e.g., n - 1)
It will always work if the base case is correct
It fails only for large n; small n are guaranteed to reach the base case
items.explanation: Corrective: “Each recursive call must move toward the base case by shrinking the problem (e.g. n - 1), or the base case is never reached.”

items.stem: What is the type and value of int(3.9)?
options: float, 3.9
int, 3
str, '3'
float, 3
items.explanation: int() converts a value to an integer and removes any fractional part, so int(3.9) is 3. That makes the result an integer, not a float.

items.stem: A program needs to print 'Score: 7'. Which choice works?
options: 'Score: ' + 7
'Score: ' + str(7)
'Score: ' / 7
int('Score: ') + 7
items.explanation: Convert the number with str() before joining it to text, or use formatting; Python will not silently turn an int into a string inside a + with a str. In this case, str(7) makes the pieces the same type so the message can be built.

items.stem: Which statement best describes what an expression does?
options: It names a value and changes its type
It combines values and produces a value
It always produces an int
It is the same thing as a variable name
items.explanation: Every Python value has a data type, and expressions combine values. The result is another value with its own type.

items.stem: You see a file named demo.py. What does that name tell you?
options: It is a Python source file
It is a code editor
It is the Python interpreter
It must already be running
items.explanation: Python source files conventionally use the .py extension, and a program is executed by passing the file to the interpreter or running it from an IDE/terminal. The name points to a source file, not to the editor or interpreter itself.

items.stem: You want to check whether age is between 14 and 18, inclusive of neither endpoint. Which test matches that idea?
options: if age > 13 and < 19:
if age > 13 and age < 19:
if age > 13 or age < 19:
if not age > 13 and age < 19:
items.explanation: Each comparison needs its own operands joined by and: age > 13 and age < 19. The bare < 19 has nothing on its left. That is the form to use when both limits must be true.

items.stem: What does Python produce for 7 / 2?
items.explanation: In Python 3 the / operator always returns a float, so 7 / 2 is 3.5; use // for whole-number floor division, which gives 3. This matters any time you expect a fractional result from division.

items.stem: A student writes 'Total: ' + 7 to label a score. What should they do?
options: Leave it as is; Python converts 7 to text automatically.
Use 'Total: ' + int(7).
Convert the number with str(7) before joining it to text.
Replace + with and.
items.explanation: Convert the number with str() before joining it to text, or use formatting; Python will not silently turn an int into a string inside a + with a str. That makes the types match before the join happens.

items.stem: A lunch check should print 'Teen' when age is over 13 and under 19, and 'Other' otherwise. Which structure fits best?
options: if age > 13 and age < 19: print('Teen') else: print('Other')
if age > 13 or age < 19: print('Teen')
if not age > 13 and age < 19: print('Teen') else: print('Other')
if age > 13: print('Teen') else: print('Other')
items.explanation: A conditional statement chooses which block of code to run based on whether a condition is true; if-else takes exactly one branch, and boolean operators (and, or, not) build compound conditions. Here the test must make both comparisons true before the Teen branch runs.

items.stem: Which statement about if and else is correct?
options: Both blocks run every time, but one runs first.
if runs its body only when the condition is true; else runs when it is false.
else can run without an if condition.
and means the same thing as or.
items.explanation: An if statement runs its body only when the condition is true, and skips it when the condition is false. An else clause holds statements that run when the if condition is false.

items.stem: Which condition correctly tests whether score equals 100?
options: if score = 100:
if score == 100:
if score != 100:
if score = = 100:
items.explanation: Comparison uses == (two equals signs); a single = is assignment. A condition that asks whether two values are equal must be written score == 100. That is the form to use when you want the if statement to test equality.

items.stem: Which if-else version runs the else block only when the condition is false?
options: if passed: run the if block; else: run the else block
if passed == false: run the if block; else: run the else block
if passed: run the else block; else: run the if block
if passed or false: run the if block; else: run the else block
items.explanation: An if statement runs its body only when the condition is true, and an else clause holds statements that run when the if condition is false. So the if block goes with the true case, and else covers the false case.

items.stem: You want a loop to run exactly five times. Which header matches that goal?
options: for i in range(5):
for i in range(1, 5):
for i in range(5, 1):
for i in range(1, 6):
items.explanation: range(5) yields 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 — it starts at 0 and stops before the endpoint, giving exactly five values. That is the clean way to get five passes through the loop body.

items.stem: Which loop correctly visits each character in the word `cat`?
options: for ch in range('cat'):
for ch in cat:
for ch in range(3):
while ch in cat:
items.explanation: A string is a container of characters, and a for loop can iterate over each character one at a time. `for ch in cat:` binds `ch` to `c`, then `a`, then `t`.

items.stem: A list has five items. You want to process the items by index from first to last. Which header fits that plan?
options: for i in range(5):
for i in range(6):
for i in range(1, 5):
while i in range(5):
items.explanation: range(5) gives the indices 0 through 4, which matches a list with five items. That lets the loop visit each valid index exactly once.

items.stem: You want a loop to run exactly five times. Which range fits that goal?
options: range(1, 5)
range(5)
range(0, 5, 2)
range(6)
items.explanation: range(5) yields 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 — it starts at 0 and stops before the endpoint, giving exactly five values. That makes it the right choice when you need five passes through the loop.

items.stem: A program uses a for loop with range(5) and then asks for the values produced. Which answer is correct?
items.explanation: range(5) yields 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 — it starts at 0 and stops before the endpoint, giving exactly five values. If you expected 1 through 5, the loop count and the indices would be off by one.

items.stem: You have a list with five items: ['a', 'b', 'c', 'd', 'e']. Which expression gets the last item?
options: lst[0]
lst[4]
lst[5]
lst[-1]
items.explanation: The last valid index is one less than the length, so a 5-item list ends at index 4. Index 0 is the first item, and index 5 is out of range. Here, lst[4] gets 'e'.

items.stem: A function sets a variable inside itself, then the code below the function tries to print that variable name. What is the best fix?
options: Move the print statement inside the function body
Rename the variable to make it global automatically
Return the value from the function and capture it outside
Call the function definition again with def
items.explanation: Local variables exist only during the call that created them; to use a result outside, the function must return it and the caller must capture the returned value. That is the way to move a result from inside the function to the rest of the program.

items.stem: You see this code: def greet(): print('hi'). What does that line by itself do?
options: It prints 'hi' right away
It stores the function for later use
It creates a global variable named greet
It runs only if the name greet is already defined
items.explanation: Defining a function only stores it; the body runs when the function is called by name, such as greet(). So this line makes the function available, but it does not execute the body yet.

items.stem: A program has x = 10 outside a function, and a function also creates x = 3 inside its body. Which statement is true?
options: The inner x is accessible everywhere after the call
The outer x is local to the function
The inner x has local scope inside the function call
Both x values become the same variable
items.explanation: A variable created inside a function has local scope and cannot be accessed outside the function. A variable created outside any function has global scope and can be accessed anywhere in the program.

items.stem: You are storing a student record with labeled fields like name, major, and year. Which structure fits best for retrieving the major by label?
options: A list, because order always matters most
A dictionary, because you can look up the value by key
A string, because it can hold labels
A set, because it keeps one copy of each label
items.explanation: A dictionary fits because it stores key-value pairs and looks up each value by its key rather than by position. Here, 'major' is a label, so it should be a key.

items.stem: You want to normalize the text in a comment before searching it. Which approach matches Python string behavior?
options: Call replace() and assume the original comment changed
Call lower() or replace() and save the returned string
Use a dictionary key to rename the comment
Insert the text into a list so it becomes mutable
items.explanation: String methods return new strings, so the cleaned text must be stored or used directly. That makes the normalized version available for the later search step.

items.stem: You have a dictionary d = {'name': 'Ava', 'age': 20}. Which expression gets the value Ava?
options: d['name']
d['age']
items.explanation: Dictionaries are accessed by key, not position; use d['name'] to get the value stored under the key 'name', not d[0]. Here, 'name' is the label tied to 'Ava'.

items.stem: A program builds a dictionary of exam scores like {'quiz': 8, 'quiz': 9}. What does Python keep?
options: Both values, under the same key
The first value only
The second value only
Neither value; duplicate keys are rejected as lists
items.explanation: Keys are unique; assigning to an existing key overwrites its previous value rather than adding a second entry. The later score replaces the earlier one under the key 'quiz'.

items.stem: A function is meant to compute the sum of 1 through n. It keeps calling itself with n - 1 until n reaches 1, where it returns 1. What feature makes this recursion stop?
options: The function name is different on each call
The base case at n = 1
The answer is computed only after all calls finish
The input becomes a string
items.explanation: The base case is the simplest input solved directly without another call, so the chain of self-calls stops there. In this item, n = 1 ends the recursion and lets the result unwind back through the earlier calls.

items.stem: A student says, 'If the final answer is wrong, no credit can be earned.' What is the best response?
options: That is correct because grading only checks the final output
That is correct unless the code runs without errors
Partial credit can come from correct reasoning and intermediate steps
Partial credit only applies to multiple-choice questions
items.explanation: Explain that instructors often award partial credit for correct reasoning, valid intermediate steps, and mostly correct code structure even when the final output is not perfect. On exam problems, showing the recursive setup and the shrinking step can still earn credit even if a later line is mistaken.

items.stem: Which exam habit best fits a fixed-time, independent midterm?
options: Spend all your time on one hard item and never check your work
Skip reading the question until the end
Use visible reasoning, then check answers as you go
Wait for hints from classmates
items.explanation: Midterm work is completed independently and within a fixed time, so efficient problem-solving and checking answers matter. Showing your reasoning also helps if partial credit is available.

items.stem: Two Cat objects start with different names. After changing one cat's name, the other cat still has its old name. Why?
options: Because each instance has its own attributes.
Because methods are unique to each instance.
Because the class stores one shared name for all objects.
Because changing one object automatically changes all objects.
items.explanation: Each instance has its own attributes, so changing one Dog's name does not change another Dog's name; only the methods are shared. That same idea explains why the two Cat objects keep separate names.

items.stem: A function is meant to count down from n to 0 recursively, but it calls itself with n again. What is the main problem?
options: The class is missing an instance.
The recursive call does not shrink the problem.
The base case is too large.
The function should use shared methods instead.
items.explanation: Each recursive call must move toward the base case by shrinking the problem (e.g. n - 1), or the base case is never reached. Calling the function with n again keeps the problem the same size.

items.stem: What is the safest way to build the message `You scored 8 points` if `score` is an integer variable?
options: "You scored " + score + " points"
"You scored " + str(score) + " points"
"You scored " + int(score) + " points"
"You scored " + score.toString() + " points"
items.explanation: Convert the number with str() before joining it to text, or use formatting; Python will not silently turn an int into a string inside a + with a str. So `"You scored " + str(score) + " points"` works. The other options either keep the type mismatch or use a method Python ints do not have.

items.stem: A script prints a number message and fails with a type error when you add text and a number. Which fix matches Python’s rules?
options: Convert the number to str() before using + with text
Use / instead of + so Python converts the number automatically
Wrap the number in int() so it becomes text
Put quotes around the variable name
items.explanation: The correct fix is to convert the number to text first, or use formatting. Convert the number with str() before joining it to text, or use formatting; Python will not silently turn an int into a string inside a + with a str. Wrapping a number in int() does not make it text.

items.stem: You installed a package with `pip`, but your script still raises `ModuleNotFoundError`. What should you check first?
options: Whether the file name contains a dot
Whether you used `//` instead of `/`
Which Python interpreter is running the script and where that interpreter was installed
Whether the variable names are uppercase
items.explanation: This usually means the package was installed into one interpreter or virtual environment, but the script is running under another. Instructor has students confirm the interpreter via `python --version` and `python -c "import sys; print(sys.executable)"`, then (re)install the dependency in that exact environment (e.g., activate the venv before running `pip install ...`) and re-run the script. That keeps the install and the runtime aligned.

items.stem: Which expression gives the whole-number quotient of 7 divided by 2?
items.explanation: Floor division returns the whole-number quotient directly. In Python 3 the / operator always returns a float, so 7 / 2 is 3.5; use // for whole-number floor division, which gives 3. For this task, 7 // 2 is the clean answer.

items.stem: A student writes print('Score: ' + 98). What is the best fix?
options: Leave it; Python will convert 98 to text automatically.
Change + to * so the types match.
Convert 98 with str(98) before joining it to the string.
Replace 98 with 98.0 so it becomes a string.
items.explanation: Strings and numbers do not automatically combine this way. Convert the number with str() before joining it to text, or use formatting; Python will not silently turn an int into a string inside a + with a str. So print('Score: ' + str(98)) works.

items.stem: You want to print the numbers 0 through 4 using a for loop. Which header is correct?
options: for i in range(5):
for i in range(1, 5):
for i in range(0, 5, 2):
for i in range(5, 0, -1):
items.explanation: range(5) yields 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 — it starts at 0 and stops before the endpoint, giving exactly five values. That is why it matches the numbers 0 through 4.

items.stem: What is the value of 7 / 2 in Python 3?
options: An error
items.explanation: In Python 3 the / operator always returns a float, so 7 / 2 is 3.5; use // for whole-number floor division, which gives 3. Use / when you want a true division result, not an integer result.

items.stem: Which expression correctly joins the number 5 onto the string "Item: "?
options: "Item: " + 5
"Item: " + str(5)
"Item: " + int(5)
items.explanation: Convert the number with str() before joining it to text, or use formatting; Python will not silently turn an int into a string inside a + with a str. So "Item: " + str(5) works.

items.stem: Which loop runs exactly five times?
options: for n in range(1, 5):
for n in range(5):
for n in range(0, 6):
for n in range(2, 5):
items.explanation: range(5) produces five values: 0, 1, 2, 3, 4. That makes the loop body run exactly five times.

items.stem: A loop needs to repeat exactly five times. Which range should the student use?
options: range(5)
range(1, 5)
range(5, 1)
range(0, 5, 2)
items.explanation: `range(5)` is the standard way to get five loop values starting at zero. range(5) yields 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 — it starts at 0 and stops before the endpoint, giving exactly five values.

items.stem: Which statement best describes the scope of a variable created outside any function?
options: It is local to the first function that uses it.
It can be accessed anywhere in the program.
It disappears as soon as the program reaches a for loop.
It can only be used inside range().
items.explanation: A variable created outside any function has global scope and can be accessed anywhere in the program.

items.stem: A program stores the days of the week in a list. Which expression gets the last day in a 7-item list named days?
options: days[7]
days[6]
days[1]
days[-1]
items.explanation: Lists are indexed starting at 0, so a 7-item list has valid indexes 0 through 6. days[6] is the last item. Index 7 is out of range for a 7-item list.

items.stem: You want the first ingredient from a list named recipe. Which access is correct?
options: recipe[1]
recipe[0]
recipe[-1]
recipe[2]
items.explanation: The first element is at index 0, so recipe[0] returns the first ingredient. recipe[1] is the second ingredient.

items.stem: A function makes a local variable total inside its body. After the function finishes, which statement is true?
options: total can be used anywhere in the program
total exists only during that call unless returned
total becomes a global variable automatically
total must be inside a list to be used later
items.explanation: Local variables exist only during the call that created them; to use a result outside, the function must return it and the caller must capture the returned value.

items.stem: A student writes a loop to print every item in names = ['Ana', 'Bo', 'Cy']. Which loop visits the elements in order?
options: for i in names:
for i in range(names):
for i in names[3]:
for i = 0 to 3:
items.explanation: A for loop can iterate through a list, visiting each element in order. for i in names: gives you each item directly.

items.stem: A list has 5 items. Which index points to the last item?
items.explanation: Indexes run from 0 to length minus 1, so a 5-item list's last index is 4; lst[5] is out of range.

items.stem: A student writes `d = {'color': 'blue'}; d['color'] = 'green'`. What is true after the assignment?
options: The dictionary now has two keys named `color`.
The old value is kept and the new one is added under `color_new`.
The value for `color` becomes `green`.
Python raises an error because keys must never be changed.
items.explanation: Assigning to an existing key updates that entry. Keys are unique; assigning to an existing key overwrites its previous value rather than adding a second entry.

items.stem: Which structure best fits data where each student has a unique ID and a stored grade?
options: A dictionary, because the grade is retrieved by the student ID key.
A list, because lists are always better for labels.
A string, because it can hold the ID and grade together.
A set, because it keeps values in order.
items.explanation: This is labeled data, so a dictionary is the right fit. Dictionaries are written with curly braces in key: value form and are ideal when data is naturally labeled rather than ordered.

items.stem: What does `strip()` do in this code: `"  hi  ".strip()`?
options: It removes every space anywhere in the string.
It removes only the spaces at the beginning and end.
It turns the string into uppercase.
It removes the letters `h` and `i`.
items.explanation: `strip()` removes leading and trailing whitespace by default, not all spaces inside the string. Instructor contrasts `strip()` with `replace()` by using examples (e.g., `"a x a".strip()` vs `"a x a".replace("a", "")`) and emphasizes that `strip()` targets only the beginning/end when whitespace characters are specified.

items.stem: A dictionary is written as `{'a': 1, 'b': 2}`. Which statement best explains why there is only one value for each key?
options: Because keys are sorted automatically.
Because a dictionary cannot hold duplicate keys.
Because values must always be numbers.
Because curly braces mean the data is ordered.
items.explanation: A dictionary uses keys to look up values, so the keys must be unique. Because a dictionary looks up values using keys, it cannot hold duplicate keys.

items.stem: What does `s[1:4]` return for a string `s`?
options: The characters at positions 1, 2, 3, and 4.
The characters from index 1 up to but not including 4.
Only the character at index 4.
The last four characters of the string.
items.explanation: Slicing includes the start index and stops before the end index. Slicing `s[a:b]` returns a substring from index `a` up to but not including `b` and accepts negative indices; `s[a:]` means from `a` to the end.

items.stem: A program opens a text file and calls read() to get its contents. What does read() return?
options: A single string containing the entire file
A list of lines from the file
Only the first line of the file
A dictionary of file contents
items.explanation: read() returns the whole file as one string, which is why it is useful when you want all the text at once. It does not split the file into lines by itself.

items.stem: Your code does this: data = f.read(); more = f.read(). What should you expect for more if the file was not reopened or reset?
options: The file name
The first line again
A list of remaining lines
items.explanation: Reading advances a position marker through the file; once read() reaches the end, a second read() returns '' until the file is reopened or the position is reset. That empty string is the signal that there is nothing left to read from that open file object.

items.stem: You need the next single line from a text file without loading the whole file. Which method should you use?
options: open()
read()
readlines()
readline()
items.explanation: readline() returns the next single line. Use it when you want one line at a time instead of the entire file or a list of every line.

items.stem: What happens if you assign a new value to a key that already exists in a dictionary?
options: Python adds a second copy of the key
The dictionary becomes a list
The old value is kept and the new one is ignored
Keys are unique; assigning to an existing key overwrites its previous value rather than adding a second entry.
items.explanation: Keys are unique; assigning to an existing key overwrites its previous value rather than adding a second entry. That is why dictionaries are good for labeled data, but not for storing multiple separate values under the same label.

items.stem: Which statement best describes recursion?
options: A function that always uses print instead of return.
A problem-solving method that reduces a problem to a simpler version of itself until a base case is reached.
A variable that is accessible everywhere in the program.
A function definition that automatically executes when Python reads it.
